briefs.title: Determining withdrawal rates using historical data
briefs.summary: Bengen tests rolling historical stock, bond, and inflation data and shows that a roughly 4 percent starting withdrawal, increased with inflation, survived the toughest 30-year periods in his dataset.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the paper that made the modern safe-withdrawal debate concrete.

briefs.title: Exploring the retirement consumption puzzle
briefs.summary: Blanchett shows that retiree spending often falls in real terms over time, instead of rising neatly with inflation every year. He estimates average real spending declines of about 1 percent a year and describes a spending smile across retirement.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a retirement spending baseline that matches how households actually age, not a flat inflation-only rule.

briefs.title: Retirement savings: Choosing a withdrawal rate that is sustainable
briefs.authors: Cooley P. L., Hubbard C. M., & Walz D. T.
briefs.summary: The Trinity study tests historical stock and bond mixes against different withdrawal rates and retirement lengths to see which combinations held up over time. It helped popularize the idea that around 4 percent was a workable starting point for many 30-year retirements.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps show where retirement spending plans fail and where they stay durable.

briefs.title: Decision rules and maximum initial withdrawal rates
briefs.summary: Guyton and Klinger test withdrawal guardrails that let spending rise or fall with portfolio conditions instead of following one fixed inflation rule. Their results suggest higher starting withdrawals may work when retirees follow strict spending rules after good and bad markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want to know what guardrails add beyond a fixed 4 percent rule.

briefs.title: Making sense out of variable spending strategies for retirees
briefs.summary: Pfau compares a range of variable spending rules, from fixed real withdrawals to rules that recalculate spending from the remaining portfolio. He frames the choice as a tradeoff between steadier income now and lower risk of severe cuts later.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a withdrawal rule that survives bad timing, inflation, and long retirements.

briefs.title: Value and momentum everywhere
briefs.authors: Asness C. S., Moskowitz T. J., & Pedersen L. H.
briefs.summary: Asness, Moskowitz, and Pedersen show that value and momentum patterns appear across countries and asset classes rather than in one narrow corner of the market.
briefs.whyItMatters: This broadens the value and momentum debate from one stock market to a cross-asset pattern.

briefs.title: On persistence in mutual fund performance
briefs.summary: Examines which risks, company traits, or market frictions the paper links to differences in long-run returns.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on which risks or traits investors have historically been paid for.

briefs.title: The cross‐section of expected stock returns
briefs.authors: Fama E. F., & French K. R.
briefs.summary: Fama and French test which stock traits line up with higher returns and find that size and value explain a large share of the gap between stronger and weaker performers.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the core papers behind modern factor investing and return attribution.

briefs.title: A five-factor asset pricing model
briefs.authors: Fama E. F., & French K. R.
briefs.summary: Fama and French expand the standard stock-return model by adding profitability and investment behavior to the usual market, size, and value factors.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need the modern Fama-French baseline rather than the older three-factor version.

briefs.title: Capital asset prices: A theory of market equilibrium under conditions of risk
briefs.summary: Sharpe sets out the classic CAPM claim that expected return should mainly reflect how much market risk a stock adds to a diversified portfolio.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the canonical starting point for the idea that market risk should drive expected return.

briefs.title: Trading is hazardous to your wealth: The common stock investment performance of individual investors
briefs.summary: Barber and Odean study household brokerage accounts and find that the people who trade the most earn worse returns than those who trade less. The gap is not just bad luck. Trading costs and poor timing do real damage.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearest empirical warnings that more trading often means worse investor outcomes.

briefs.title: Luck versus skill in the cross‐section of mutual fund returns
briefs.authors: Fama E. F., & French K. R.
briefs.summary: Fama and French test mutual fund returns to see how much is true manager skill and how much is random variation. Their results suggest that strong performance is rare and that most apparent winners can be explained by luck once costs are counted.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when a hot manager track record may simply be randomness wearing the mask of skill.

briefs.title: Returns from investing in equity mutual funds 1971 to 1991
briefs.summary: This paper looks at how equity mutual funds did over two decades and compares investor results with simple market benchmarks. The broad result is that fees and costs made it hard for the average fund to beat the market in a lasting way.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real question is whether paying more produces a better investor outcome.

briefs.title: The arithmetic of active management
briefs.summary: Sharpe lays out a simple but powerful point: before costs, active investors as a group must match the market, and after costs they must trail it. The argument is mathematical, not rhetorical.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the shortest and cleanest argument for why active management has to lose after costs in aggregate.

briefs.title: SPIVA U.S. scorecard
briefs.summary: The SPIVA scorecard tracks how often active funds beat their benchmarks over different time periods. Its recurring pattern is that most active funds fall behind over longer horizons, especially after survivorship is handled properly.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the practical scorecard most investors need before paying active-fund fees.

briefs.title: The importance of default options for retirement saving outcomes: Evidence from the United States
briefs.authors: Beshears J., Choi J. J., Laibson D., & Madrian B. C.
briefs.summary: This paper reviews evidence showing that default settings have a large effect on whether people join retirement plans, how much they contribute, and where the money goes. People often stay close to the default even when better choices are available.
briefs.whyItMatters: This shows that plan design can matter as much as investor intent.

briefs.title: Can small victories help win the war? Evidence from consumer debt management
briefs.summary: The paper studies debt repayment behavior and finds that early progress on a small balance can help people stay engaged with a payoff plan. The psychological effect can matter even when the math would favor a different order of attack.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how bias and framing change real money decisions, not just abstract preferences.

briefs.title: Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk
briefs.summary: Builds on prospect theory, the idea that people feel losses more sharply than gains and often take different risks depending on how choices are framed.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the foundation for understanding loss aversion, framing effects, and many later investor-bias papers.

briefs.title: The power of suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) participation and savings behavior
briefs.authors: Madrian B. C., & Shea D. F.
briefs.summary: Madrian and Shea study what happened when a company moved from opt-in enrollment to automatic enrollment in its 401(k) plan. Participation jumped, and many workers stayed with the default contribution rate and fund choice.
briefs.whyItMatters: This paper explains why opt-in systems underperform automatic enrollment by so much.

briefs.title: Save More Tomorrow: Using behavioral economics to increase employee saving
briefs.summary: Thaler and Benartzi test a program that commits workers in advance to raise saving rates when future pay raises arrive. The design helps people save more without feeling the full pain of a current pay cut.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the goal is higher saving rates without relying on constant self-control.

briefs.title: Loss harvesting: What’s it worth to the taxable investor?
briefs.authors: Arnott R. D., Berkin A. L., & Ye J.
briefs.summary: Stein and Narasimhan estimate the value of tax-loss harvesting for taxable investors by modeling how realized losses can offset gains and reduce current tax drag. The paper treats harvesting as a measurable after-tax benefit, not just a slogan.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a direct answer to whether tax-loss harvesting is worth real money or just marketing copy.

briefs.title: Optimal consumption and investment with capital gains taxes
briefs.authors: Dammon R. M., Spatt C. S., & Zhang H.
briefs.summary: This paper studies how capital gains taxes change the best mix of spending, investing, and trading over time. It shows that taxes do not just lower returns. They also change when and how investors should realize gains.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps quantify decisions that look small on paper but compound once taxes are included.

briefs.title: Optimal savings with taxable and tax-advantaged accounts
briefs.authors: Gomes F., Michaelides A., & Polkovnichenko V.
briefs.summary: The paper compares saving across taxable accounts and tax-advantaged accounts and asks how households should split contributions between them. It shows that account choice can materially change long-run after-tax wealth.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when account order, loss use, or asset placement is part of the real decision.

briefs.title: Tax-efficient sequencing of accounts to tap in retirement
briefs.summary: This paper studies which account retirees should spend from first, including taxable, tax-deferred, and tax-free pools. The order changes taxes, portfolio life, and how much money can be spent over retirement.
briefs.whyItMatters: This matters when withdrawal order changes taxes, Medicare effects, and how long the portfolio lasts.

briefs.title: Asset location in tax-deferred and conventional savings accounts
briefs.summary: The paper looks at where different assets should be placed when an investor has both taxable and tax-deferred accounts. It tests whether certain holdings belong in sheltered accounts while others belong in taxable ones.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the real question is where each asset should live, not just what to buy.

briefs.title: Portfolio Selection
briefs.summary: Markowitz introduces the core idea that a portfolio should be judged by both expected return and risk, not by return alone. The paper lays out the mean-variance framework that became the base model for modern portfolio construction.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the paper that turned diversification into a formal portfolio problem instead of a slogan.

briefs.title: Mutual Fund Performance
briefs.summary: Sharpe tests whether mutual funds beat what would be expected from the market risk they take. The paper helped establish risk-adjusted performance as a more serious way to judge managers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real issue is how to build a portfolio instead of how to pick a single winner.

briefs.title: The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945-1964
briefs.summary: Jensen studies mutual fund returns over a long historical period and compares them with a risk-adjusted market benchmark. He finds little evidence that the average fund delivered persistent superior performance after costs.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real issue is how to build a portfolio instead of how to pick a single winner.

briefs.title: How to Rate Management of Investment Funds
briefs.summary: Treynor proposes an early framework for judging portfolio managers by comparing return with the market risk taken to earn it. The paper helped shape later performance measures that focus on skill rather than raw outcome.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real issue is how to build a portfolio instead of how to pick a single winner.

briefs.title: A critique of the asset pricing theory's tests
briefs.summary: Roll argues that testing asset-pricing models is harder than it looks because the true market portfolio is unobservable. That means many clean-looking tests depend on benchmark choices that are less solid than they appear.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps frame portfolio construction as a trade-off between concentration, volatility, and expected return.

briefs.title: The arbitrage theory of capital asset pricing
briefs.summary: Ross offers an alternative to the single-market-factor view of expected returns by arguing that several common risks can help price assets. The paper helped open the door to multifactor investing frameworks.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand what diversification is buying you and what it is not.

briefs.title: Capital market equilibrium with restricted borrowing
briefs.summary: Black shows that asset-pricing results change when investors cannot borrow and lend freely at the same rate. That makes real-world portfolio constraints part of the model instead of an afterthought.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand what diversification is buying you and what it is not.

briefs.title: The relationship between return and market value of common stocks
briefs.summary: Banz shows that smaller companies have historically earned higher returns than larger ones, laying out the classic size effect.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: Investment performance of common stocks in relation to their price-earnings ratios
briefs.summary: Basu tests whether low price-to-earnings stocks beat high price-to-earnings stocks and finds evidence in favor of a value effect.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: Returns to buying winners and selling losers: Implications for stock market efficiency
briefs.summary: Jegadeesh and Titman document momentum by showing that recent winning stocks often keep outperforming for a time while recent losers keep lagging.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the central papers behind momentum as a serious return pattern.

briefs.title: Does the stock market overreact?
briefs.authors: De Bondt W. F. M., & Thaler R.
briefs.summary: Explains how bias, framing, and social cues can change saving, spending, and investing decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: Do stock prices move too much to be justified by subsequent changes in dividends?
briefs.summary: Shiller compares stock-price swings with later changes in dividends and argues that prices seem to move more than fundamentals alone would justify. The paper became one of the landmark challenges to a strict efficient-market view.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a classic challenge to the idea that price swings mostly reflect changing fundamentals.

briefs.title: The equity premium: A puzzle
briefs.summary: Mehra and Prescott show that stocks have beaten safe assets by so much that standard consumption models struggle to explain the gap.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is still the cleanest statement of how hard it is to explain long-run stock outperformance.

briefs.title: Myopic loss aversion and the equity premium puzzle
briefs.summary: Explains how bias, framing, and social cues can change saving, spending, and investing decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: Determinants of portfolio performance
briefs.authors: Brinson G. P., Hood L. R., & Beebower G. L.
briefs.summary: Brinson, Hood, and Beebower decompose pension fund results and find that asset allocation explains far more of return variation than manager selection or market timing. The paper became famous for focusing attention on allocation first.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real issue is how to build a portfolio instead of how to pick a single winner.

briefs.title: How many stocks make a diversified portfolio?
briefs.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
briefs.summary: Statman studies how many stocks are needed before diversification removes most single-stock risk. The answer is more than many investors expect, especially if they want diversification to be meaningful rather than symbolic.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a concrete answer to how concentrated a stock portfolio can be before diversification stops being real.

briefs.title: Investor diversification and international equity markets
briefs.authors: French K. R., & Poterba J. M.
briefs.summary: This paper studies whether investors can reduce risk by spreading equity exposure across countries instead of staying only in their home market. It shows that international diversification can improve the mix, especially when markets do not move in lockstep.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand what diversification is buying you and what it is not.

briefs.title: Stocks bonds bills and inflation: Year-by-year historical returns (1926-1974)
briefs.authors: Ibbotson R. G., & Sinquefield R. A.
briefs.summary: Ibbotson and Sinquefield assemble one of the core long-run U.S. return datasets for stocks, bonds, bills, and inflation.
briefs.whyItMatters: This dataset underpins a large share of U.S. long-run return analysis.

briefs.title: Proof that properly anticipated prices fluctuate randomly
briefs.summary: Samuelson gives the formal argument that if information is already reflected in prices, price changes should look unpredictable. It is one of the classic statements behind the random-walk view of markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the foundational formal statements behind the random-walk view of prices.

briefs.title: Efficient Capital Markets: A Review of Theory and Empirical Work
briefs.summary: Fama reviews the theory and evidence for efficient capital markets and organizes the idea into a clear research agenda. The paper became the standard reference point for what market efficiency means in finance.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the baseline statement of market efficiency that later anomaly papers are arguing with.

briefs.title: Lifetime portfolio selection under uncertainty: The continuous-time case
briefs.publication: The Review of Economics and Statistics
briefs.summary: Merton develops a lifetime framework for choosing portfolio risk and consumption under uncertainty rather than treating investment as a one-period problem. The model helped connect saving, spending, and asset mix into one decision system.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand what diversification is buying you and what it is not.

briefs.title: Advances in prospect theory: Cumulative representation of uncertainty
briefs.summary: Builds on prospect theory, the idea that people feel losses more sharply than gains and often take different risks depending on how choices are framed.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how bias and framing change real money decisions, not just abstract preferences.

briefs.title: Prospect theory and asset prices
briefs.authors: Barberis N., Huang M., & Santos T.
briefs.summary: Builds on prospect theory, the idea that people feel losses more sharply than gains and often take different risks depending on how choices are framed.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: By force of habit: A consumption-based explanation of aggregate stock market behavior
briefs.authors: Campbell J. Y., & Cochrane J. H.
briefs.summary: Links asset prices to household consumption risk and asks whether shifts in spending patterns help explain stock returns.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: Liquidity risk and expected stock returns
briefs.summary: Studies whether harder-to-trade assets earn extra return as compensation for being less liquid.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: The other side of value: The gross profitability premium
briefs.summary: Novy-Marx shows that highly profitable firms have tended to outperform weakly profitable firms even after controlling for value.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on which risks or traits investors have historically been paid for.

briefs.title: Betting against beta
briefs.summary: Frazzini and Pedersen show that high-beta stocks have often underdelivered while lower-beta stocks have done better than standard theory predicts.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: Quality minus junk
briefs.authors: Asness C. S., Frazzini A., & Pedersen L. H.
briefs.summary: Asness, Frazzini, and Pedersen build a quality factor that favors profitable, stable, conservatively financed businesses over weaker peers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on which risks or traits investors have historically been paid for.

briefs.title: ...and the cross-section of expected returns
briefs.authors: Harvey C. R., Liu Y., & Zhu H.
briefs.summary: Studies which company traits, risks, or signals line up with higher future returns across many stocks rather than in one isolated case.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps anchor stock-return debates in an explicit pricing model instead of loose intuition.

briefs.title: Stock market prices do not follow random walks: Evidence from a simple specification test
briefs.authors: Lo A. W., & MacKinlay A. C.
briefs.summary: Lo and MacKinlay test the random-walk idea directly and find patterns inconsistent with a pure random walk in stock prices. The paper gave strong empirical pushback against the simplest form of market efficiency.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the classic empirical challenges to the strict random-walk view of markets.

briefs.title: On the impossibility of informationally efficient markets
briefs.authors: Grossman S. J., & Stiglitz J. E.
briefs.summary: Grossman and Stiglitz argue that perfectly efficient markets cannot exist in a literal sense because someone must have an incentive to gather costly information. If prices were perfectly informative, nobody would pay to produce that information.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the classic argument that perfectly efficient markets would destroy the incentive to gather information.

briefs.title: The limits of arbitrage
briefs.summary: Shleifer and Vishny argue that even when mispricing is obvious, investors may be unable or unwilling to bet aggressively enough to fix it. Capital constraints, career risk, and withdrawal risk can keep bad prices alive.
briefs.whyItMatters: This paper explains why apparent mispricing can persist even when smart investors see it.

briefs.title: Characteristics of risk and return in risk arbitrage
briefs.summary: This paper studies merger arbitrage and shows that the return pattern is tied to deal-specific risks rather than a free lunch. The strategy can look smooth until deal breaks expose the hidden downside.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want merger arbitrage described as a risky strategy rather than a mechanical free spread.

briefs.title: Investor psychology and security market under- and overreactions
briefs.authors: Daniel K., Hirshleifer D., & Subrahmanyam A.
briefs.summary: Explains how bias, framing, and social cues can change saving, spending, and investing decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: A unified theory of underreaction momentum trading and overreaction in asset markets
briefs.summary: Barberis, Shleifer, and Vishny offer a model in which investor bias can produce both slow underreaction and later overreaction in asset prices.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a key theoretical bridge between behavioral bias and return patterns like momentum and reversal.

briefs.title: Boys will be boys: Gender overconfidence and common stock investment
briefs.summary: Barber and Odean compare men and women in brokerage data and find that men trade more and, on average, hurt their returns more as a result. The paper links overconfidence to real investing mistakes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful because it ties overconfidence to an actual return penalty, not just a survey result.

briefs.title: Familiarity breeds investment
briefs.summary: Shows that investors often prefer familiar names, local markets, or nearby firms even when broader diversification would be safer.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: How distance language and culture influence stockholdings and trades
briefs.summary: Shows that investors often prefer familiar names, local markets, or nearby firms even when broader diversification would be safer.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: Home bias at home: Local equity preference in domestic portfolios
briefs.authors: Coval J. D., & Moskowitz T. J.
briefs.summary: Shows that investors often prefer familiar names, local markets, or nearby firms even when broader diversification would be safer.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: Returns-chasing behavior mutual funds and beta's death
briefs.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
briefs.summary: The paper studies how investors chase recent fund returns and how that flow behavior can distort measured performance. It focuses on what happens when money arrives for the wrong reason.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when recent outperformance may owe more to return chasing than to durable process quality.

briefs.title: Costly search and mutual fund flows
briefs.summary: The paper looks at how hard it is for investors to search the fund universe and how that friction shapes where money flows. Limited search can keep expensive or mediocre funds alive longer than expected.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why bad funds can still gather assets in a market that looks competitive on paper.

briefs.title: Risk taking by mutual funds as a response to incentives
briefs.summary: This paper examines how mutual fund managers change risk when pay, rankings, or career pressure push them to reach for a better-looking result. Incentives can alter the portfolio even without changing skill.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is useful when manager behavior may be responding to incentives rather than investor interests.

briefs.title: Of tournaments and temptations: An analysis of managerial incentives in the mutual fund industry
briefs.authors: Brown K. C., Harlow W. V., & Starks L. T.
briefs.summary: Brown, Harlow, and Starks study how mutual fund managers change behavior when rankings create tournament-like incentives. Managers who are behind may take different risks than managers who are ahead.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why end-of-period fund behavior may reflect career games, not steady investment logic.

briefs.title: Mutual fund performance: An empirical decomposition into stock-picking talent style transactions costs and expenses
briefs.summary: The paper breaks mutual fund performance into stock picking, style exposure, trading costs, and fees. It shows that any stock-picking skill has to survive a heavy layer of costs before investors benefit.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate genuine manager edge from fees, taxes, and benchmark noise.

briefs.title: On the industry concentration of actively managed equity mutual funds
briefs.authors: Kacperczyk M., Sialm C., & Zheng L.
briefs.summary: The paper studies how concentrated active-fund positions are within industries and whether that concentration reflects conviction or hidden risk. It connects portfolio concentration to fund outcomes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know whether concentration inside an active fund is a sign of skill or just a larger bet.

briefs.title: How active is your fund manager? A new measure that predicts performance
briefs.authors: Cremers K. J. M., & Petajisto A.
briefs.summary: Cremers and Petajisto introduce Active Share, a measure of how different a fund is from its benchmark. They show that funds that look active on paper but hug the index tend to disappoint, while genuinely differentiated funds are a separate category.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether active management adds enough skill to justify its cost.

briefs.title: Mutual fund flows and performance in rational markets
briefs.authors: Berk J. B., & Green R. C.
briefs.summary: Berk and Green model why money chases recent winners even in a rational market. If skill exists but is scarce, fund flows can bid away the surplus that new investors hope to capture.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why a manager can be skilled while still being a weak buy for fresh capital.

briefs.title: On the size of the active management industry
briefs.summary: Pastor and Stambaugh study how large the active-management business can get before competition erodes its value to investors. The paper links industry size to diminishing edge.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the question is not whether skill exists, but whether too much money can crowd it away.

briefs.title: Disappearing dividends: changing firm characteristics or lower propensity to pay?
briefs.authors: Fama E. F., & French K. R.
briefs.summary: Fama and French show that fewer firms pay dividends largely because the market has more young, lower-profit companies than it once did.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when falling dividend rates are being blamed on management preference alone.

briefs.title: A catering theory of dividends
briefs.summary: Baker and Wurgler argue that managers sometimes shape dividend policy around investor appetite for dividend-paying stocks, not only around operating needs.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether dividend policy partly follows investor taste rather than pure corporate finance logic.

briefs.title: Multi-factor asset pricing models: Factor construction choices and the revisit of pricing factors
briefs.publication: Journal of international financial markets institutions and money
briefs.summary: Tests how well different return models explain stock performance, usually by comparing one-factor and multi-factor approaches.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the return model behind common claims about risk, value, size, or profitability.

briefs.title: Empirical tests of asset pricing models with individual assets: Resolving the errors-in-variables bias in risk premium estimation
briefs.authors: Narasimhan Jegadeesh Joonki Noh Kuntara Pukthuanthong et al.
briefs.summary: This paper focuses on a measurement problem in asset-pricing tests and asks whether correcting that bias changes the estimated risk premia.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know how much the econometrics affects the apparent success of a pricing model.

briefs.title: Benchmarking asset pricing models in emerging markets: evidence from Borsa Istanbul
briefs.summary: This paper compares asset-pricing models in the Turkish market and asks which factor setup travels best outside the usual U.S. sample.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a direct test of whether standard pricing models survive in an emerging-market setting.

briefs.title: Dispersed Ownership and Asset Pricing: An Unpriced Premium Associated with Free Float
briefs.authors: B. Hearn Igor Filatotchev Marc Goergen
briefs.summary: The paper studies whether free float and ownership dispersion help explain return differences across stocks. It asks whether market-access characteristics carry a premium that standard models miss.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether who can actually trade a stock matters for pricing.

briefs.title: Is Human Capital Premium Price in Asset Pricing? Insights from South Africa During the COVID-19 Era
briefs.publication: Journal of Innovative Research in Management Sciences
briefs.summary: This paper tests whether human-capital risk was priced in South African equities during the COVID period.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a crisis-period application of labor-risk ideas in asset pricing.

briefs.title: Empirical Tests of Asset Pricing Models with Individual Assets: Resolving the Errors-in-Variables Bias in Risk Premium Estimation by
briefs.authors: Narasimhan Jegadeesh Joonki Noh Kuntara Pukthuanthong et al.
briefs.summary: Tests how well different return models explain stock performance, usually by comparing one-factor and multi-factor approaches.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as a map of which traits the paper treats as priced and which ones it does not.

briefs.title: An empirical investigation of Tobin’s-Q augmented various Asset Pricing Models: Evidence from Pakistan
briefs.publication: Journal of Social Sciences and Management  Studies
briefs.summary: This paper adds Tobin’s Q to asset-pricing models in Pakistan and tests whether investment-related valuation signals improve model fit.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether balance-sheet investment signals add value in an applied pricing model.

briefs.title: Human capital in asset pricing: The case of the Brazilian stock market during crisis periods
briefs.authors: N. Khan Mustafa Afeef Hassan Zada
briefs.summary: This paper tests whether human-capital risk helps explain stock returns in Brazil, especially during stressed market periods.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a market-specific test of whether labor-income risk belongs in asset-pricing models.

briefs.title: Further tests of asset pricing models: Liquidity risk matters
briefs.authors: Xiuli Ma Xindong Zhang Weimin Liu

briefs.summary: This paper studies investor bias in a local setting and discusses whether awareness of behavioral errors can improve decision quality. It is narrower and more context-specific than the canonical bias papers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a regional application of investor-bias research, not as the main source on the topic.

briefs.title: Research on the Development and Application of the Behavioral Finance
briefs.publication: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
briefs.summary: This is a broad review of how behavioral-finance ideas developed and where they have been applied across investing and decision-making topics.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a general orientation paper when you want breadth more than depth.

briefs.title: Behavioral Finance: Understanding Investor Psychology and Its Impact on Stock Price
briefs.summary: This paper gives a straightforward overview of how investor psychology can move prices away from what a purely rational model would predict.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a plain introduction to the investor-psychology side of market behavior.

briefs.title: Scientific and Methodological Foundations for Studying the Impact of Behavioral Finance on the Managerial Decision-Making Process
briefs.summary: This paper focuses on how to study behavioral-finance effects in managerial settings and what methods are best suited to that work.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if your interest is behavioral finance inside firms rather than only in markets.

briefs.title: Artificial intelligence in behavioral finance: a global review of cognitive bias modeling in investor decision-making
briefs.authors: Sadi Evren Şeker Başak Turan Içke Serhat Yanik et al.
briefs.summary: This review looks at how AI tools are being used to model investor bias and decision patterns in behavioral-finance research.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how behavioral-finance research is starting to intersect with machine-learning methods.

briefs.title: The Impact of Behavioral Finance on Sustainable Investing in the Stock Market: A Comprehensive Analysis of Investor Behaviour Biases and Decision-Making Processes
briefs.authors: Bipin Chauhan Ravi Shekhar Santosh Kumar et al.
briefs.publication: 2025 2nd International Conference on Recent Trends in Electrical Electronics and Computing Technologies (ICRTEECT)
briefs.summary: This paper looks at how common investor biases interact with sustainable-investing choices and ESG narratives in the stock market.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how sustainability preferences and behavioral bias can reinforce each other.

briefs.title: Investor Psychology and Market Bubbles: A Behavioral Finance Perspective
briefs.publication: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
briefs.summary: This paper focuses on how optimism, fear, and crowd belief can feed bubbles and keep them going longer than fundamentals alone would justify.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the question is how investor mood helps inflate and sustain a bubble.

briefs.title: Behavioral Finance: an investigation based on the prospect theory and the investor profile of portuguese stricto sensu graduate students
briefs.authors: Fabricio Haubert Carlos Rogério Montenegro de Lima M. Lima
briefs.summary: This paper studies prospect-theory behavior in a graduate-student investor sample and links it to investor profile differences.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a small-sample behavioral application rather than as a field-defining paper.

briefs.title: A Critical Comparison of SEUT and Prospect Theory
briefs.publication: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
briefs.summary: This paper compares standard expected-utility theory with prospect theory and lays out where the two models make different predictions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand what prospect theory changed relative to the older rational benchmark.

briefs.title: Asymmetric dependence between the prospect theory value and stock returns in India: a quantile regression approach
briefs.summary: This paper applies prospect-theory ideas to stock returns in India and asks whether the behavioral relationship changes across different return environments.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a narrower empirical test of prospect-theory ideas in one market.

briefs.authors: Abraham J. Fetterman Ellie Kitanidis Joshua Albrecht et al.
briefs.summary: Focuses on portfolio construction, diversification, and the trade-off between seeking return and controlling risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps frame portfolio construction as a trade-off between concentration, volatility, and expected return.

briefs.authors: Huachao Dong Jinglu Li Peng Wang et al.

briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real issue is how to build a portfolio instead of how to pick a single winner.

briefs.authors: A. Hoffmann Alex Y. D. Siem Dick den Hertog et al.
briefs.summary: This paper is mainly about optimization methods and efficient-frontier mathematics rather than about real-world portfolio evidence.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you care about optimization technique; weaker as a direct source for household or portfolio decisions.

briefs.title: Portfolio optimization in stocks using mean–variance optimization and the efficient frontier
briefs.summary: This paper applies mean-variance optimization directly to stock portfolios and examines how the efficient frontier behaves in a practical investing setup.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a direct applied example of efficient-frontier portfolio construction.

briefs.title: Uncertainty of Efficient Frontier in Portfolio Optimization
briefs.summary: This paper asks how stable the efficient frontier is once estimation uncertainty is admitted into portfolio optimization.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know how fragile optimized portfolios can become once inputs are noisy.

briefs.title: An analytic derivation of the efficient frontier in biobjective cash management and its implications for policies
briefs.authors: Francisco Salas‐Molina D. Plà-Santamaria J. Rodríguez-Aguilar
briefs.summary: This paper derives an efficient frontier for cash-management choices, balancing competing goals in a treasury-style setting rather than a stock portfolio.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if cash management is part of the allocation problem you care about.

briefs.title: Learning the Efficient Frontier
briefs.authors: Philippe Chatigny Ivan Sergienko Ryan Ferguson et al.
briefs.summary: Centers on the efficient frontier, the trade-off between return and risk when investors combine assets into a portfolio.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps frame portfolio construction as a trade-off between concentration, volatility, and expected return.

briefs.title: Limits of arbitrage and mispricing: evidence from mergers and acquisitions
briefs.authors: Qingzhong Ma David A. Whidbee Wei Zhang
briefs.summary: This paper uses merger situations to show how limits to arbitrage can leave prices away from their likely end value. It treats M&A spreads as a live example of why mispricing can persist even in watched markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a live transactional setting where mispricing survives despite plenty of professional attention.

briefs.title: Investor sentiment limits to arbitrage and hard-to-value stocks
briefs.publication: Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting
briefs.summary: The paper studies how investor sentiment matters most in stocks that are difficult to value and hard to arbitrage. In those names, mood and narrative can push prices farther away from fundamentals.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearer papers on where sentiment bites hardest: stocks that are difficult to value and difficult to arbitrage.

briefs.title: Liquidity cognition and limits of arbitrage
briefs.summary: Explains why obvious mispricing can survive when shorting is costly, capital is limited, or investors face funding and career risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a more specialized limits-to-arbitrage paper with liquidity and cognition at the center.

briefs.title: Limits of Arbitrage
briefs.summary: Explains why obvious mispricing can survive when shorting is costly, capital is limited, or investors face funding and career risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a broad conceptual entry point into why mispricing can survive.

briefs.title: Asymmetric effect of FEARS Sentiment on Stock Returns: Short-sale constraints limits to arbitrage and behavioural biases
briefs.authors: Garima Goel S. R. Dash R. Brooks et al.
briefs.summary: Examines whether investor mood and narrative push prices away from fundamentals, especially in hard-to-value securities.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when sentiment, short-sale limits, and behavior all need to be considered together in one return pattern.

briefs.title: Biased short: Short sellers' disposition effect and limits to arbitrage
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know whether even short sellers show the same bias patterns seen in long-only investors.

briefs.title: Investor sentiment limits on arbitrage and the performance of cross-country stock market anomalies
briefs.summary: Examines whether investor mood and narrative push prices away from fundamentals, especially in hard-to-value securities.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether sentiment weakens cross-country anomaly results in the same way across markets.

briefs.title: Limits to Arbitrage: An introduction to Behavioral Finance and a Literature Review
briefs.summary: Reviews the main behavioral explanations for mispricing, including bias, slow learning, and the practical limits on arbitrage.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a survey of the limits-to-arbitrage literature rather than a single empirical test.

briefs.title: Industry Momentum and Behavioral Limits to Arbitrage
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want momentum discussed at the industry level rather than only at the single-stock level.

briefs.title: A survey of behavioral finance
briefs.authors: N. Barberis N. Barberis Richard H. Thaler et al.
briefs.summary: Barberis and Thaler review the main ideas in behavioral finance, including sentiment, overreaction, underreaction, and limits to arbitrage. The paper became a standard map of the field.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is still one of the best general maps of how behavioral finance explains underreaction, overreaction, and sentiment-driven mispricing.

briefs.title: How Constraining Are Limits to Arbitrage? Evidence from a Recent Financial Innovation
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a modern test of how much new instruments really reduce arbitrage frictions.

briefs.title: How Constraining are Limits to Arbitrage? Evidence from a Recent Financial Innovation
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a modern test of how much new instruments really reduce arbitrage frictions.

briefs.title: Benchmarks as Limits to Arbitrage: Understanding the Low-Volatility Anomaly
briefs.authors: Malcolm P. Baker Brendan O. Bradley Jeffrey Wurgler
briefs.summary: This paper argues that benchmark structure itself can limit arbitrage by pushing professional managers toward index-relative behavior. That helps explain why low-volatility stocks can perform better than a simple theory would suggest.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know why benchmark-aware managers may fail to arbitrage away low-volatility outperformance.

briefs.title: Behavioral Factors in Risk Arbitrage∗
briefs.summary: Examines merger arbitrage through a behavioral lens and asks whether investor bias changes how deal risk gets priced.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want merger arbitrage interpreted through investor behavior rather than only deal mechanics.

briefs.title: The Dynamics of Limits to Arbitrage: An Empirical Investigation
briefs.summary: This paper studies how constraints on arbitrage change over time instead of treating them as fixed. It shows that the force keeping mispricing alive can intensify during stress and relax during calmer periods.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know whether arbitrage constraints are stable or cyclical.

briefs.title: Behavioral Biases and the Asset Growth Anomaly
briefs.authors: Qingzhong Ma David A. Whidbee Wei Zhang
briefs.summary: The paper examines whether investor behavior helps explain why firms with rapid asset growth often earn weaker later returns. It links a well-known market anomaly to behavioral overreaction or misplaced optimism.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a behavioral explanation for why fast asset growth can precede weaker later returns.

briefs.title: Ambiguity no Arbitrage and the Limits to Rational Expectations
briefs.authors: H. Adriaens B. Donkers B. Melenberg
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if ambiguity itself is the friction you care about, rather than simple cost or funding limits.

briefs.title: Influencing Limits to Arbitrage: Corporate Disclosure in Inefficient Markets
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether disclosure policy can change how far mispricing persists.

briefs.title: Why Do Firms Fail to Engage Diversity? A Behavioral Strategy Perspective
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful mainly as a behavioral strategy paper, not as a core capital-markets efficiency reference.

briefs.title: Behavioral Finance Research in 2020: Cui Bono et Quo Vadis?
briefs.summary: Reviews the main behavioral explanations for mispricing, including bias, slow learning, and the practical limits on arbitrage.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a state-of-the-field review rather than as a core empirical anomaly paper.

briefs.title: Behavioral biases in the corporate bond market
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether behavioral distortions show up in credit as well as equities.

briefs.title: Short- and Long-Horizon Behavioral Anomalies and Institutional Investors’ Nudge Behavior: Based on the Data of Listed Chinese Tobacco Companies
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a narrow market-specific anomaly study rather than a general market-efficiency reference.

briefs.title: Behavioral Finance-A Review
briefs.summary: Reviews the main behavioral explanations for mispricing, including bias, slow learning, and the practical limits on arbitrage.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a general review when you need breadth more than a sharp empirical test.

briefs.title: A Review of Overconfidence in Behavioral Finance
briefs.summary: Reviews how overconfidence can increase trading, weaken discipline, and leave prices less tethered to intrinsic value.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if overconfidence is the specific bias you want isolated from the rest of behavioral finance.

briefs.title: Influence of Behavioral Biases on Professional Investment Decision in Kenya
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a professional-investor application in one market, not as a field-defining paper.

briefs.title: A Look at Behavioral Finance
briefs.summary: Reviews the main behavioral explanations for mispricing, including bias, slow learning, and the practical limits on arbitrage.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a quick review of the main behavioral-finance ideas behind mispricing.

briefs.title: Chapter 18 A survey of behavioral finance
briefs.summary: Reviews the main behavioral explanations for mispricing, including bias, slow learning, and the practical limits on arbitrage.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a chapter-length survey rather than as a single decisive paper.

briefs.title: Chapter 17 Behavioral Finance in Theory and Practice
briefs.summary: Reviews the main behavioral explanations for mispricing, including bias, slow learning, and the practical limits on arbitrage.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a chapter-length orientation to behavioral finance rather than a core source paper.

briefs.title: A Survey of Behavioral Macro-Finance
briefs.summary: This survey connects behavioral finance with larger macro questions such as asset booms, crashes, and cycles. It expands the discussion from single-stock anomalies to economy-wide behavior and pricing patterns.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want behavioral mispricing linked to macro booms, busts, and broad asset cycles.

briefs.title: The Conventional Past Behavioral Present and Algorithmic Future of Risk and Finance
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a broad framing piece on how behavioral finance fits into a changing market structure.

briefs.title: Three Essays on Behavioral Economics
briefs.summary: Examines where prices track fundamentals and where behavior or market frictions let mispricing linger.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful only if the essays line up with your subtopic; otherwise it is broader and less direct than the canonical papers.

briefs.title: Mistaking bad news for good news: investor optimism and mispricing of strategic alternatives announcements
briefs.authors: H. J. Rim Jenny Zha Giedt
briefs.summary: Studies a case where investor interpretation drifts away from fundamentals and creates a measurable pricing mistake.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a concrete example of optimism turning corporate-event news into a pricing mistake.

briefs.title: The Relationship Between Stock Price and Intrinsic Value of a Company
briefs.summary: Compares market price with estimated intrinsic value and asks how closely the two stay linked in practice.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the price-versus-value question stated directly rather than through a broader anomaly paper.

briefs.title: The Economics of Liquid Staking Derivatives: Basis Determinants and Price Discovery
briefs.summary: Studies how a newer market instrument finds its price and whether spreads or basis gaps reflect risk, friction, or mispricing.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how efficiency questions carry into newer crypto-market instruments.

briefs.title: On informational efficiency of the banking sector: a behavioral model of the credit boom
briefs.authors: David Peón Anxo Calvo M. Antelo
briefs.summary: Applies an efficiency lens to credit markets and asks whether boom-period prices reflected fundamentals or behavioral overshoot.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when credit booms are being discussed without enough attention to behavioral overshoot.

briefs.title: Resolving the paradox: is the safe withdrawal rate sometimes too safe?
briefs.summary: Kitces argues that safe withdrawal rates are not equally low in every market environment. He shows that starting valuation levels, especially the Shiller P/E, line up strongly with how safe future withdrawal rates are likely to be.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps show where retirement spending plans fail and where they stay durable.

briefs.title: Safe savings rates: A new approach to retirement planning over the life cycle
briefs.summary: Pfau argues that retirement planning works better when saving years and spending years are treated as one combined life-cycle problem. He shows that a safe savings rate can be more stable and more useful than aiming for one fixed safe withdrawal rule.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when you care more about spending resilience than about a single headline withdrawal rate.

briefs.title: A dynamic and adaptive approach to distribution planning and monitoring
briefs.summary: Blanchett and Frank propose reviewing the sustainability of a withdrawal rate every year instead of deciding once at retirement and never revisiting it. Their method raises or lowers the rate based on the remaining horizon and the portfolio’s current condition.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a withdrawal rule that survives bad timing, inflation, and long retirements.

briefs.title: Conserving client portfolios during retirement
briefs.summary: Bengen extends his retirement-withdrawal research beyond one fixed rule and looks at alternatives such as spending more early in retirement or adjusting withdrawals to portfolio performance. The work keeps the central question the same: how much can a retiree take without running out too soon.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a withdrawal rule that survives bad timing, inflation, and long retirements.

briefs.title: Spending flexibility and safe withdrawal rates
briefs.authors: Finke M., Pfau W. D., & Williams D.
briefs.summary: Finke, Pfau, and Williams model withdrawal decisions around risk tolerance instead of treating everyone as if they want the same retirement tradeoff. They find that more risk-tolerant retirees may rationally choose higher withdrawal rates and riskier portfolios than the usual 4 percent guidance suggests.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when you care more about spending resilience than about a single headline withdrawal rate.

briefs.title: Pension design and structure: New lessons from behavioral finance
briefs.authors: Mitchell O. S., & Utkus S. P.
briefs.summary: Connects retirement plan design to the way real people react to defaults, complexity, and payout choices.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a withdrawal rule that survives bad timing, inflation, and long retirements.

briefs.title: A sustainable spending rate without simulation
briefs.summary: Milevsky and Robinson build a forward-looking way to estimate sustainable spending without relying only on backward-looking historical tests or black-box Monte Carlo results. Their framework suggests payout rates may need to be lower than many advisers assume.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a withdrawal rule that survives bad timing, inflation, and long retirements.

briefs.title: Global portfolio optimization
briefs.summary: This work studies how portfolios should be optimized when investors draw from several markets at once instead of one domestic universe. It treats cross-market diversification as a core design problem.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real issue is how to build a portfolio instead of how to pick a single winner.

briefs.title: Optimal versus naive diversification: How inefficient is the 1/N portfolio strategy?
briefs.authors: DeMiguel V., Garlappi L., & Uppal R.
briefs.summary: DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal compare optimized portfolios with a simple equal-weight strategy and find that the naive 1/N rule is hard to beat in many practical settings. Estimation error can wipe out the theoretical gains from more sophisticated optimization.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the practical check on how much optimization really beats a simple equal-weight rule.

briefs.title: Toward maximum diversification
briefs.summary: Choueifaty and Coignard propose a portfolio approach that explicitly tries to maximize diversification rather than only balancing mean and variance. The method focuses on spreading risk contributions more broadly across holdings.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a portfolio rule that spreads risk more deliberately than classic mean-variance optimization.

briefs.title: Minimum-variance portfolios in the US equity market
briefs.authors: Clarke R., de Silva H., & Thorley S.
briefs.summary: This paper studies portfolios built to minimize volatility rather than maximize expected return. It documents that low-volatility portfolios can produce surprisingly competitive results in the US equity market.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want evidence that lower-volatility equity portfolios can stay competitive without heroic forecasts.

briefs.title: The Markowitz optimization enigma: Is optimized optimal?
briefs.summary: Michaud argues that classic mean-variance optimization can produce unstable and unrealistic portfolios because it overreacts to noisy input estimates. The paper questions whether mathematically optimal portfolios are actually robust in practice.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real issue is how to build a portfolio instead of how to pick a single winner.

briefs.title: Modern investment management: An equilibrium approach
briefs.summary: This book presents portfolio construction through an equilibrium lens and helped popularize ideas that later fed into Black-Litterman and other practical allocation frameworks.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a bridge from theoretical allocation models to practical institutional portfolio design.

briefs.title: The diversification puzzle
briefs.summary: This source examines why many investors remain underdiversified even when diversification is widely taught and easy to explain. It treats underdiversification as a persistent behavioral and structural problem.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know why investors still stay underdiversified even after diversification became common knowledge.

briefs.title: The cross-section of volatility and expected returns
briefs.authors: Ang A., Hodrick R. J., Xing Y., & Zhang X.
briefs.summary: Studies which company traits, risks, or signals line up with higher future returns across many stocks rather than in one isolated case.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as a map of which traits the paper treats as priced and which ones it does not.

briefs.title: The volatility effect
briefs.summary: Examines whether different forms of risk, such as volatility or tail exposure, help explain why some assets earn more than others.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a cleaner view of what the paper thinks actually drives returns over time.

briefs.title: The efficient market inefficiency of capitalization-weighted stock portfolios
briefs.authors: Haugen R. A., & Baker N. L.
briefs.summary: This paper argues that cap-weighted indexes can lock investors into owning more of whatever has already become expensive, which can reduce efficiency in practice.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: Do stock prices fully reflect information in accruals and cash flows about future earnings?
briefs.summary: Sloan shows that investors often treat accrual-heavy earnings as if they were as reliable as cash earnings, which helps explain later return reversals.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on which risks or traits investors have historically been paid for.

briefs.title: Contrarian investment extrapolation and risk
briefs.authors: Lakonishok J., Shleifer A., & Vishny R. W.
briefs.summary: Lakonishok, Shleifer, and Vishny argue that cheap stocks often outperform because investors extrapolate recent bad news too far into the future.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on which risks or traits investors have historically been paid for.

briefs.title: Evidence on the characteristics of cross sectional variation in stock returns
briefs.summary: Examines which risks, company traits, or market frictions the paper links to differences in long-run returns.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps anchor stock-return debates in an explicit pricing model instead of loose intuition.

briefs.title: Value investing: The use of historical financial statement information to separate winners from losers
briefs.summary: Piotroski uses accounting data to separate stronger and weaker value stocks and shows that simple balance-sheet and earnings signals improve value selection.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know whether momentum is a real return pattern or just a backtest artifact.

briefs.title: Capital investments and stock returns
briefs.authors: Titman S., Wei K. C. J., & Xie F.
briefs.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
briefs.summary: Examines which risks, company traits, or market frictions the paper links to differences in long-run returns.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: Do industries explain momentum?
briefs.summary: Examines momentum, the tendency for recent winning assets to keep outperforming for a period before the pattern fades.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth using when you want evidence on why recent winners can keep winning for a while.

briefs.title: Are investors reluctant to realize their losses?
briefs.summary: Examines the tendency to sell gains too fast and hold losses too long, even when that hurts long-run results.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how bias and framing change real money decisions, not just abstract preferences.

briefs.title: Naive diversification strategies in defined contribution saving plans
briefs.summary: Benartzi and Thaler show that many retirement savers use simple split-the-difference rules instead of building a thoughtful portfolio. The menu itself can distort the final allocation.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: The disposition to sell winners too early and ride losers too long: Theory and evidence
briefs.summary: Examines the tendency to sell gains too fast and hold losses too long, even when that hurts long-run results.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how bias and framing change real money decisions, not just abstract preferences.

briefs.title: A model of investor sentiment
briefs.authors: Barberis N., Shleifer A., & Vishny R.
briefs.summary: Links mood, narrative, or crowd psychology to trading behavior and short-run market moves.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how bias and framing change real money decisions, not just abstract preferences.

briefs.title: Overconfidence and trading volume
briefs.publication: The Geneva Risk and Insurance Review
briefs.summary: Examines overconfidence and shows how it can push investors into more trading than skill really supports.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: Good day sunshine: Stock returns and the weather
briefs.summary: Links mood, narrative, or crowd psychology to trading behavior and short-run market moves.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: Sports sentiment and stock returns
briefs.authors: Edmans A., Garcia D., & Norli O.
briefs.summary: Links mood, narrative, or crowd psychology to trading behavior and short-run market moves.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: Animal spirits: How human psychology drives the economy
briefs.authors: Akerlof G. A., & Shiller R. J.
briefs.summary: Links mood, narrative, or crowd psychology to trading behavior and short-run market moves.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: Behavioral biases and investment
briefs.summary: This paper provides a broad overview of the main behavioral biases that shape investment choices, from overconfidence to loss aversion and herd effects.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a general survey when you want the major investor biases in one place.

briefs.title: Optimal withdrawal strategies for retirees with multiple savings accounts
briefs.summary: This paper models how retirees should withdraw from several account types rather than treating retirement wealth as one single pool. The goal is to improve after-tax spending and reduce avoidable tax drag over time.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps quantify decisions that look small on paper but compound once taxes are included.

briefs.title: Asset location for retirement savers
briefs.authors: Poterba J. M., Shoven J. B., & Sialm C.
briefs.publication: In Pensions in the US Economy
briefs.summary: This source explains the practical logic of asset location for retirement investors, focusing on which assets are better suited to taxable versus tax-sheltered accounts.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps quantify decisions that look small on paper but compound once taxes are included.

briefs.title: Optimal stock trading with personal taxes: Implications for prices and the abnormal January returns
briefs.summary: Constantinides studies how personal taxes affect the timing of stock trades and how those choices can feed back into market prices. The paper links tax behavior to seasonal market effects such as January return patterns.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you care about after-tax wealth rather than pretending pretax returns are the whole story.

briefs.title: Tax management loss harvesting and HIFO accounting
briefs.summary: This paper looks at tax-loss harvesting together with high-in first-out accounting, which can reduce realized gains by choosing the highest-cost shares first. It treats tax management as a detailed implementation problem, not a generic idea.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you care about after-tax wealth rather than pretending pretax returns are the whole story.

briefs.title: Tax changes and asset pricing
briefs.summary: The paper studies how changes in tax rules can alter asset prices and expected returns. It treats taxes as part of the market structure rather than as a side issue for accountants only.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you care about after-tax wealth rather than pretending pretax returns are the whole story.

briefs.title: Tax-motivated trading by individual investors
briefs.authors: Ivkovic Z., Poterba J., & Weisbenner S.
briefs.summary: This paper studies whether individual investors trade partly to manage taxes, including delaying gains or realizing losses at useful times. It shows that tax motives can be seen directly in trading behavior.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when account order, loss use, or asset placement is part of the real decision.

briefs.title: How mutual fund capital gains distributions affect retail investor behavior
briefs.summary: The paper studies how retail investors react when mutual funds distribute taxable capital gains. It shows that tax events tied to fund structure can influence investor behavior even when investors did not actively sell anything themselves.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when account order, loss use, or asset placement is part of the real decision.

briefs.title: The relation between price and performance in the mutual fund industry
briefs.summary: This paper asks whether higher-priced mutual funds actually deliver better results. It examines whether investors are paying for genuine performance or simply paying more for the same exposure.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if a higher fee is being sold as evidence of higher quality.

briefs.title: Unobserved actions of mutual funds
briefs.summary: Kacperczyk, Sialm, and Zheng show that the holdings funds report can miss part of what managers are doing between disclosures. That gap matters when investors judge skill from stale snapshots.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why fund disclosures do not always tell the full story about manager behavior.

briefs.title: Measuring skill in the mutual fund industry
briefs.authors: Berk J. B., & van Binsbergen J. H.
briefs.summary: Fama and French test whether mutual fund outperformance survives once luck, factor exposure, and costs are stripped out. They find very little evidence that many managers deliver persistent skill net of fees.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when a fund’s past outperformance may just be noise rather than repeatable manager edge.

briefs.title: Scale and skill in active management
briefs.authors: Pastor L., Stambaugh R. F., & Taylor L. A.
briefs.summary: Berk and Green argue that money tends to flow toward successful active managers until the edge gets competed away. The result is that even skilled managers may not leave a large surplus for new investors after they become popular.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether active management adds enough skill to justify its cost.

briefs.title: The value of active mutual fund management: An examination of the stockholdings and trades of fund managers
briefs.authors: Chen H. L., Jegadeesh N., & Wermers R.
briefs.publication: The Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
briefs.summary: This paper studies what active mutual fund managers actually hold and trade, rather than just their headline returns. It finds that some managers show stock selection skill, but that the value to investors depends on costs and implementation.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real question is whether paying more produces a better investor outcome.

briefs.title: The cost of active investing
briefs.summary: French estimates the total cost investors pay for active investing, not just fund fees but the full system cost of trying to beat the market. His conclusion is that the aggregate price of active management is large relative to the value most investors receive.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real question is whether paying more produces a better investor outcome.

briefs.title: Orange juice and weather
briefs.summary: Roll studies whether weather affects orange juice prices and uses a very specific market to show how information gets into prices. It is often cited as an example of a market where fundamentals can dominate cleanly.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as the textbook example of a market where information processing can look unusually clean.

briefs.title: Stock returns and the weekend effect
briefs.summary: This paper documents that stock returns differ by day of the week, with unusually weak performance around the Monday opening. It became one of the classic calendar-anomaly papers.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the standard calendar anomalies used to test how cleanly markets absorb information.

briefs.title: Capital market seasonality: The case of stock returns
briefs.authors: Rozeff M. S., & Kinney W. R.
briefs.summary: The paper studies recurring seasonal patterns in stock returns rather than treating returns as uniform through the calendar. It helped expand the literature on market seasonality beyond a single anomaly.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the seasonality literature broadened beyond a single weekend or January effect.

briefs.title: Size-related anomalies and stock return seasonality: Further empirical evidence
briefs.summary: This paper studies whether small-cap return anomalies are tied to specific parts of the calendar. It strengthens the case that market seasonality and firm size can interact in important ways.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether size effects strengthen or weaken in specific calendar windows.

briefs.title: The P/E effect: Risk or anomaly?
briefs.authors: Boudreaux D. O., & Rozeff M. S.
briefs.summary: This paper studies whether low price-to-earnings stocks earn higher returns because they are riskier or because markets misprice them. It is part of the early debate over whether value effects are compensation for risk or an anomaly.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want an early direct test of whether cheap stocks win because of risk or mispricing.

briefs.title: The information in long-maturity forward rates
briefs.authors: Fama E. F., & Bliss R. R.
briefs.summary: Fama studies whether forward rates contain useful information about future interest rates and risk premia. The paper helps separate what a yield curve is forecasting from what it is charging as compensation for risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need to separate rate expectations from term premia in the yield curve.

briefs.title: Yield spreads and interest rate movements: A bird's eye view
briefs.authors: Campbell J. Y., & Shiller R. J.
briefs.summary: Campbell and Shiller study how yield spreads relate to later rate moves. They show that spreads carry information, but not always in the simple expectations-only way that textbook term-structure stories suggest.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know what the yield curve says about future rates without oversimplifying it.

briefs.title: Bond risk premia
briefs.summary: Cochrane and Piazzesi show that expected bond returns move over time and can be forecast using a combination of forward rates. Bond risk premia are not constant. They expand and contract with the cycle.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the strongest papers showing that expected bond returns move over time instead of staying fixed.

briefs.title: Some theoretical problems suggested by the movements of interest rates bond yields and stock prices in the United States since 1856
briefs.summary: Hicks lays out early theoretical questions about why interest rates and bond yields move the way they do over long history. It is a foundational attempt to explain term structure rather than merely describe it.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want an early attempt to explain the yield curve before modern models took over.

briefs.title: An equilibrium characterization of the term structure
briefs.summary: Cox, Ingersoll, and Ross develop an equilibrium model for how interest rates evolve across maturities. The paper became one of the classic foundations for term-structure modeling.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the term structure treated as an equilibrium object, not just a fitted curve.

briefs.title: A theory of the term structure of interest rates
briefs.authors: Cox J. C., Ingersoll J. E., & Ross S. A.
briefs.summary: Vasicek presents a tractable model of interest-rate movements that became a workhorse for pricing bonds and rate-sensitive securities. It is simple enough to use and rich enough to matter.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the classic workhorse models behind later rate and bond-pricing work.

briefs.title: Common factors affecting bond returns
briefs.summary: Litterman and Scheinkman show that a small number of factors explain most Treasury return movements, especially level, slope, and curvature shifts in the curve. This became one of the most influential organizing ideas in bond investing.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the standard references for thinking about level, slope, and curvature as the main bond-return drivers.

briefs.title: Economic forces and the stock market
briefs.authors: Chen N. F., Roll R., & Ross S. A.
briefs.summary: Chen, Roll, and Ross study how broad economic forces affect stock returns and connect those forces to asset-pricing risk. The paper helps bridge macro variables and market returns across asset classes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a macro bridge paper when you want rates and markets discussed in one framework.

briefs.title: Common risk factors in the returns on stocks and bonds
briefs.authors: Fama E. F., & French K. R.
briefs.summary: Fama and French identify factors that help explain returns across both stocks and bonds, not just within one market. The paper helped unify cross-asset return thinking.
briefs.whyItMatters: This matters if you want one paper that links stock and bond returns through shared drivers.

briefs.title: Explaining the rate spread on corporate bonds
briefs.authors: Elton E. J., Gruber M. J., Agrawal D., & Mann C.
briefs.summary: Collin-Dufresne, Goldstein, and Martin examine why corporate bond spreads are wider than simple default models predict. They find that changing credit conditions and other nondefault forces matter a lot.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a core paper for understanding why credit spreads move beyond pure default risk.

briefs.title: The determinants of credit spread changes
briefs.authors: Collin-Dufresne P., Goldstein R. S., & Martin J. S.
briefs.summary: This paper studies what drives changes in corporate credit spreads and shows that spreads move with more than just firm default risk. Marketwide and liquidity-related forces also play a role.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a core paper for anyone who wants to know why credit spreads move more than default models predict.

briefs.title: Modeling term structures of defaultable bonds
