briefs.summary: Duffie and Singleton build a framework for pricing bonds that carry default risk rather than assuming Treasuries and corporates behave the same way. The model became a key building block in credit pricing.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need a proper framework for combining interest-rate risk with default risk.

briefs.title: A simple approach to valuing risky fixed and floating rate debt
briefs.authors: Longstaff Francis A., & Schwartz E. S.
briefs.summary: Merton offers a structural way to think about risky debt by linking debt value to the value and volatility of the underlying firm. It is a foundational step in modern credit-risk modeling.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the foundational links between firm value and risky debt pricing.

briefs.title: Market transparency liquidity externalities and institutional trading costs in corporate bonds
briefs.authors: Bessembinder H., Maxwell W., & Venkataraman K.
briefs.summary: This paper studies how transparency and market structure affect the cost of trading corporate bonds. It shows that bond-market frictions can be large and that better transparency can change who pays them.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know who pays for opacity in the corporate bond market.

briefs.title: The illiquidity of corporate bonds
briefs.authors: Bao J., Pan J., & Wang J.
briefs.summary: This paper measures how illiquid corporate bonds can be relative to more transparent or actively traded markets. It shows that trading frictions are an important part of corporate bond returns.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you suspect part of a bond yield is really a payment for not being able to trade easily.

briefs.title: Time-varying expected returns in international bond markets
briefs.summary: This paper studies whether expected bond returns change through time across countries rather than staying fixed. The evidence suggests that bond return opportunities shift with global and local conditions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when bond opportunities are being described as stable even though the evidence says otherwise.

briefs.title: On biases in tests of the expectations hypothesis of the term structure of interest rates
briefs.authors: Bekaert G., Hodrick R. J., & Marshall D. A.
briefs.summary: Bekaert, Hodrick, and Marshall study why simple tests of the expectations hypothesis can be misleading. They show that statistical bias can distort the apparent evidence on how the yield curve works.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether a clean yield-curve result is real or partly a testing artifact.

briefs.title: A no-arbitrage vector autoregression of term structure dynamics with macroeconomic and latent variables
briefs.summary: This paper combines no-arbitrage bond pricing with macro variables and hidden state factors to model the yield curve more realistically. It links rates to both observable economics and latent dynamics.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the yield curve tied to macro forces rather than treated as a standalone shape.

briefs.title: The US Treasury yield curve: 1961 to the present
briefs.authors: Gürkaynak R. S., Sack B., & Wright J. H.
briefs.summary: Gurkaynak, Sack, and Wright build a long historical Treasury yield curve dataset that became a standard reference for fixed-income research. It gives researchers a cleaner continuous curve across decades.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a foundational curve dataset behind a large share of later fixed-income research.

briefs.title: Factor investing in the corporate bond market
briefs.summary: This paper studies whether factor-style ideas such as value, carry, low risk, or momentum can also work in corporate bonds. It applies the factor lens to a market often treated as yield-only.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know whether factor language survives outside equities and into credit.

briefs.title: Common factors in corporate bond returns
briefs.authors: Israel R., Palhares D., & Richardson S.
briefs.summary: The paper studies whether corporate bond returns can be organized around a small set of common drivers rather than many isolated security stories. It helps simplify a market that often looks fragmented.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the bond-market version of factor thinking rather than a single-issuer story.

briefs.title: Corporate bond market transaction costs and transparency
briefs.authors: Edwards A. K., Harris L. E., & Piwowar M. S.
briefs.summary: This paper measures how transparency changes transaction costs in the corporate bond market. It shows that market structure can materially affect investor execution.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a direct check on whether market structure quietly eats part of bond returns.

briefs.title: The performance of corporate-bond mutual funds: Evidence based on security-level holdings
briefs.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
briefs.summary: This paper studies corporate-bond mutual funds using their actual holdings rather than only fund-level returns. It asks whether managers add value through security selection after costs and constraints.
briefs.whyItMatters: This matters when a bond manager claims security-selection skill rather than simple yield collection.

briefs.title: Secondary trading costs in the municipal bond market
briefs.authors: Harris L. E., & Piwowar M. S.
briefs.summary: This paper measures the costs investors face when trading municipal bonds in the secondary market. It shows that transaction costs can be meaningful in a market many households treat as safe and sleepy.
briefs.whyItMatters: This matters if tax-free income is being judged without counting trading friction.

briefs.title: Smoothing in appraisal-based returns
briefs.publication: The Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics
briefs.summary: This paper shows that appraisal-based real estate return series often look smoother than the real market because appraisals lag and mute price changes. Reported property volatility can therefore look lower than actual economic risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the classic warning that appraisal-based property volatility is often understated.

briefs.title: The efficiency of the market for single-family homes
briefs.authors: Case K. E., & Shiller R. J.
briefs.summary: Case and Shiller test whether single-family home prices behave like an efficient market. They find evidence that past price movements can help predict future movements, which is awkward for a fully efficient-market story.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the classic papers questioning whether housing markets are as efficient as stock markets.

briefs.title: Economic risk factors and commercial real estate returns
briefs.publication: The Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics
briefs.summary: The paper links commercial real estate returns to broader economic risk factors rather than treating property as a world of its own. It shows that property returns move with macro conditions in ways investors can measure.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want commercial property tied back to macro risk rather than treated as a standalone world.

briefs.title: Commercial real estate valuation: Fundamentals versus investor sentiment
briefs.authors: Clayton J., Ling D. C., & Naranjo A.
briefs.publication: The Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics
briefs.summary: This paper compares commercial property values with underlying fundamentals and investor mood. It argues that sentiment can push valuations away from the income and macro drivers that would normally anchor them.
briefs.whyItMatters: This matters when commercial property pricing may be reflecting narrative as much as cash flow.

briefs.title: Value indices of commercial real estate: A comparison of index construction methods
briefs.authors: Fisher J. D., Geltner D. M., & Webb R. B.
briefs.publication: The Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics
briefs.summary: The paper compares different ways to build commercial real estate price indices and shows that the method used can materially change the picture of returns and volatility.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a reminder that property-index methodology can change the apparent return story.

briefs.title: Understanding recent trends in house prices and home ownership
briefs.summary: This NBER paper looks at why house prices and homeownership changed so sharply in the 2000s, with attention to credit conditions, demand, and supply. It tries to separate structural drivers from simple bubble talk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the 2000s housing run-up broken into structural drivers rather than sloganized as a bubble.

briefs.title: Housing supply and housing bubbles
briefs.authors: Glaeser E. L., Gyourko J., & Saiz A.
briefs.summary: The paper argues that housing bubbles behave differently in places where supply is slow to respond. When new building is constrained, demand shocks can translate into much bigger price moves.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to know why some housing booms become far more extreme than others.

briefs.title: Assessing high house prices: Bubbles fundamentals and misperceptions
briefs.authors: Himmelberg C., Mayer C., & Sinai T.
briefs.summary: Himmelberg, Mayer, and Sinai examine whether high house prices necessarily imply a bubble. They show that financing costs, rent equivalents, and local conditions can justify more of the price level than simple ratio-based arguments suggest.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the better papers for separating expensive housing from obvious bubble claims.

briefs.title: Money illusion and housing anomalies
briefs.summary: This paper argues that homebuyers may think in nominal rather than real terms, which can distort housing demand and pricing. Inflation and nominal interest rates can therefore change housing behavior in ways standard models miss.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why nominal rates and inflation can distort housing behavior in ways buyers do not fully notice.

briefs.title: Determinants of real house price dynamics
briefs.authors: Capozza D. R., Hendershott P. H., Mack C., & Mayer C. J.
briefs.summary: The paper studies what drives real house prices over time, including income, construction costs, demographics, and financing conditions. It treats house prices as the result of several interacting forces rather than one single cycle story.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a direct look at which variables actually move real house prices over time.

briefs.title: What does the stock market tell us about real estate returns?
briefs.summary: The paper asks whether stock market information, especially from listed property vehicles, can help explain or forecast real estate returns. Public markets may reveal information faster than appraisals or private deals do.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want faster public-market signals for an asset class often measured slowly.

briefs.title: Do real estate prices and stock prices move together? An international analysis
briefs.summary: This paper tests how closely stock and real estate prices move together across countries. The answer is mixed: there is some connection, but the link is not stable enough to treat the two assets as the same thing.
briefs.whyItMatters: This matters when property is being treated as either totally separate from equities or just an equity proxy.

briefs.title: The variation of economic risk premiums in real estate returns
briefs.authors: Karolyi G. A., & Sanders A. B.
briefs.publication: The Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics
briefs.summary: The paper studies how the risk premium in real estate changes over time rather than staying constant. Property returns can therefore look very different across calm periods and stressed periods.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether property risk premia stay stable across cycles.

briefs.title: International real estate returns: A multifactor multicountry approach
briefs.authors: Bond S. A., Karolyi G. A., & Sanders A. B.
briefs.summary: This paper models real estate returns across countries using several common drivers instead of one local story at a time. It shows that global property returns share some common risk factors even when local details differ.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when global property is being sold as local intuition rather than a set of shared risk exposures.

briefs.title: Diversification issues in real estate investment
briefs.authors: Seiler M. J., Webb J. R., & Myer F. C. N.
briefs.publication: The Journal of Real Estate Literature
briefs.summary: The paper studies how much diversification real estate actually adds and where the limits appear. Property can diversify a portfolio, but concentration by region, type, or cycle can shrink the benefit.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if the diversification case for property is being made without enough attention to concentration risk.

briefs.title: International evidence on real estate as a portfolio diversifier
briefs.authors: Hoesli M., Lekander J., & Witkiewicz W.
briefs.summary: This paper tests real estate as a diversifier across several countries. It finds that property can improve portfolio mix in some settings, but the strength of the benefit depends on market structure and correlation patterns.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the diversification case for property tested across countries rather than assumed.

briefs.title: Expected returns and expected growth in commercial real estate
briefs.authors: Plazzi A., Torous W., & Valkanov R.
briefs.summary: The paper separates current income from expected growth when thinking about commercial property returns. It shows that return expectations depend on more than cap rates alone.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when cap rates are being treated as the whole return story.

briefs.title: Forecasting real estate prices
briefs.authors: Ghysels E., Plazzi A., Valkanov R., & Torous W.
briefs.summary: This paper examines how well real estate prices can be forecast and which variables help. It suggests that prediction is possible to a degree, but far less cleanly than many market narratives imply.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a reality check on how predictable property prices really are.

briefs.title: The value added from investment managers: An examination of funds of REITs
briefs.authors: Kallberg J. G., Liu C. H., & Trzcinka C.
briefs.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
briefs.summary: The paper looks at whether managers running funds of REITs add value through selection and allocation. It tests whether layering active management on top of listed property vehicles actually improves investor outcomes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether active management adds value even after you already chose listed real estate.

briefs.title: Risk and return on real estate: Evidence from equity REITs
briefs.authors: Chan K. C., Hendershott P. H., & Sanders A. B.
briefs.summary: This paper studies the return and risk profile of equity REITs using public-market evidence. It helps frame listed real estate as a serious asset class with its own mix of income, leverage, and market sensitivity.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want listed real estate treated as a real capital-market asset rather than a housing anecdote.

briefs.title: Risk and the performance of real estate investment trusts: A multiple index approach
briefs.summary: The paper uses multiple benchmark indices to understand what drives REIT performance. It shows that listed property returns reflect more than one source of risk at the same time.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when one benchmark is not enough to explain REIT behavior.

briefs.title: Privately versus publicly held asset investment performance
briefs.authors: Riddiough T. J., Moriarty M., & Yeatman P. J.
briefs.summary: This paper compares private and public asset performance and highlights the valuation and liquidity issues that complicate direct comparisons. Private assets can look smoother partly because they are priced differently.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know how much private-asset smoothness is real and how much is measurement.

briefs.title: Public versus private real estate equities: A more refined long-term comparison
briefs.authors: Pagliari J. L., Scherer K. A., & Monopoli R. T.
briefs.summary: The paper compares listed and private real estate over a long horizon with a more careful method than simple headline return charts. It tries to isolate what is real performance difference and what is just measurement difference.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when listed and private property are being compared as if the data were directly interchangeable.

briefs.title: Two decades of commercial property returns: A repeated-measures regression-based version of the NCREIF index
briefs.publication: The Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics
briefs.summary: This paper builds a commercial property return series using a repeated-measures method to improve on simpler index construction. It aims to give a cleaner long-run picture of private commercial real estate performance.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when private-commercial-property returns need a cleaner long-run benchmark.

briefs.title: Search and liquidity in real estate markets
briefs.authors: Ang A., Nabar S., & Wald J. K.
briefs.summary: This paper looks at how search frictions and illiquidity shape real estate prices and transactions. Unlike stocks, property markets often involve slow matching, delayed sales, and uneven information.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a clean explanation of why real estate can look stable while actually being slow and hard to clear.

briefs.title: The Millionaire Next Door: The Surprising Secrets of America's Wealthy
briefs.authors: Stanley T. J., & Danko W. D.
briefs.summary: Stanley and Danko profile affluent households and argue that wealth often comes from steady saving, modest consumption, and business ownership rather than visible luxury.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a behavioral picture of how ordinary wealth accumulation usually works in practice.

briefs.title: The Intelligent Investor
briefs.summary: Graham sets out the core value-investing framework: demand a margin of safety, focus on price versus underlying value, and avoid speculation disguised as investing.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is still the clearest plain-language statement of margin-of-safety investing.

briefs.title: Security Analysis
briefs.summary: Graham and Dodd build a detailed framework for valuing securities through balance-sheet strength, earnings power, and conservative appraisal.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the deeper technical foundation underneath later value-investing books.

briefs.title: A Random Walk Down Wall Street
briefs.summary: Argues that low-cost indexing beats most attempts to outpick the market once fees, taxes, and trading mistakes are counted.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read when the real question is whether paying more produces a better investor outcome.

briefs.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
briefs.summary: Argues that low-cost indexing beats most attempts to outpick the market once fees, taxes, and trading mistakes are counted.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know whether active management adds enough skill to justify its cost.

briefs.title: The Psychology of Money
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: The Simple Path to Wealth
briefs.summary: Collins presents a straightforward household-investing framework built around high savings rates, broad index funds, and simple withdrawal rules.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a stripped-down household investing system that favors consistency over complexity.

briefs.title: Die With Zero: Getting All You Can from Your Money and Your Life
briefs.summary: Perkins argues that the goal is not to die rich but to time spending, saving, and gifting so money is used when it can create the most value.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the real decision is timing spending, not only maximizing the estate left behind.

briefs.title: Just Keep Buying
briefs.summary: Maggiulli focuses on the math of saving, investing, and staying invested, with an emphasis on behavior people can actually sustain.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a practical saving-and-investing framework that leans on consistency instead of optimization.

briefs.title: Margin of Safety: Risk-Averse Value Investing Strategies for the Thoughtful Investor
briefs.summary: Klarman lays out a cautious value-investing framework centered on downside protection, patience, and buying only when the discount is large enough.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearest modern statements of value investing as downside control first.

briefs.title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
briefs.summary: Fisher argues for buying outstanding businesses that can compound for long periods rather than trading in and out of average companies.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you care more about finding exceptional businesses than buying statistically cheap ones.

briefs.title: One Up On Wall Street
briefs.summary: Lynch argues that ordinary investors can find useful ideas by paying attention to products, industries, and businesses they actually know.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to see how everyday business observation can feed stock ideas.

briefs.title: Beating the Street
briefs.summary: Lynch extends his stock-picking approach and shows how business observation, category thinking, and patience fit together in practice.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want Lynch's stock-picking style extended beyond the first book.

briefs.title: The Little Book That Beats the Market
briefs.summary: Greenblatt presents the magic formula, a simple ranking system that mixes earnings yield with return on capital.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a very simplified systematic value screen, not a full valuation framework.

briefs.title: Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how bias and framing change real money decisions, not just abstract preferences.

briefs.title: Thinking Fast and Slow
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: Fooled by Randomness: The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: The Most Important Thing: Uncommon Sense for the Thoughtful Investor
briefs.summary: Marks centers investing on cycles, risk control, price discipline, and second-level thinking rather than forecasting brilliance.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want value investing framed through cycles, risk control, and second-level thinking.

briefs.title: The Intelligent Asset Allocator
briefs.summary: Bernstein explains asset allocation in practical language, with a strong emphasis on diversification, rebalancing, and staying realistic about risk. The book translates portfolio theory into decisions a household investor can actually use.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want portfolio theory translated into plain household-investing language.

briefs.title: The Four Pillars of Investing
briefs.summary: Bernstein organizes investing around theory, history, psychology, and business practice. The book aims to show why portfolio success depends on behavior and structure, not just return chasing.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a behavior-aware explanation of why asset allocation and investor discipline matter more than prediction.

briefs.title: Unconventional Success: A Fundamental Approach to Personal Investment
briefs.summary: Swensen argues for a low-cost, disciplined, diversified approach for individual investors rather than manager chasing or stock picking. The book stresses structure, simplicity, and cost control.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a disciplined, low-cost portfolio philosophy built around asset allocation rather than manager selection.

briefs.title: Winning the Loser's Game
briefs.summary: Ellis argues that for most investors the winning move is not to outplay everyone else but to make fewer costly mistakes than the crowd. The book pushes discipline over cleverness.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if the real edge comes from avoiding self-inflicted errors rather than chasing brilliance.

briefs.title: Common Sense on Mutual Funds
briefs.summary: Argues that low-cost indexing beats most attempts to outpick the market once fees, taxes, and trading mistakes are counted.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate genuine manager edge from fees, taxes, and benchmark noise.

briefs.title: The Wealthy Barber
briefs.summary: Chilton packages basic money habits such as paying yourself first, controlling debt, and investing regularly into a simple household system.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a simple habit-based savings system rather than a complex financial plan.

briefs.title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
briefs.summary: Kiyosaki frames wealth building around assets, liabilities, cash flow, and financial independence, though the book is more motivational than empirical.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a motivational framing device, but weaker than evidence-led books on household finance.

briefs.title: Your Money or Your Life
briefs.summary: Robin and Dominguez treat money as life energy and build a framework around spending awareness, savings discipline, and intentional work choices.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want household finance tied to spending awareness and life-design choices.

briefs.title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
briefs.summary: Sethi emphasizes automation, low-cost investing, targeted spending, and system design over constant budgeting.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if automation and system design matter more to you than meticulous budgeting.

briefs.title: The Only Investment Guide You'll Ever Need
briefs.summary: Tobias gives a broad household-finance overview that covers saving, investing, taxes, and portfolio basics in plain language.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a broad household-finance overview, not as a single-topic authority.

briefs.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
briefs.summary: Clason uses short parables to teach saving first, living below means, and putting money to work.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want timeless saving rules presented as simple parables rather than formal analysis.

briefs.title: Stocks for the Long Run
briefs.summary: Siegel argues from long-run historical data that diversified stocks have tended to beat bonds, bills, and inflation over very long holding periods.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the long-horizon case for equities stated in historical rather than promotional terms.

briefs.title: What Works on Wall Street
briefs.summary: O Shaughnessy compiles long-run market tests of simple ranking rules, especially value, momentum, and shareholder-yield screens.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on which risks or traits investors have historically been paid for.

briefs.title: Your Money and Your Brain
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: Predictably Irrational
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: Principles: Life and Work
briefs.summary: Dalio frames decision-making around principles, feedback loops, and error correction, blending practical management advice with a system view of judgment.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a decision-framework book, though it is not a primary evidence source in the same way as the core papers.

briefs.title: When Genius Failed: The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management
briefs.summary: Lowenstein reconstructs how a highly sophisticated hedge fund collapsed when leverage, crowded trades, and funding pressure hit at the same time.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the best real-world studies of how leverage and crowding can break elite strategies.

briefs.title: Liar's Poker
briefs.summary: Lewis uses Salomon Brothers to show how incentives, status games, and trading culture shaped Wall Street in the bond-boom era.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a culture-and-incentives portrait of bond trading rather than a technical market manual.

briefs.title: Flash Boys: A Wall Street Revolt
briefs.summary: Lewis examines high-frequency trading, market structure, and how speed advantages can shape execution quality for ordinary investors.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when market structure and execution quality matter more than broad market direction.

briefs.title: Devil Take the Hindmost: A History of Financial Speculation
briefs.summary: Chancellor surveys major speculative booms and busts to show how recurring patterns of leverage, crowd psychology, and narrative excess keep resurfacing.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a long historical pattern of speculative booms rather than a single crisis story.

briefs.title: Manias Panics and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises
briefs.summary: Kindleberger and Aliber lay out a recurring crisis sequence in which credit expansion, speculation, and reversal feed one another.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the standard historical frameworks for how crises build and unwind.

briefs.title: Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds
briefs.summary: Mackay collects historical episodes of financial and social mania to show how group behavior can overpower sober judgment.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a long-history catalog of how crowd behavior can overwhelm individual judgment.

briefs.title: The Alchemy of Finance
briefs.summary: Soros explains reflexivity, the idea that market beliefs can change the underlying reality and then feed back into prices again.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if reflexivity is the concept you want, rather than a standard market-efficiency framework.

briefs.title: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator
briefs.summary: This classic market memoir follows a speculator through booms, losses, and trading errors, with constant attention to timing, leverage, and psychology.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want market psychology and speculation shown through a lived trading narrative.

briefs.title: Why Smart People Make Big Money Mistakes
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how bias and framing change real money decisions, not just abstract preferences.

briefs.title: What Investors Really Want
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why sensible plans often break once habit, emotion, or social cues get involved.

briefs.title: Behavioural Investing: A Practitioners Guide to Applying Behavioural Finance
briefs.summary: Translates behavioral research into a practical account of how money decisions are shaped by bias, habit, and story rather than pure calculation.
briefs.whyItMatters: Best read as evidence on why people do not behave like frictionless spreadsheet optimizers.

briefs.title: The Quants: How a New Breed of Math Whizzes Conquered Wall Street and Nearly Destroyed It
briefs.summary: Patterson traces the rise of quantitative trading firms and shows how leverage, crowding, and model similarity can turn smart systems into shared failure points.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate a return story with evidence behind it from a loose investing slogan.

briefs.title: A Man for All Markets
briefs.summary: Thorp recounts how probability, hedging, and disciplined sizing shaped his work in blackjack, options, and hedge funds.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a first-person record of probability, hedging, and disciplined risk-taking applied in markets.

briefs.title: The Warren Buffett Way
briefs.summary: Hagstrom distills Buffett's approach into business quality, management judgment, capital allocation, and sensible purchase price.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want Buffett-style investing broken into repeatable business-quality heuristics.

briefs.title: Buffett: The Making of an American Capitalist
briefs.summary: Lowenstein traces Buffett's development from cigar-butt investing toward buying superior businesses at fair prices.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want Buffett's development treated historically rather than as a rules-only summary.

briefs.title: SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2024
briefs.authors: Ganti A. R., Edwards T., Di Gioia D., Chapman F., & Didio N.
briefs.summary: S&P Dow Jones finds that most U.S. active equity managers still trailed their benchmarks in 2024, and the gap widened over longer holding periods even after a year with some small-cap and fixed-income pockets of strength.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want recent scorekeeping on how rarely active fund selection keeps up over a full market cycle.

briefs.title: SPIVA After-Tax Scorecard Year-End 2024: The Effect of Taxes on Indices and Active Funds
briefs.summary: This scorecard compares index funds with active U.S. equity funds after taxes and shows that taxable distributions made it even harder for the median active manager to keep up with broad benchmarks.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when the real question is not pre-tax alpha but what actually stays in a taxable investor account after turnover and distributions.

briefs.title: Mind the Gap US 2025
briefs.summary: Morningstar measures the investor return gap, the difference between fund returns and the returns investors actually earn after their cash-timing decisions. The report links larger gaps to volatility, poor timing, and fee drag.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a practical reminder that behavior can do more damage than fund selection when investors buy and sell at the wrong times.

briefs.title: Morningstar’s 2024 Annual US Fund Fee Study
briefs.summary: Morningstar shows that investor-paid fund fees kept falling in 2024, but the decline slowed as index-fund price wars approached a floor and newer ETFs launched with more varied price points.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good context for why cost discipline still matters even after years of headline fee compression.

briefs.title: Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2026
briefs.authors: Dimson E., Marsh P., & Staunton M.
briefs.summary: The 2026 Yearbook extends the long-run DMS database through 2025 and uses more than a century of market history to revisit diversification, currency hedging, geopolitical risk, gold, and the recurring debate over technology booms.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the best reference points for checking whether current market stories look exceptional or just unusually loud versions of older patterns.

briefs.title: How America Saves 2025
briefs.summary: Vanguard reviews nearly five million defined-contribution participants and finds stronger use of auto-enrollment, professionally managed allocations, and higher savings rates, alongside a rise in hardship withdrawals.
briefs.whyItMatters: It gives a large-sample view of how workers actually save, invest, and tap retirement accounts rather than how idealized retirement plans are supposed to work.

briefs.title: Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The Fed’s 2024 SHED shows that overall financial well-being stayed below the 2021 peak, inflation remained the dominant concern, and many households still lacked emergency savings even with a solid labor market.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good reality check on day-to-day household balance-sheet stress that does not show up in market indexes.

briefs.title: Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022
briefs.authors: Aladangady A., Bricker J., Chang A. C., Goodman S., Krimmel J., Moore K. B., Reber S., Volz A. H., & Windle R.
briefs.summary: The 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances captures a large jump in median net worth, higher stock-market participation, stronger retirement-plan participation, and a housing affordability squeeze after the pandemic shock.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the broadest household balance-sheet snapshot in the United States and one of the best anchors for claims about wealth inequality, debt, and saving behavior.

briefs.title: Pensions at a Glance 2023
briefs.summary: The OECD surveys pension rules across member countries, updates replacement-rate projections for today’s workers, and examines how inflation, reform design, and early-retirement rules shape retirement income security.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need retirement policy evidence that goes beyond one country and shows how pension design changes the spending floor retirees can rely on.

briefs.title: The Great Inequality Transfer
briefs.summary: Urban Institute studies how homeownership and housing wealth shape intergenerational transfers and shows that the coming wealth handoff is likely to reinforce existing racial wealth gaps rather than narrow them.
briefs.whyItMatters: It connects housing wealth to inheritance, which matters if you want to understand why property ownership compounds inequality across generations.

briefs.title: Beyond the Retirement Crisis Headlines
briefs.summary: Using Morningstar’s new retirement-outcomes model, this paper estimates that retirement shortfalls are concentrated among workers who lack access to employer plans, lower-income workers, and people retiring earlier.
briefs.whyItMatters: It moves the retirement-crisis debate away from slogans and toward which households are actually at risk of running short.

briefs.title: The Overlooked Cost: How Long-Term Services and Supports Impacts Retirement-Income Adequacy
briefs.summary: Morningstar estimates that adding long-term care risk pushes the share of households projected to fall short in retirement from 26 percent to 41 percent, with single women especially exposed.
briefs.whyItMatters: Strong reminder that retirement plans built around market returns alone can badly understate late-life spending risk.

briefs.title: Does Pension Automatic Enrollment Increase Debt? Evidence from a Large-Scale Natural Experiment
briefs.authors: Beshears J., Blakstad M., Choi J. J., Firth C., Gathergood J., Laibson D., Notley R., Sheth J. D., Sandbrook W., & Stewart N.
briefs.summary: This natural experiment on U.K. auto-enrollment finds that workers do save more in pensions, but part of the gain is offset by higher unsecured borrowing and somewhat larger mortgage balances.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a more realistic view of what forced saving does to the whole household balance sheet, not just the retirement account.

briefs.title: Asset Demand of U.S. Households
briefs.authors: Gabaix X., Koijen R. S. J., Mainardi F., Oh S., & Yogo M.
briefs.summary: Using security-level portfolio data, the authors show that less wealthy households tend to sell equities in downturns while ultra-wealthy households are more likely to buy, with most households showing substantial inertia overall.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives unusually direct evidence on who stabilizes markets and how household rebalancing differs across the wealth distribution.

briefs.title: Portfolio flows and household portfolios
briefs.authors: te Kaat D. M., Ma C., & Rebucci A.
briefs.summary: This paper finds that cross-border portfolio inflows during the European crisis pushed households with larger bond and stock allocations to rebalance more heavily into housing.
briefs.whyItMatters: It shows that housing demand can move with financial-market shocks and portfolio reallocations, not only with mortgage rates or local supply constraints.

briefs.title: Household Mobility and Mortgage Rate Lock
briefs.summary: Liebersohn and Rothstein estimate that higher mortgage rates in 2022 and 2023 cut mobility for mortgaged homeowners by about 16 percent because moving meant giving up older low-rate loans.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearest explanations for why housing supply can feel frozen even when owners have large home-equity gains.

briefs.title: Suboptimal household investment and information-processing frictions: Evidence from 529 college savings plans
briefs.authors: Li J. J., Mitchell O. S., & Zhu C.
briefs.publication: Journal of Financial Literacy and Wellbeing
briefs.summary: The authors find that most 529 accounts opened between 2010 and 2020 were placed in tax-inefficient or high-cost plans, producing expected lifetime losses on a large share of accounts.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good evidence that tax wrappers only help when households understand which account location actually preserves the benefit.

briefs.title: Retirees Spend Lifetime Income, Not Savings
briefs.summary: Blanchett and Finke find that retirees spend far more freely from Social Security, pensions, and annuity income than from portfolio balances, and actual withdrawal rates from savings sit well below common planning guidance.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why many retirees underspend despite having enough assets on paper.

briefs.title: To plan, or not to plan? Optimal planning and saving for retirement
briefs.authors: Kalemli-Ozcan S., Markov A., & Rauh J.
briefs.summary: This model shows how households can rationally postpone retirement planning when planning itself is costly, which helps explain why many people save too little early in life even when they are forward-looking.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a cleaner bridge between behavioral-looking under-saving and standard economic optimization.

briefs.title: A mean-variance benchmark for household portfolios over the life cycle
briefs.summary: Munk extends the Markowitz framework to include human capital and shows that simple mean-variance logic can recover much of the life-cycle allocation guidance produced by more complex dynamic models.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a practical bridge between textbook portfolio theory and the real problem of allocating financial assets around labor income and housing.

briefs.title: Household willingness to take financial risk: Stockmarket movements and life-cycle effects
briefs.authors: Cardak B. A. & Martin V. L.
briefs.summary: Using panel data, the paper shows that household risk tolerance rises after long runs of stronger stock returns and follows an age pattern that peaks around middle age before falling near retirement.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a useful reminder that stated risk tolerance is not fixed and can move with the market cycle and household age.

briefs.title: The long-term impact of financial literacy on wealth: Evidence from longitudinal data
briefs.summary: Using Dutch longitudinal data, this paper finds that higher financial literacy predicts more income and savings years later, with different effects across age groups and a notable gender split.
briefs.whyItMatters: This strengthens the case that financial literacy is not only correlated with wealth but can shape later balance-sheet outcomes.

briefs.title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning
briefs.authors: Gu S., Kelly B., & Xiu D.
briefs.summary: Gu, Kelly, and Xiu compare machine-learning methods for expected-return estimation and show that nonlinear models can outperform standard linear approaches while repeatedly surfacing momentum, liquidity, and volatility as dominant signals.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong modern reference for how return forecasting changed once researchers let flexible models handle interaction effects and large predictor sets.

briefs.title: Household Finance in Retrospect and Prospect
briefs.summary: Campbell and Ramadorai survey how household finance matured into a serious research field, from portfolio choice and debt behavior to financial advice, literacy, and administrative-data work.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want one recent map of what household finance research explains well and where the biggest unanswered questions still sit.

briefs.title: Why Do Households Save and Work?
briefs.authors: Borella M., De Nardi M., Yang F., & Torres Chain J. P.
briefs.summary: This paper estimates a life-cycle model with wages, health shocks, medical spending, family transitions, and bequests, then shows which forces actually drive saving and work decisions across households.
briefs.whyItMatters: It helps separate retirement saving stories that sound plausible from the specific risks and motives that move wealth in the data.

briefs.title: Life Cycle Portfolio Choice with Human Capital and Social Security
briefs.authors: Scott J., Shoven J. B., Slavov S., & Watson J. G.
briefs.summary: Scott, Shoven, Slavov, and Watson revisit the usual target-date-fund logic and show that labor-income risk and Social Security make optimal stock-bond paths differ more by income than standard glide paths imply.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a good check on whether one default glide path is really sensible for households with very different earnings risk and retirement backstops.

briefs.title: What Drives Investors' Portfolio Choices? Separating Risk Preferences from Frictions
briefs.summary: Using 401(k) defaults as a quasi-experiment, the authors estimate that low stock exposure in retirement accounts mostly reflects participation frictions and adjustment costs, not unusually low risk tolerance.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want evidence that bad portfolio outcomes often come from inertia and process friction, not from deeply revealed investor preferences.

briefs.title: Household Portfolios and Retirement Saving over the Life Cycle
briefs.authors: Parker J. A., Schoar A., Cole A. T., & Simester D.
briefs.summary: The paper shows that U.S. middle-class households now hold more equity than in the 1990s and ties much of the age pattern to target-date funds becoming default options after the Pension Protection Act.
briefs.whyItMatters: It shows how plan defaults can reshape real household portfolios without households actively redesigning their own investing rules.

briefs.title: The Design of Defined Contribution Plans
briefs.summary: Bhattacharya and Illanes study how employers and recordkeepers shape 401(k) quality, then argue that plan design problems often persist because employer incentives do not line up cleanly with worker outcomes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand why weak retirement plans keep showing up even when low-cost better designs are already known.

briefs.title: Selection into Financial Education and Effects on Portfolio Choice
briefs.authors: Gemmo I., Michaud P.-C., & Mitchell O. S.
briefs.summary: Gemmo, Michaud, and Mitchell run an incentivized experiment and find that financial education improved portfolio efficiency and welfare, with the biggest gains showing up among people most willing to buy the education.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is stronger than generic literacy talk because it measures whether education changes actual portfolio choices in a controlled setting.

briefs.title: Financial Literacy, Schooling, and Wealth Accumulation
briefs.authors: Behrman J. R., Mitchell O. S., Soo C., & Bravo D.
briefs.summary: Using instrumental-variable methods, the authors find that financial literacy has a large positive relationship with household wealth even after trying to separate it from schooling and ability.
briefs.whyItMatters: This remains one of the better-known attempts to move the literacy debate from correlation toward a more causal estimate.

briefs.title: Financial Literacy, Retirement Planning, and Household Wealth
briefs.authors: van Rooij M., Lusardi A., & Alessie R. J.
briefs.summary: Van Rooij, Lusardi, and Alessie link stronger financial knowledge with higher net worth and show that part of the channel runs through stock-market participation and actual retirement planning.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a useful bridge between literacy, planning behavior, and the long-run wealth gap between otherwise similar households.

briefs.title: Defaulting 401(k) Assets into Payout Annuities for "Pretty Good" Lifetime Incomes
briefs.authors: Horneff V., Maurer R., & Mitchell O. S.
briefs.summary: Horneff, Maurer, and Mitchell model what happens when plans default part of a retiree's 401(k) balance into annuity income and find that modest automatic annuitization can improve retirement security for many households.
briefs.whyItMatters: This makes the annuity debate concrete by testing a practical plan default instead of an all-or-nothing product choice.

briefs.title: Retirement Consumption and Pension Design
briefs.authors: Kolsrud J., Landais C., Reck D., & Spinnewijn J.
briefs.summary: Using Swedish administrative data, the authors show that earlier retirees face larger consumption drops and use those patterns to evaluate which pension reforms smooth spending and which shift pain onto vulnerable households.
briefs.whyItMatters: It grounds pension-design debates in actual retirement consumption rather than replacement-rate rules alone.

briefs.title: Failures of Contingent Reasoning in Annuitization Decisions
briefs.authors: Luttmer E. F. P., de Oliveira P., & Taubinsky D.
briefs.summary: Luttmer, de Oliveira, and Taubinsky find that many people undervalue annuities because they fail to connect annuity income with the less efficient saving they would otherwise need to self-insure retirement risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why annuities stay unpopular even when they make economic sense on paper.

briefs.title: The Mortgage Piggy Bank: Building Wealth through Amortization
briefs.summary: Bernstein and Koudijs show that required mortgage amortization can raise net worth almost one-for-one because many households do not fully offset the extra principal payments by cutting other saving.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a cleaner view of why forced home-equity buildup can matter for wealth beyond simple housing appreciation.

briefs.title: Temptation and Incentives to Wealth Accumulation
briefs.authors: Attanasio O., Kovacs A., & Moran P.
briefs.summary: This paper models housing as a commitment device and finds that mortgage-interest deductions and required amortization can raise wealth partly by making saving less easy to reverse.
briefs.whyItMatters: It connects present bias to real housing policy and shows why some illiquid saving tools can still increase household wealth.

briefs.title: Pensions at a Glance 2025
briefs.summary: The 2025 OECD pension compendium updates retirement-income rules across member countries and adds a focused review of the gender pension gap, aging pressure, and recent reform choices.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is one of the cleanest cross-country references for checking how pension promises and retirement-policy tradeoffs compare in practice.

briefs.title: Pension Markets in Focus 2025
briefs.summary: OECD tracks global pension assets, contributions, payouts, and investment gains through end-2024, showing how much recent retirement-asset growth came from markets versus cash flows.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to separate headline pension-asset growth from the mechanics that actually produced it.

briefs.title: US Active/Passive Barometer Report: Mid-Year 2025
briefs.summary: Morningstar compares more than nine thousand active and passive funds and reports that only about one-third of active strategies both survived and beat their passive peers over the prior year.
briefs.whyItMatters: It gives a broad, current check on whether paying for active management improved outcomes after survivorship and category matching are handled.

briefs.title: 2025 Retirement Plan Landscape Report
briefs.summary: Morningstar reviews plan coverage, asset growth, fees, investment menus, and defined-benefit health across the U.S. retirement system, with extra attention to how smaller plans still lag on costs and quality.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a practical snapshot of where the retirement system is improving and where scale and plan design still leave workers behind.

briefs.title: U.S. Persistence Scorecard Year-End 2024
briefs.authors: Di Gioia D., Ganti A. R., & Malinowski A.
briefs.summary: S&P Dow Jones shows that even the minority of active U.S. funds that outperform in one period rarely keep doing it, with virtually no top-quartile persistence over the following four years.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is the cleaner follow-up question after any beat-the-benchmark claim: did the outperformance last, or was it mostly luck?

briefs.title: SPIVA Institutional Scorecard Year-End 2024
briefs.authors: Di Gioia D., & Ganti A. R.
briefs.summary: This institutional SPIVA edition extends the active-versus-benchmark test to separate accounts and institutional mandates, then finds that long-run equity underperformance still looks common even before fees.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when someone argues that active management only fails in retail mutual funds and looks better once you move upmarket.

briefs.title: Friends with Benefits: Social Capital and Household Financial Behavior
briefs.authors: Cannon B., Hirshleifer D., & Thornton J.
briefs.summary: Using Facebook friendship data, the authors find that households with more high-income connections are much more likely to save and own stocks, with evidence that the link is partly causal rather than just correlational.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives a concrete mechanism for why investing habits cluster inside social circles instead of spreading evenly across households.

briefs.title: Stock Market Wealth and Entrepreneurship
briefs.authors: Chodorow-Reich G., Nenov P. T., Santos V., & Simsek A.
briefs.summary: Using Norwegian portfolio records, the paper shows that gains in household stock wealth increase the odds of starting a business and improve later firm profitability by easing financing constraints.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want evidence that household portfolio gains can change real economic options, not just paper net worth.

briefs.title: To Pay or Autopay? Fintech Innovation and Credit Card Payments
briefs.summary: Studying a fintech credit-card portfolio, Wang finds that a small enrollment nudge explains about half of autopay adoption and sharply raises the odds that cardholders make only the minimum payment.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is directly relevant for how default settings can reduce missed payments while still leaving borrowers stuck in revolving debt.

briefs.title: Monetary Policy Transmission Through Online Banks
briefs.authors: Erel I., Liebersohn J., Yannelis C., & Earnest S.
briefs.summary: The paper shows that online banks pass policy-rate changes through to depositors faster than traditional banks, pulling deposits toward households willing to move cash for better yields.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for understanding why some savers benefit quickly from higher rates while others remain trapped in low-yield accounts.

briefs.title: Refinancing Frictions, Mortgage Pricing and Redistribution
briefs.authors: Berger D. W., Milbradt K., Tourre F., & Vavra J. S.
briefs.summary: Berger and coauthors model mortgage markets and show that borrowers who rarely refinance can end up subsidizing those who refinance often, with reforms creating large distributional tradeoffs.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why mortgage pricing can quietly transfer value from less attentive households to more sophisticated ones.

briefs.title: Optimal Mortgage Refinancing with Inattention
briefs.authors: Berger D. W., Milbradt K., Tourre F., & Vavra J. S.
briefs.summary: This paper shows that many mortgage refinance mistakes can be explained by borrowers paying attention to rates only intermittently, not just by high transaction costs.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a cleaner explanation for why households leave mortgage savings on the table even when refinancing looks obvious.

briefs.title: Efficiency in Household Decision-Making: Evidence from the Retirement Savings of US Couples
briefs.authors: Choukhmane T., Goodman L., & O'Dea C.
briefs.summary: Using administrative data on more than a million workers, the authors show that couples often fail to direct retirement contributions to the spouse with the better employer match, leaving money unclaimed.
briefs.whyItMatters: This quantifies an expensive household coordination mistake that standard retirement calculators usually ignore.

briefs.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
briefs.summary: Choukhmane finds that auto-enrollment lifts retirement saving strongly in the first year, but much of the effect fades over longer horizons even as savings inequality narrows.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the medium-run evidence on whether retirement-plan defaults change wealth building or mainly shift timing.

briefs.title: Household Labor Supply and the Value of Social Security Survivors Benefits
briefs.authors: Coyne D., Fadlon I., Ramnath S. P., & Tong P. K.
briefs.summary: Using tax records and age eligibility rules, the paper shows that widowed households cut labor supply sharply when survivors benefits begin, implying that the program provides real liquidity and insurance.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is useful when evaluating Social Security as a household balance-sheet stabilizer rather than just a retirement transfer.

briefs.title: Dynamic Spending Responses to Wealth Shocks: Evidence from Quasi Lotteries on the Stock Market
briefs.authors: Andersen A. L., Johannesen N., & Sheridan A.
briefs.summary: The authors use lottery-like variation in stock gains to show that household spending rises quickly after portfolio windfalls, with responses accumulating over several years rather than one month.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want an estimate of how stock-market gains actually feed into consumer spending instead of staying inside brokerage accounts.

briefs.title: Home Price Expectations and Spending: Evidence from a Field Experiment
briefs.authors: Chopra F., Roth C., & Wohlfart J.
briefs.summary: A U.S. field experiment finds that higher expected home-price growth barely changes homeowner spending but leads renters to cut spending as future housing costs look harder to reach.
briefs.whyItMatters: This separates owner and renter responses in a way that standard housing-wealth stories often blur together.

briefs.title: Homeownership and Portfolio Choice over the Generations
briefs.summary: Paz-Pardo shows that riskier earnings paths for younger cohorts help explain weaker homeownership and lower wealth accumulation relative to earlier generations.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a housing explanation that ties affordability to labor-income risk instead of prices alone.

briefs.title: Borrowing and Spending in the Money: Debt Substitution and the Cash-Out Refinance Channel of Monetary Policy
briefs.authors: Anenberg E., Scharlemann T., & van Straelen E.
briefs.summary: The paper finds that when mortgage rates rise and cash-out refinancing falls, households often substitute toward other borrowing, leaving total new borrowing less sensitive than refinance counts suggest.
briefs.whyItMatters: This narrows the gap between mortgage headlines and actual household credit behavior during rate shocks.

briefs.title: Why Do Retired Households Draw Down Their Wealth So Slowly?
briefs.authors: French E., Jones J. B., & McGee R.
briefs.summary: French, Jones, and McGee review the evidence on why many retirees spend principal slowly, emphasizing longevity risk, medical-cost risk, housing, and bequest motives.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a compact reference for why retirees often behave very differently from simple spend-down models.

briefs.title: Household Finance
briefs.authors: Gomes F., Haliassos M., & Ramadorai T.
briefs.summary: This survey maps the modern household-finance literature across saving, portfolios, insurance, retirement, mortgages, credit, financial literacy, and advice.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a high-level entry point when you want one rigorous source that connects the main subfields on the shelf.

briefs.title: Cyclical Attention to Saving
briefs.summary: Macaulay shows that savers pay closer attention to deposit products during downturns, improving the rates they earn and amplifying the macro effects of shocks.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives a rare bridge between household attention mistakes and actual cash-yield outcomes in savings markets.

briefs.title: Public Education and Intergenerational Housing Wealth Effects
briefs.authors: Gilraine M., Graham J., & Zheng A.
briefs.summary: The authors show that local house-price gains can improve school quality and then raise children's future earnings, creating an intergenerational housing-wealth channel.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want evidence that housing wealth can shape long-run family outcomes beyond resale gains alone.

briefs.title: Housing Wealth and Consumption: The Role of Heterogeneous Credit Constraints
briefs.authors: Aruoba S. B., Elul R., & Kalemli-Ozcan S.
briefs.summary: Using individual-level data, the paper argues that much of the spending response to falling house prices came from tighter credit constraints, not a pure housing-wealth effect.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate liquidity stress from paper wealth when thinking about housing crashes and household consumption.

briefs.title: Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2025
briefs.authors: Dimson E., Marsh P., & Staunton M.
briefs.summary: This yearbook uses 125 years of data across 35 markets to show how stocks, bonds, bills, and inflation behaved over full cycles, with a fresh emphasis on diversification in a more concentrated market era.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want long-run return history that puts current market concentration and diversification claims in context.

briefs.title: The Global Findex Database 2025
briefs.summary: The 2025 Global Findex updates how adults in 141 economies save, borrow, pay, and handle financial shocks, while adding globally comparable measures of digital access and safety.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the best broad scorecards for how households actually use financial services, not just how economists model them.

briefs.title: 2025 Global Market Accessibility Review Report
briefs.summary: MSCI reviews how easy it is for global investors to enter, exit, and operate across developed, emerging, frontier, and standalone equity markets, using investor-focused accessibility criteria.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when you want a concrete view of which markets are investable in practice, not just attractive on paper.

briefs.title: Global Financial Stability Report, April 2025: Enhancing Resilience amid Uncertainty
briefs.summary: The IMF argues that high valuations, leverage in nonbank finance, and sovereign debt stress left global markets more fragile as policy uncertainty and geopolitical risk rose in 2025.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a current cross-market map of where funding stress and bond-market instability could spill into portfolios.

briefs.title: Financial Advice and Investor Beliefs: Experimental Evidence on Active vs. Passive Strategies
briefs.summary: In a randomized experiment, the authors show that investors rate advice more favorably when it matches their priors, yet many still update their beliefs after seeing passive or active arguments.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why good evidence alone does not settle the active versus passive debate for most investors.

briefs.title: Investor Memory and Biased Beliefs: Evidence from the Field
briefs.authors: Jiang Z., Liu H., Peng C., & Yan H.
briefs.summary: Using survey and transaction data, the paper finds that investors recall prior market experiences selectively, and those memories shape both return expectations and trading decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a concrete mechanism for why recent market experiences can distort belief formation and risk-taking.

briefs.title: Higher-Order Beliefs and Risky Asset Holdings
briefs.summary: The authors distinguish between what investors expect the market to do and what they think other investors expect, then show those higher-order beliefs affect risky asset allocations in different ways.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is useful if you want a cleaner explanation for why sentiment can move portfolios even when first-order return expectations look similar.

briefs.title: A Housing Portfolio Channel of QE Transmission
briefs.authors: Boddin D., te Kaat D. M., Ma C., & Rebucci A.
briefs.summary: This paper finds that quantitative easing can push households with existing bond wealth to rotate toward second homes, affecting both house prices and local rental supply.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to trace how central-bank policy can reach property markets through portfolio rebalancing rather than mortgages alone.

briefs.title: Convenience Yields and Exchange Rate Puzzles
briefs.authors: Jiang Z., Krishnamurthy A., Lustig H., & Sun J.
briefs.summary: The paper ties exchange-rate behavior to safe-asset demand for dollar bonds, arguing that convenience yields help explain why currencies often disconnect from standard macro fundamentals.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives fixed-income and macro investors a cleaner way to connect Treasury demand, currency moves, and risk premia.

briefs.title: Building Costs and House Prices
briefs.summary: Looking across long U.S. housing history, the authors find that construction costs explain less of house-price behavior than many market narratives assume.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to separate land scarcity, regulation, and demand shocks from the simpler claim that homes just cost more to build.

briefs.title: Housing Supply and Housing Affordability
briefs.summary: This review pulls together the evidence on housing supply constraints, showing why affordability has worsened as regulations and land-use frictions have become more binding.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a strong entry point if you want the affordability debate framed around supply mechanics instead of slogans.

briefs.title: Tax Preferences and Housing Affordability: Explorations using a Life-Cycle Model
briefs.summary: The model tests how owner-occupied housing tax breaks, mortgage-interest deductions, and alternative credits affect ownership rates, affordability, and welfare across households.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to evaluate housing tax policy as a distributional tool rather than treating all subsidies as automatically pro-homeownership.

briefs.title: On the Optimality of Deferred Public Annuities
briefs.summary: The authors show that when retirees lack private annuities, an optimal public retirement income path can look like a deferred annuity that starts later and then pays steadily.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a useful framework for thinking about Social Security timing and late-life income design as insurance, not just income smoothing.

briefs.title: The Unintended Consequences of Rebalancing
briefs.authors: Harvey C. R., Mazzoleni M. G., & Melone A.
briefs.summary: This paper argues that routine institutional rebalancing moves prices in predictable ways and creates measurable execution costs that other traders can exploit.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you treat rebalancing as harmless housekeeping rather than a trading decision with market impact.

briefs.title: What Hundreds of Economic News Events Say About Belief Overreaction in the Stock Market
briefs.authors: Bianchi F., Ludvigson S. C., & Ma S.
briefs.summary: Combining structural asset pricing with machine learning, the authors argue that investors systematically overreact to several kinds of economic news shocks.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want evidence that market mispricing can show up in how investors process news, not only in slow-moving anomalies.

briefs.title: The How and Why of Household Reactions to Income Shocks
briefs.authors: Colarieti R., Mei P., & Stantcheva S.
briefs.summary: Using new survey evidence, the paper estimates how households split income shocks across spending, saving, and debt paydown, then studies the reasoning behind those choices.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when you want household-finance evidence that explains both the observed response and the decision logic behind it.

briefs.title: Fixed and Variable Longevity Annuities in Defined Contribution Plans: Optimal Retirement Portfolios Taking Social Security into Account
briefs.authors: Horneff V., Maurer R., & Mitchell O. S.
briefs.summary: The paper compares fixed and variable longevity annuities inside defined-contribution plans and finds that deferred annuity access can improve retirement outcomes once Social Security is included.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when evaluating whether annuities belong inside retirement plans rather than being treated as an after-market purchase.

briefs.title: Passive Investing and the Rise of Mega-Firms
briefs.authors: Jiang H., Vayanos D., & Zheng L.
briefs.summary: The authors argue that flows into passive funds disproportionately lift the prices of the largest companies, helping explain the rise of mega-cap dominance.
briefs.whyItMatters: This sharpens the passive-investing debate by focusing on market-structure effects, not only fees and manager skill.

briefs.title: NAR Settlement, House Prices, and Consumer Welfare
briefs.authors: Buchak G., Matvos G., Piskorski T., & Seru A.
briefs.summary: Modeling the post-settlement real-estate market, the authors argue that lower broker commissions can raise house values even while improving welfare overall.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand why cutting transaction costs does not automatically make housing more affordable for buyers.

briefs.title: Monetary Transmission Through Bank Securities Portfolios
briefs.authors: Greenwald D., Krainer J., & Paul P.
briefs.summary: Using supervisory data, the authors show that losses on banks' bond portfolios during the 2022-23 tightening cycle reduced credit supply, especially where rate risk was unhedged.
briefs.whyItMatters: This ties bond-duration risk directly to lending capacity, which matters for both financial stability and rate-sensitive asset pricing.

briefs.title: Playing Catch-up with Health Savings
briefs.authors: Berman J., Bloomfield A., & Slavov S.
briefs.summary: Using tax records, the authors show that HSA catch-up contribution rules meaningfully raise saving among households near the cap and do not appear to crowd out retirement contributions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for understanding whether HSA tax incentives genuinely increase saving or just rearrange money already being set aside.

briefs.title: Optimizing Retirement Financial Strategies: Integrating Annuities, Defined Contribution Plans, and Long-Term Care Costs
briefs.authors: Horneff V., Maurer R., Mitchell O. S., & Odenbreit J.
briefs.summary: This paper models retirement drawdown decisions with taxes, required minimum distributions, annuities, bequests, and long-term-care shocks in one framework.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want retirement-income research that treats late-life care risk as a central planning input rather than an afterthought.

briefs.title: The Mortgage Debt Channel of Monetary Policy when Mortgages are Liquid
briefs.authors: Elias M., Gillitzer C., Kaplan G., La Cava G., & Prasad N. V.
briefs.summary: Using Australian bank-transaction data, the authors find that large payment shocks on adjustable-rate mortgages changed spending much less than expected because borrowers had redraw buffers.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a useful caution against assuming that mortgage-rate resets translate mechanically into household spending cuts.

briefs.title: Glass Box Machine Learning and Corporate Bond Returns
briefs.authors: Bell S., Kakhbod A., Lettau M., & Nazemi A.
briefs.summary: Bell, Kakhbod, Lettau, and Nazemi use interpretable machine-learning models on bond characteristics and macro data to predict corporate bond returns. They show that the strongest signals come from term-structure conditions, macro uncertainty, and interactions that matter more for smaller issuers and longer maturities.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a bond-return model that does more than sort by duration and credit spread.

briefs.title: One Factor to Bind the Cross-Section of Returns
briefs.authors: Borri N., Chetverikov D., Liu Y., & Tsyvinski A.
briefs.summary: Borri, Chetverikov, Liu, and Tsyvinski propose a non-linear single-factor model that fits the cross-section of returns across 171 major assets better than many multi-factor setups. The paper argues that what looks like many separate factors may partly be one common pricing force expressed nonlinearly.
briefs.whyItMatters: A sharp challenge to the idea that every new anomaly needs its own factor.

briefs.title: The Distributional Effects of Asset Returns
briefs.summary: Fernandez-Villaverde and Levintal estimate a model in which households hold different portfolios and earn different returns, then trace how weaker returns reshape wealth and consumption shares. They find that lower expected returns can raise inequality between the top tail and the rest by hitting broad wealth accumulation harder.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good for understanding why return assumptions matter for both retirement math and wealth concentration.

briefs.title: Aggregation, Liquidity, and Asset Prices with Incomplete Markets
briefs.authors: Di Tella S., Hebert B. M., & Kurlat P.
briefs.summary: Di Tella, Hebert, and Kurlat show how trading frictions and household liquidity needs can explain high demand for safe assets, a flat security market line, and a sizable liquidity premium. The paper ties everyday cash constraints directly to broad asset-pricing patterns.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when the usual split between household finance and asset pricing feels too clean.

briefs.title: Steering a Ship in Illiquid Waters: Active Management of Passive Funds
briefs.authors: Koont N., Ma Y., Pastor L., & Zeng Y.
briefs.summary: Koont, Ma, Pastor, and Zeng show that corporate bond ETFs do not simply hold their indexes mechanically. They actively adjust creation and redemption baskets to manage liquidity, which can help arbitrage in normal periods but can also worsen liquidity strains during large flow shocks.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful corrective to the idea that passive fixed-income vehicles stay purely passive under stress.

briefs.title: Subjective Income Expectations and Household Debt Cycles
briefs.authors: D'Acunto F., Weber M., & Yin X.
briefs.summary: D'Acunto, Weber, and Yin match transactions, credit, and survey data to show that households extrapolate recent income shocks too far into the future. That optimism and pessimism then feed directly into spending, borrowing, and default cycles.
briefs.whyItMatters: Strong evidence that household debt booms are partly about expectations errors, not only rates or wages.

briefs.title: Why Do Index Funds Have Market Power? Quantifying Frictions in the Index Fund Market
briefs.authors: Brown Z. Y., Egan M. L., Jeon J., Jin C., & Wu A. A.
briefs.summary: Brown, Egan, Jeon, Jin, and Wu study why nearly identical index funds can keep charging different fees. Their model points to inertia and information frictions, with only a small share of households updating index holdings in a typical month.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you assume competition should automatically crush index fund fees.

briefs.title: The Rise of Factor Investing: "Passive" Security Design and Market Implications
briefs.authors: Cong L. W., Huang S., & Xu D.
briefs.summary: Cong, Huang, and Xu treat factor funds and related vehicles as securities designed to package common exposures efficiently. They argue that these products can improve incorporation of systematic information into prices while also raising co-movement and changing liquidity patterns.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good bridge between ETF product design and the broader debate about market structure.

briefs.title: Longevity, Health and Housing Risks Management in Retirement
briefs.summary: Michaud and St. Amour model why households use so few annuities, reverse mortgages, and long-term care policies even when these products address obvious retirement risks. They find that risk aversion, bequest motives, housing substitutability, and inertia explain much of the reluctance.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a more realistic view of why retirement-risk products stay niche.

briefs.title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Housing Wealth
briefs.authors: Daysal N. M., Lovenheim M. F., & Wasser D. N.
briefs.summary: Daysal, Lovenheim, and Wasser use Danish administrative data to trace how shifts in parents' housing wealth affect children's later balance sheets. They find meaningful pass-through into both overall wealth and later housing wealth, especially when shocks occur early in childhood.
briefs.whyItMatters: Shows that housing wealth is not only a current asset. It also shapes the next generation's starting line.

briefs.title: Consumer Credit Reporting Data
briefs.authors: Gibbs C. N., Guttman-Kenney B., Lee D., Nelson S. T., van der Klaauw W., & Wang J.
briefs.summary: Gibbs, Guttman-Kenney, Lee, Nelson, van der Klaauw, and Wang explain what consumer credit bureau data actually measure and how researchers can use them to study borrowing, distress, mobility, and credit access. The paper is both a methods guide and a map of the modern household credit dataset.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth keeping close if you rely on credit-score or delinquency research and want to know what is really inside the data.

briefs.title: Credit Scores: Performance and Equity
