briefs.summary: Albanesi and Vamossy benchmark a standard credit score against a machine-learning default model and find meaningful misclassification, especially among lower-score borrowers. The gains from a better model are largest for young, lower-income, and minority borrowers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to separate credit risk measurement from the fairness claims built on top of it.

briefs.title: Taxes and the Revaluation of Household Wealth
briefs.summary: Wolff recalculates household wealth after netting out deferred taxes on retirement accounts, capital gains, defined-benefit pensions, and Social Security. The exercise shows that pre-tax net worth can materially overstate what households can actually spend or pass on.
briefs.whyItMatters: A reminder that headline net worth is not the same thing as after-tax usable wealth.

briefs.title: Book-Value Wealth Taxation, Capital Income Taxation, and Innovation
briefs.authors: Guvenen F., Kambourov G., Kuruscu B., & Ocampo-Diaz S.
briefs.summary: Guvenen, Kambourov, Kuruscu, and Ocampo-Diaz build a model in which heterogeneous returns and collateral constraints make capital allocation inefficient. In that setting, a wealth tax can push capital away from low-productivity uses and toward higher-productivity firms.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the serious theoretical case for why wealth taxation can be about allocation, not only redistribution.

briefs.title: Putting the "Finance" into "Public Finance": A Theory of Capital Gains Taxation
briefs.authors: Aguiar M. A., Moll B., & Scheuer F.
briefs.summary: Aguiar, Moll, and Scheuer study capital gains taxation in a world where asset prices move for discount-rate reasons, not only cash-flow changes. They argue that once price movements matter, optimal taxation looks different from both classic income-tax logic and simple mark-to-market wealth-tax proposals.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when tax debates treat asset-price gains as if they were just delayed wages.

briefs.title: The Gender Gap in Housing Returns
briefs.summary: Goldsmith-Pinkham and Shue show that single women earn lower housing returns than single men, with much of the gap tied to transaction timing, location, and execution prices. Because housing is the dominant asset for many households, the return gap compounds into a meaningful wealth gap over time.
briefs.whyItMatters: This connects housing-market mechanics directly to long-run wealth inequality.

briefs.title: Global Wealth Report 2024
briefs.summary: UBS reports that global household wealth rebounded 4.2 percent in U.S. dollar terms in 2023 after the 2022 drop, with recoveries across regions and continued movement up the wealth distribution. The report also emphasizes wealth mobility and an expected USD 83.5 trillion intergenerational transfer over the coming decades.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful high-level map of where household wealth is recovering, concentrating, and moving next.

briefs.title: Global Financial Stability Report, October 2024
briefs.summary: The IMF's October 2024 GFSR argues that calm markets are masking a continued buildup of vulnerability through high debt, stretched asset valuations, leverage in nonbanks, and commercial real estate strain. It also links elevated macro uncertainty to fatter downside tails for markets, credit, and growth.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when portfolio risk looks tame in prices but not in the balance-sheet plumbing underneath.

briefs.title: Social Interaction Intensity and Investor Behavior
briefs.authors: Gelman M., Hirshleifer D., Levi Y., & Reiter-Gavish L.
briefs.summary: Gelman, Hirshleifer, Levi, and Reiter-Gavish use local soccer-game density as a measure of social interaction and find that stronger in-person interaction amplifies buying, risk-taking, and trading volume. The effect is strongest in riskier stocks and in places where investors look more alike.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want evidence that investor herding can intensify through ordinary social contact, not only through screens.

briefs.title: Household Debt Balances Continue Steady Increase; Delinquency Transition Rates Remain Elevated for Auto and Credit Cards
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The New York Fed reports that total household debt reached USD 18.04 trillion in Q4 2024, with mortgage balances still rising and serious delinquency pressure remaining elevated in auto loans and credit cards. The release is a concise snapshot of where household leverage is still building strain.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when strong headline consumption data hide where credit stress is already reappearing on household balance sheets.

briefs.title: The Offshore World According to FATCA: New Evidence on the Foreign Wealth of U.S. Households
briefs.authors: Johannesen N., Reck D., Risch M., Slemrod J., Guyton J., & Langetieg P.
briefs.summary: Using FATCA account-level filings, the authors estimate that U.S. taxpayers hold about $4 trillion in foreign accounts, with almost half in tax havens and extremely high ownership rates at the very top of the income distribution.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a modern measure of offshore wealth, tax-haven concentration, and what cross-border reporting changed.

briefs.title: Households' Response to the Wealth Effects of Inflation
briefs.authors: Schnorpfeil P., Weber M., & Hackethal A.
briefs.summary: Combining bank data with an information experiment, the paper shows that many households understand inflation erodes cash but miss how it also erodes nominal debt, and that learning this changes both spending and debt choices.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong guide to how inflation affects behavior through beliefs about real wealth, not only through prices.

briefs.title: Financial Windfalls, Portfolio Allocations, and Risk Preferences
briefs.authors: Briggs J. S., Cesarini D., Lee S. C., Lindqvist E., & Ostling R.
briefs.summary: Using randomized Swedish lottery prizes, the authors find that a $100,000 windfall reduces the risky share of household portfolios by about 5 percentage points instead of pushing winners toward more risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when thinking about whether bigger balances automatically make investors more aggressive. The answer here is often no.

briefs.title: The Economics of Financial Stress
briefs.authors: Sergeyev D., Lian C., & Gorodnichenko Y.
briefs.summary: Survey evidence and a dynamic model tie financial stress to binding constraints, lower cognitive bandwidth, weaker work outcomes, and the risk of getting stuck in high-stress low-wealth states.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives a disciplined framework for why household strain can worsen economic decisions instead of merely reflecting them.

briefs.title: Why Do Couples and Singles Save during Retirement? Household Heterogeneity and its Aggregate Implications
briefs.authors: De Nardi M., French E., Jones J. B., & McGee R.
briefs.summary: The model shows that retired households save for different reasons depending on marital status, income, age, medical expense risk, and bequest motives, with richer couples saving heavily for bequests.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good context for why retirement wealth can stay high long after labor income ends, especially in upper-balance households.

briefs.title: Asset Demand and Real Interest Rates
briefs.authors: Beaudry P., Kartashova K., & Meh C.
briefs.summary: The authors link falling real rates to a substantial increase in demand for retirement wealth and show how retirement motives and Social Security shape asset demand across income groups.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful bridge between secular-rate debates and the portfolio behavior of households saving for retirement.

briefs.title: Inflation's Impact on American Households
briefs.authors: Altig D., Auerbach A. J., Eidschun E. F., Kotlikoff L. J., & Ye V. Y.
briefs.summary: Running Survey of Consumer Finances households through a lifetime fiscal model, the paper finds that a permanent jump from zero to 10 percent inflation cuts median lifetime spending by 6.82 percent, with smaller damage when COLAs are less delayed.
briefs.whyItMatters: This quantifies how inflation hits households through taxes, transfers, and benefit indexing rather than only through market prices.

briefs.title: The Impact of Unconditional Cash Transfers on Consumption and Household Balance Sheets: Experimental Evidence from Two US States
briefs.authors: Bartik A. W., Rhodes E., Broockman D. E., Krause P. K., Miller S., & Vivalt E.
briefs.summary: In a three-year experiment, $1,000 monthly transfers lifted spending by at least $300 per month, improved self-reported financial health and credit scores, but did not create durable net-worth gains because higher debt offset modest asset growth.
briefs.whyItMatters: A concrete look at what large cash infusions change first: consumption, mobility, and felt financial slack more than long-run balance-sheet strength.

briefs.title: Household Climate Finance: Theory and Survey Data on Safe and Risky Green Assets
briefs.authors: Aron-Dine S., Beutel J., Piazzesi M., & Schneider M.
briefs.summary: Using survey data and an asset-pricing model, the paper finds unmet demand for green deposit accounts and argues that beliefs about green equity returns, more than pure taste, help explain the current greenium.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want to separate values-based investing from return expectations and product design.

briefs.title: The Extraordinary Rise in the Wealth of Older American Households
briefs.summary: Using Survey of Consumer Finances data from 1983 to 2022, Wolff shows that households aged 75 and older gained wealth share sharply, driven mainly by homeownership, stock ownership, and lower relative mortgage burdens.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a compact explanation for why younger households have fallen further behind older owners in the recent wealth cycle.

briefs.title: Credit Access in the United States
briefs.authors: Bakker T. J., DeLuca S., English E. A., Fogel J. S., Hendren N., & Herbst D.
briefs.summary: Linked administrative data show that by age 25, Black adults, people from low-income families, and people raised in the Southeast or Appalachia already face materially worse credit scores, thinner access, and heavier use of high-cost alternatives.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong empirical baseline for how early credit gaps become long-lived household finance gaps.

briefs.title: Credit Scores and Inequality across the Life Cycle
briefs.authors: Chatterjee S., Corbae D., Dempsey K. P., & Rios-Rull J.-V.
briefs.summary: The paper models why credit scores spread out with age alongside income and consumption inequality, and uses that framework to test how data-rich screening or legal limits on adverse information can change access.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful for understanding credit scores as a dynamic inequality mechanism instead of a static household snapshot.

briefs.title: Portfolio Choice and Settlement Frictions: A Theory of Endogenous Convenience Yields
briefs.summary: The model shows how settlement frictions create convenience yields and shape liquidity premia, overnight funding conditions, and optimal holdings of liquid assets.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need a cleaner explanation for why liquidity services can matter as much as headline yield in portfolio design.

briefs.title: Practical Finance: An Approximate Solution to Lifecycle Portfolio Choice
briefs.authors: Choi J. J., Liu C., & Liu P.
briefs.summary: This paper offers spreadsheet-friendly approximations to lifecycle portfolio choice that stay within 0.06 percent of the optimal solution across 5,103 parameter sets.
briefs.whyItMatters: A rare bridge between academic lifecycle models and something an advisor or investor can actually implement.

briefs.title: Nonpayment and Eviction in the Rental Housing Market
briefs.authors: Humphries J. E., Nelson S. T., Nguyen D. L., van Dijk W., & Waldinger D. C.
briefs.summary: Lease-level rental ledgers show that landlords often tolerate missed payments, that eviction filings cost roughly two to three months of rent, and that broad procedural delays prevent fewer evictions than targeted financial incentives.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a grounded picture of rental distress, landlord tradeoffs, and which interventions actually change housing outcomes.

briefs.title: Housing Betas
briefs.summary: Piazzesi documents that stock and housing cash flows move together but their long-horizon returns changed from negative comovement before the Global Financial Crisis to positive comovement afterward, then explains the shift with segmentation and credit links.
briefs.whyItMatters: This sharpens how housing behaves as an investment asset rather than just a consumption good.

briefs.title: Wealth and Insurance Choices: Evidence from US Households
briefs.authors: Gropper M. J. & Kuhnen C. M.
briefs.summary: Contrary to standard theory, administrative data show that wealthier households hold better life and property insurance coverage, and standard explanations such as pricing, literacy, and legal risk explain little of the gap.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good reminder that lower-wealth households often face weaker protection exactly where they are most fragile.

briefs.title: A Family Affair: The Effects of College on Parent and Student Finances
briefs.authors: Bhargava P., Black S. E., Denning J. T., Fairlie R. W., & Gurantz O.
briefs.summary: Linked aid and credit records show that college costs reshape family borrowing, with lower-income parents taking on more education debt and higher prices pushing some families toward home-equity borrowing and worse delinquency outcomes.
briefs.whyItMatters: This captures how education finance spills into household balance sheets well beyond the student borrower.

briefs.title: Dynamic Optimization Meets Budgeting: Unraveling Financial Complexities
briefs.summary: Experimental evidence shows that people struggle with multi-period consumption-saving choices even in clean settings, tend to over-smooth consumption, and rarely reoptimize once an initial plan is set.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong explanation for why households often underuse compounding, inflation adjustment, and long-horizon planning tools.

briefs.title: The Complexity of Economic Decisions
briefs.summary: The paper formalizes complexity as the productivity of thinking about a decision and shows how more components, weaker dominance, and limited cognition create larger mistakes in tasks like saving, taxes, and forecasting.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for understanding why some financial choices stay hard even when information is available and incentives are clear.

briefs.title: Consumption Wedges: Measuring and Diagnosing Distortions
briefs.authors: Indarte S., Kluender R., Malmendier U., & Stepner M.
briefs.summary: Using transaction records and expectation surveys, the authors measure how far real households deviate from frictionless consumption plans and separate mistakes tied to liquidity frictions, behavioral biases, and expectation errors.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives a cleaner way to diagnose whether household money mistakes come from cash constraints, beliefs, or behavior.

briefs.title: How Do Interest Rates Affect Consumption? Household Debt and the Role of Asset Prices
briefs.authors: Foulis A. K., Hazell J., Mian A. R., & Tracey B.
briefs.summary: Using millions of UK mortgage resets, the paper finds that rate cuts raise spending mostly by lifting house prices and collateral values, while lower monthly debt service does less work than standard cash-flow stories imply.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand why rates move household demand through balance sheets as much as through borrowing costs.

briefs.title: Till the IRS Do Us Part: (Optimal) Taxation of Households
briefs.authors: Holter H. A., Krueger D., & Stepanchuk S.
briefs.summary: The model compares joint household taxation with progressive individual taxation and finds that taxing spouses separately can expand labor supply, raise human capital, and materially shift the revenue-maximizing tax schedule.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong reference for how tax-unit design changes both family incentives and the fiscal room governments can create.

briefs.title: A Macroeconomic Perspective on Stock Market Valuation Ratios
briefs.authors: Atkeson A., Heathcote J., & Perri F.
briefs.summary: The paper argues that unusually high U.S. valuation ratios can persist when labor takes a smaller share of output and corporate investment stays weak, even without assuming lower discount rates or faster growth.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a disciplined answer to whether elevated market multiples automatically imply a near-term mean reversion.

briefs.title: Dementia and Long-run Trajectories in Household Finances
briefs.authors: Li J., McGarry K. M., Nicholas L. H., & Skinner J. S.
briefs.summary: Health and Retirement Study data show that household wealth starts diverging about six years before a dementia diagnosis, with the evidence pointing to impaired financial decision-making rather than higher medical spending or deliberate spend-down.
briefs.whyItMatters: It sharpens the case for earlier oversight and simpler financial systems as cognition declines.

briefs.title: Experiences, Expectations, and Asset Prices
briefs.summary: Nagel reviews evidence that investors overweight the market and inflation regimes they have personally lived through, creating age-dependent beliefs that feed into return predictability, valuation swings, and long-run real-rate shifts.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a concise bridge between household experience, investor expectations, and market pricing.

briefs.title: Lands of Opportunity: Differences in the Geography of Wealth and Income Mobility in the United States
briefs.authors: Binder A. J., Risch M., & Voorheis J. L.
briefs.summary: Using linked survey and administrative data, the authors build county-level estimates of wealth mobility, housing wealth mobility, and homeownership mobility and show that the geography of wealth persistence differs from the geography of income persistence.
briefs.whyItMatters: It adds local structure to the question of where families actually build wealth, not just where they earn more.

briefs.title: Risky Insurance: Life-Cycle Insurance Portfolio Choice with Incomplete Markets
briefs.authors: Briggs J. S., Rogers C., & Tonetti C.
briefs.summary: Survey evidence and a life-cycle model show that households see real nonpayment risk in annuities, life insurance, and long-term care insurance, and those beliefs materially suppress ownership even before price loads are considered.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful explanation for why insurance markets stay thin even when the underlying risks are large.

briefs.title: Intermediaries and Asset Prices
briefs.summary: Haddad and Muir review how dealer and institutional balance-sheet constraints help explain excess volatility, cross-asset dislocations, and the cross section of expected returns in modern markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a compact way to update a household-risk view of markets with the balance-sheet capacity of intermediaries.

briefs.title: Quick-Fixing: Near-Rationality in Consumption and Savings Behavior
briefs.authors: Andre P., Flynn J. P., Nikolakoudis G., & Sastry K.
briefs.summary: The paper shows that many households use simple adjustment rules after income shocks, such as fully saving or fully spending small shocks, because re-optimizing a full consumption plan is costly and rarely worth the effort.
briefs.whyItMatters: It explains why rough budgeting rules can be common without implying that households are wildly irrational.

briefs.title: Monetary Policy and Housing Overvaluation
briefs.authors: Biljanovska N., Espuny Diaz E., Kermani A., & Mano R.
briefs.summary: Using metro-level U.S. data, the paper finds that house prices in overvalued markets react more strongly to monetary shocks, with investor demand falling especially hard after tightening in places where price-to-rent ratios were already stretched.
briefs.whyItMatters: This shows why the same rate move can cool one housing market modestly and another one sharply.

briefs.title: The Prestakes of Stock Market Investing
briefs.authors: Bianchi F., Lee D. Q., Ludvigson S. C., & Ma S.
briefs.summary: Machine-learning benchmarks are used to identify predictable expectation errors in investors, analysts, and professionals, with those errors spiking during turbulent markets and linking to defensive alpha opportunities.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a concrete test of where market beliefs depart from disciplined information processing.

briefs.title: Heterogeneous Beliefs, Asset Prices, and Business Cycles
briefs.authors: Bigio S., Silva D., & Zilberman E.
briefs.summary: The model links extrapolative investor beliefs to higher equity volatility, a larger equity premium, and more cyclical hiring by making firm discount rates depend on the wealth-weighted beliefs of market participants.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong framework for seeing optimism and pessimism as drivers of both prices and real economic swings.

briefs.title: Externalities and the Taxation of Top Earners
briefs.summary: Kleven derives top-tax formulas that explicitly account for whether very high earners generate innovation spillovers or rent-extraction losses, and shows that those externalities can materially shift the efficient top rate.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a sharper way to discuss top-bracket tax design than debates that only focus on labor-supply elasticities.

briefs.title: Pricing Protection: Credit Scores, Disaster Risk, and Home Insurance Affordability
briefs.authors: Blonz J., Hossain M., Keys B. J., Mulder P., & Weill J. A.
briefs.summary: Drawing on 70 million policies, the authors show that homeowners with low credit pay insurance premiums about 24 percent above otherwise identical high-credit households, a gap comparable to the effect of disaster risk itself.
briefs.whyItMatters: It shows that home affordability is shaped by insurance pricing and credit scoring, not just mortgage rates and house prices.

briefs.title: Firm Emissions and Credit Allocation
briefs.authors: Gu G. W., Hale G., Sharma B., & Wu J.
briefs.summary: Bank-loan data from the U.S., EU, and Denmark show only limited evidence that lenders actively steer credit toward greener borrowers, with much of the observed shift reflecting firm growth rather than bank stewardship.
briefs.whyItMatters: This matters if you want to know whether credit markets are genuinely reallocating capital for the transition or mostly following firm scale.

briefs.title: Monetary Policy According to Households: Perceptions, Reactions and Channels
briefs.authors: Grigoli F., Sandri D., Gorodnichenko Y., & Coibion O.
briefs.summary: Survey experiments with more than 25,000 U.S. households show that people often read higher policy rates as higher future inflation, and those inflation beliefs then drive lower planned consumption and portfolio shifts.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good reminder that monetary policy works through household interpretation, not just textbook transmission channels.

briefs.title: Bank Fees and Household Financial Well-Being
briefs.authors: Pagel M., Sridhar S., & Williams E.
briefs.summary: Transaction-level data from major banks show that removing NSF fees lowered charges across the income distribution, but looser overdraft rules produced broader downstream gains mainly for households with more income and liquidity.
briefs.whyItMatters: This separates fee relief that changes the line item from fee reform that actually improves household resilience.

briefs.title: The Financial Consequences of Being Denied Benefit Access
briefs.authors: Homonoff T., Lee M. S., & Meckel K.
briefs.summary: Linking SNAP intake variation to credit files, the paper shows that households denied benefits for procedural reasons take on more debt, miss more payments, and suffer lower credit scores.
briefs.whyItMatters: It shows that administrative friction is not a paperwork issue alone. It directly weakens household balance sheets.

briefs.title: Payment-Chain Crises
briefs.authors: Bigio S., Mendez E., & Van Patten D.
briefs.summary: The model studies what happens when firms delay payments until upstream cash arrives, showing how credit access and interest rates determine the size of payment-chain networks and the resulting amplification of downturns.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for understanding why fragile payment plumbing can turn ordinary funding stress into a broader economic shock.

briefs.title: Global Financial Stability Report, October 2025: Shifting Ground beneath the Calm
briefs.summary: The IMF argues that stretched asset prices, sovereign borrowing pressure, and the growing role of nonbank intermediaries left global bond and funding markets vulnerable even while headline volatility looked calm in late 2025.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a cross-market read on how apparently quiet conditions can still conceal rate, rollover, and liquidity risk.

briefs.title: Global Financial Stability Report, April 2026: Global Financial Markets Confront the War in the Middle East and Amplification Risks
briefs.summary: The April 2026 IMF stability report tracks how war risk, higher energy prices, sovereign refinancing strain, and fragile cross-border portfolio flows can turn market volatility into wider funding stress.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a strong map of how geopolitical shocks move through bonds, currencies, and nonbank balance sheets rather than staying isolated to one headline.

briefs.title: Financial Stability Report - November 2025
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The Federal Reserve flags elevated asset valuations, heavy hedge-fund leverage, commercial real-estate refinancing pressure, and persistent Treasury-market fragility even after the April 2025 volatility episode faded.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful U.S.-specific check on where rates, liquidity, and leverage could still hit household portfolios and credit conditions.

briefs.title: Financial Stability Report - May 2026
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The May 2026 Fed stability report says household debt stayed manageable in aggregate, but high hedge-fund leverage, private-credit strain, and still-thin Treasury liquidity kept the system exposed to shocks.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading when you need the Fed view on whether strong household balance sheets are enough to offset system-level funding and rate risk.

briefs.title: Global Wealth Report 2025
briefs.summary: UBS reports that global household wealth kept rising in 2024, with the United States and China still dominating the wealth base and the coming intergenerational transfer becoming more central to who controls assets next.
briefs.whyItMatters: A practical macro shelf item for tracking where wealth is accumulating, how concentrated it is, and how transfer dynamics may reshape portfolios and advice.

briefs.title: World Wealth Report 2026
briefs.summary: Capgemini finds that high-net-worth wealth and population both jumped sharply in 2025 on equity-market gains, while affluent clients increasingly demanded broader product access and more personalized advice.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives a current read on where millionaire wealth is growing and how wealth-management demand is shifting beyond simple asset gathering.

briefs.title: SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2025
briefs.authors: Ganti A. R., Di Gioia D., Didio N., & Flaherty L.
briefs.summary: S&P Dow Jones reports that 79 percent of active large-cap U.S. funds trailed the S&P 500 in 2025, with weak results across most bond categories as well.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is current scorekeeping on how often active managers still fail to clear a simple benchmark after fees and style drift.

briefs.title: SPIVA Europe Mid-Year 2025
briefs.authors: Edwards T., Voros B., Di Gioia D., & Didio N.
briefs.summary: The Europe scorecard finds that most actively managed equity and fixed-income funds domiciled in Europe still underperformed their category benchmarks through the first half of 2025 despite big regional dispersion.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the active-versus-passive argument tested outside the U.S. rather than assumed to travel unchanged.

briefs.title: Unlocking Mortgage Lock-In: Equilibrium Effects in a Spatial Housing Ladder Model
briefs.authors: Fonseca J., Liu L., & Mabille P.
briefs.summary: Using individual mortgage data and a housing-ladder model, the authors show that rate lock kept many owners from downsizing or moving, which propped up prices and rents more than a simple sales slump would suggest.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why higher mortgage rates did not cool housing the way many textbook stories predicted.

briefs.title: The Annuity Puzzle Revisited: Barriers, Behavior, and Policy Paths to Lifetime Income
briefs.authors: Hershfield H. E., Shu S., Brown J. R., Hurwitz A., Milevsky M. A., Mitchell O. S., & Toland T.
briefs.summary: The paper revisits why retirees rarely buy life annuities even though lifetime-income logic is strong, focusing on complexity, distrust, framing, and weak plan-sponsor adoption rather than one single market failure.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the retirement problem is not only how much to withdraw but how to turn assets into income that cannot be outlived.

briefs.title: Credit When You Need It
briefs.authors: Collier B. L., Hartley D. A., Keys B. J., & Ng J. X.
briefs.summary: Linking disaster-loan approvals to credit files, the authors find that emergency credit sharply reduces later bankruptcy and severe distress for households hit by uninsured losses.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is strong evidence that liquidity access after a shock changes real household outcomes, not just short-term cash flow.

briefs.title: Dual Credit Markets: Income Risk, Household Debt, and Consumption
briefs.authors: Gallen Y., Melzer B. T., & Zator M.
briefs.summary: The paper models how households split borrowing between cheaper secured debt and expensive unsecured debt when income risk rises, and shows how that split shapes spending responses.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when you want a cleaner explanation for why consumer debt stress can build even before headline debt totals look extreme.

briefs.title: FinTech Lending and Cashless Payments
briefs.authors: Ghosh P., Vallee B., & Zeng Y.
briefs.summary: Studying digital payment and lending data, the authors show that cashless ecosystems can expand credit access while reshaping who gets financed and how transaction data becomes part of underwriting.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good shelf item for understanding how payment rails and credit scoring are converging in consumer finance.

briefs.title: Equilibrium Evictions
briefs.authors: Corbae D., Glover A., & Nattinger M.
briefs.summary: The authors model eviction as an equilibrium feature of rental markets and argue that renter delinquency, landlord incentives, and vacancy costs can make underinvestment and unstable housing outcomes persistent.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want housing insecurity treated as a financing and market-structure problem rather than only a legal one.

briefs.title: The Economics of "Buy Now, Pay Later": A Merchant's Perspective
briefs.authors: Berg T., Burg V., Keil J., & Puri M.
briefs.summary: This paper argues that BNPL works in part by letting merchants subsidize credit for weaker borrowers, boosting sales most where customers are more credit constrained and seller market power is higher.
briefs.whyItMatters: It explains BNPL as a pricing and credit tool, not just a checkout convenience.

briefs.title: News Selection and Household Inflation Expectations
briefs.authors: Chahrour R., Shapiro A. H., & Wilson D.
briefs.summary: The authors show that households partly adjust for media selection bias, but high-inflation headlines still move inflation expectations far more than low-inflation news moves them back down.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong reminder that household beliefs react to what gets covered, not only to the underlying price data.

briefs.title: Inflation, Expectations and Monetary Policy: What Have We Learned and to What End?
briefs.summary: This review argues that inflation expectations remain more weakly anchored than many policy models assume, and that communication failures can amplify inflation cycles even after the initial shock changes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the expectations channel treated as a core monetary-policy constraint rather than a side detail.

briefs.title: Why Do We Dislike Inflation?
briefs.summary: Survey evidence shows that households mainly hate inflation because they believe wages do not keep up, daily budgeting becomes harder, and price growth feels unfair rather than merely inefficient.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is useful when inflation is being discussed as a lived household finance problem rather than only a macro statistic.

briefs.title: Homeownership and Attention to Inflation: Evidence from Information Treatments
briefs.summary: The paper finds that homeowners pay closer attention to inflation news than renters do, partly because housing debt and asset values make inflation feel more directly connected to their balance sheet.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when you want to know why inflation beliefs differ across households even before income or education enters the picture.

briefs.title: The Legacy of High Inflation on Monetary Policy Rules
briefs.authors: Magud N. E., Pienknagura S., & Uribe M.
briefs.summary: The authors argue that histories of high inflation can leave central banks needing tougher policy rules later because credibility and expectations do not reset quickly once inflation spikes fade.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to understand why rates can stay restrictive longer than current inflation prints alone would suggest.

briefs.title: Tax Policy and the Dividend Puzzle
briefs.summary: Bernheim argues that tax changes should matter more for payout choices and stock prices than simple dividend-irrelevance models allow, then uses that tension to frame why dividend behavior stays hard to explain with one clean theory.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good starting point for why payout policy still resists neat textbook answers.

briefs.title: Dividends, taxes, and common stock prices
briefs.summary: Barclay studies ex-dividend pricing and shows that stock prices do not drop by the full cash payout, which points to tax clienteles and trading frictions in how investors value dividends.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want evidence that taxes change the economics of cash payouts in live markets.

briefs.title: Dividends and Taxes
briefs.summary: Gordon and Dietz revisit how dividend taxes shape financing choices, payout policy, and the relative appeal of retained earnings versus distributions.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps connect tax policy directly to how firms decide whether to pay out or reinvest cash.

briefs.title: Lifetime Portfolio Selection by Dynamic Stochastic Programming
briefs.publication: The Review of Economics and Statistics
briefs.summary: Samuelson formalizes lifetime asset allocation as a dynamic problem and shows how optimal risk-taking depends on wealth, horizon, and future opportunities rather than one static mix.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the foundational papers behind lifecycle portfolio design.

briefs.title: Prospect Theory, Mental Accounting, and Momentum
briefs.summary: Grinblatt and Han link investor reference points and unrealized gains to momentum, arguing that mental accounting and loss aversion can delay how news gets fully reflected in prices.
briefs.whyItMatters: It gives a behavioral mechanism for why momentum can persist instead of vanishing on contact.

briefs.title: The Disposition Effect and Underreaction to News
briefs.summary: Frazzini shows that investors are slower to let prices adjust when they are sitting on paper losses, which helps explain underreaction after firm news and the persistence of return drift.
briefs.whyItMatters: Strong evidence that investor psychology can leak directly into price formation.

briefs.title: Survival Pessimism and the Demand for Annuities
briefs.summary: O'Dea and Sturrock show that many people underestimate how long they will live, which makes annuities look less valuable than they actually are when judged against objective mortality data.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a concrete behavioral explanation for the annuity puzzle.

briefs.title: The 4 Percent Rule is Not Safe in a Low-Yield World
briefs.authors: Finke M. S., Pfau W. D., & Blanchett D. M.
briefs.summary: Finke, Pfau, and Blanchett argue that safe-withdrawal rules built on twentieth-century bond yields become too optimistic when forward-looking yield levels stay low.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearest challenges to using the classic 4 percent rule without adjusting for the rate backdrop.

briefs.title: The Rate of Return on Everything, 1870-2015
briefs.authors: Jorda O., Knoll K., Kuvshinov D., Schularick M., & Taylor A. M.
briefs.summary: This paper builds a very long-run cross-country return history for housing, equities, bonds, and bills, and finds that residential real estate has been a major return engine alongside stocks.
briefs.whyItMatters: It broadens market history beyond stocks and shows how much household wealth has ridden on housing returns.

briefs.title: Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills?
briefs.summary: Bessembinder tests the stock-versus-cash question at the security level and shows how much long-run stock outperformance depends on a surprisingly small share of listed companies.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong antidote to the lazy version of "stocks always win" market history.

briefs.title: The Impact of Mortgage Rates on the Housing Market
briefs.summary: Casta traces how shifts in mortgage rates feed through to home prices, sales activity, and affordability rather than moving only one housing variable at a time.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want one paper that ties rate sensitivity directly to housing market turnover and pricing.

briefs.title: Housing, Mortgage Recourse, and Financial Fragility
briefs.summary: Gao and Reed study how recourse rules change borrower risk, default incentives, and household fragility when housing leverage meets a bad shock.
briefs.whyItMatters: This sharpens the difference between a housing downturn and a household balance-sheet crisis.

briefs.title: Inflation Exposure Expectations and Households' Portfolio Choices
briefs.summary: Yang studies how what households think inflation will do to their own budgets affects the risk they take and the assets they choose to hold.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful bridge between inflation expectations and actual portfolio behavior.

briefs.title: Optimal Retirement Wealth
briefs.summary: Daglish and Hsiao frame retirement planning around the wealth level needed to fund spending goals under uncertainty, instead of treating one static target as universally sufficient.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when retirement planning needs a state-dependent target rather than a rule of thumb.

briefs.title: Beyond the Status Quo: A Critical Assessment of Lifecycle Investment Advice
briefs.authors: Anarkulova A., Cederburg S., & O'Doherty M. S.
briefs.summary: The authors challenge standard lifecycle glide-path advice by showing that the usual stock-bond age rules can look fragile once return uncertainty and welfare tradeoffs are modeled more fully.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want a serious critique of default target-date logic rather than a marketing gloss on glide paths.

briefs.title: When Taxes Shape Dividends: Does Ownership Type Matter?
briefs.summary: Kim studies whether dividend responses to tax changes differ across owner bases, which helps separate firm-level payout decisions from investor-level tax demand.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the dividend debate needs a modern tax-incidence angle instead of only older U.S. evidence.

briefs.title: The Price of Time: The Real Story of Interest
briefs.summary: Chancellor traces how long periods of suppressed interest rates reshape speculation, debt loads, capital allocation, and the political economy around savings.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong book-length case for treating interest rates as the price that organizes the rest of finance.

briefs.title: The Missing Billionaires: A Guide to Better Financial Decisions
briefs.summary: Haghani and White use utility, sizing, and spending math to show how wealthy families still go broke when risk, diversification, and withdrawal discipline are handled badly.
briefs.whyItMatters: One of the better recent books on how portfolio math and household behavior interact over long horizons.

briefs.title: Triumph of the Optimists: 101 Years of Global Investment Returns
briefs.authors: Dimson E., Marsh P., & Staunton M.
briefs.summary: Dimson, Marsh, and Staunton assemble long-run global return histories to show how often national winners reverse, how much concentration matters, and why local hindsight misleads investors.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a canonical reminder that long-run market leadership is far less stable than recent U.S. returns suggest.

briefs.title: House of Debt
briefs.summary: Mian and Sufi argue that household leverage, not just bank fragility, turned the housing bust into a broader economic collapse by crushing consumer balance sheets and demand.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong macro-to-household account of why debt structure matters as much as house prices.

briefs.title: Baby Boomer retirement security: The roles of planning, financial literacy, and housing wealth
briefs.summary: Lusardi and Mitchell show that many older households approach retirement with weak planning, low financial literacy, and heavy reliance on home equity rather than diversified financial wealth.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a clear reminder that retirement readiness depends on planning behavior and asset mix, not just headline net worth.

briefs.title: Financial Literacy and Planning: Implications for Retirement Wellbeing
briefs.summary: Using a special Health and Retirement Study module, Lusardi and Mitchell show that financially savvy households are more likely to make retirement plans, use formal planning tools, and follow through on saving decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want evidence that retirement planning behavior is measurable and tightly connected to later financial security.

briefs.title: What Accounts for the Variation in Retirement Wealth Among U.S. Households?
briefs.authors: Bernheim B. D., Skinner J., & Weinberg S.
briefs.summary: Bernheim, Skinner, and Weinberg test standard life-cycle explanations for why otherwise similar households retire with very different wealth levels and find the data fit behavioral shortcuts better than pure optimization.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is one of the clearest papers showing that wealth gaps are not fully explained by textbook preference differences or income paths.

briefs.title: Target-Date Funds in 401(k) Retirement Plans
briefs.authors: Mitchell O. S., & Utkus S. P.
briefs.summary: Mitchell and Utkus show how automatic enrollment, reenrollment, and fund mapping pushed more workers into target-date funds, effectively turning plan design into employer-provided lifecycle advice.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why default architecture matters so much in retirement investing, even when workers appear to have free choice.

briefs.title: Heterogeneity in Target Date Funds: Strategic Risk-taking or Risk Matching?
briefs.summary: Balduzzi and Reuter document large risk differences across target-date funds with the same retirement year and argue that some fund families use higher risk profiles to win market share rather than to match investor needs.
briefs.whyItMatters: It warns that a target date alone does not tell you how conservative or aggressive a retirement default really is.

briefs.title: Retail Financial Innovation and Stock Market Dynamics: The Case of Target Date Funds
briefs.authors: Parker J. A., Schoar A., & Sun Y.
briefs.summary: Parker, Schoar, and Sun show that the growth of target-date funds creates systematic rebalancing flows that sell stocks after strong markets and buy after weak ones, dampening some market swings.
briefs.whyItMatters: It connects a retirement product design choice to broader market behavior, not just individual asset allocation.

briefs.title: Monetary Policy Communications and Their Effects on Household Inflation Expectations
briefs.authors: Coibion O., Gorodnichenko Y., & Weber M.
briefs.summary: A large randomized study finds that simple messages about the Fed's inflation target move household expectations almost as much as reading the actual FOMC statement, while news coverage has a smaller effect.
briefs.whyItMatters: It shows that how inflation is explained to households can matter nearly as much as the policy decision itself.

briefs.title: The role of information and experience for households' inflation expectations
briefs.authors: Conrad C., Enders Z., & Glas A.
briefs.summary: Using survey data from Germany, the paper shows that media channels, policy information, and lived inflation experience all shape what households expect prices to do next and how uncertain they feel about it.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when you want to know why two households can see the same economy and still form different inflation beliefs.

briefs.title: Household Inflation Expectations and Consumer Spending: Evidence from Panel Data
briefs.summary: Burke and Ozdagli find that higher expected inflation does not lift spending across the board. Durable purchases rise only for some households, while worries about unemployment can offset that effect.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a useful corrective to the simple claim that higher inflation expectations automatically pull consumption forward.

briefs.title: What matters in households' inflation expectations?
briefs.authors: Andrade P., Gautier E., & Mengus E.
briefs.summary: Studying French household surveys, the authors show that the big divide is often between people who expect stable prices and everyone else, with that split carrying more spending significance than fine differences in expected inflation rates.
briefs.whyItMatters: It sharpens the inflation-expectations debate by showing that the extensive margin of paying attention may matter more than small forecast changes.

briefs.title: Retail ETF investing
briefs.authors: Gempesaw D., Henry J. J., & Xiao H.
briefs.summary: Using order-flow data, the paper shows that retail ETF traders lean more heavily into leveraged and inverse products than institutional traders and often chase prior ETF returns rather than trade contrarian.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a practical look at what retail ETF usage actually became once low-cost wrappers met speculative behavior.

briefs.title: The Value of ETF Liquidity
briefs.authors: Khomyn M., Putnins T., & Zoican M.
briefs.summary: Khomyn, Putnins, and Zoican show that ETF liquidity can sustain higher fees because short-horizon investors value trading ease enough to pay for it, giving liquid first movers a durable edge.
briefs.whyItMatters: It explains why some higher-fee ETFs keep winning assets instead of getting priced away immediately.

briefs.title: The counterparty risk exposure of ETF investors
briefs.authors: Hurlin C., Iseli G., Perignon C., & Yeung S.
briefs.summary: Hurlin, Iseli, Perignon, and Yeung examine how ETF structures can leave investors exposed to swap and securities-lending counterparties even when the product looks simple on the surface.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a useful shelf item when comparing ETF convenience against the hidden plumbing risks inside some wrappers.

briefs.title: Active mutual funds and their passive ETF investments
briefs.summary: Chen finds that active equity mutual funds often hold passive ETFs as hedging tools, especially when managers want to adjust market exposure without fully reshaping their stock book.
briefs.whyItMatters: It blurs the clean active-versus-passive split and shows how active managers now use passive vehicles inside active strategies.

briefs.title: Sources of Inaction in Household Finance: Evidence from the Danish Mortgage Market
briefs.authors: Andersen S., Campbell J. Y., Nielsen K. M., & Ramadorai T.
briefs.summary: Using Danish administrative data, the authors separate refinancing delays into psychological barriers and lower refinancing probabilities, showing that older, poorer, and less-educated households leave more money on the table.
briefs.whyItMatters: It shows that mortgage mistakes are not only about math. Friction and inattention can become permanent household finance costs.

briefs.title: Regional Heterogeneity and the Refinancing Channel of Monetary Policy
briefs.authors: Beraja M., Fuster A., Hurst E., & Vavra J.
briefs.summary: Beraja, Fuster, Hurst, and Vavra show that interest-rate cuts do not transmit evenly because refinancing works much better in regions where households still have the equity needed to refinance.
briefs.whyItMatters: It ties housing equity distribution directly to how strongly monetary policy reaches household cash flow and spending.

briefs.title: Houses as ATMs: Mortgage Refinancing and Macroeconomic Uncertainty
briefs.authors: Chen H., Michaux M., & Roussanov N.
briefs.summary: Chen, Michaux, and Roussanov model cash-out refinancing as a liquidity-management tool and show that households extract equity more aggressively when uncertainty rises and liquidity feels scarce.
briefs.whyItMatters: It helps explain why home equity becomes a shock absorber for household balance sheets in bad times.

briefs.title: The State of the Nation's Housing 2025
briefs.authors: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University
briefs.publication: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University
briefs.summary: Harvard's annual housing report shows a market squeezed by high prices, high mortgage rates, rising insurance and tax burdens, and record rental stress, with both ownership and rental affordability deteriorating.
briefs.whyItMatters: It is a strong broad-market check on whether housing is becoming more usable as shelter, leverage, and wealth-building infrastructure.

briefs.title: America's Rental Housing 2024
briefs.authors: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University
briefs.publication: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University
briefs.summary: The report finds that half of U.S. renters were cost burdened in 2022, with rent pressure, eviction risk, shrinking low-rent supply, and record homelessness all pointing to a structurally stressed rental market.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need the clearest recent snapshot of rent burdens and why renting is becoming a weaker wealth-building and stability platform.

briefs.title: Housing America's Older Adults 2023
briefs.authors: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University
briefs.publication: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University
briefs.summary: Harvard shows that the 65-plus population is growing faster at the oldest ages, while many households cannot afford both age-appropriate housing and the care or support services they are likely to need.
briefs.whyItMatters: It connects longevity, housing stock, and late-life cash flow in one place, which matters for both retirement planning and housing policy.

briefs.title: The National Financial Capability Study 2024 Report
briefs.summary: FINRA's state-by-state study tracks how households handle budgeting, credit, emergency savings, and basic money knowledge, giving a broad benchmark for practical financial capability in the United States.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a live baseline for how well households actually manage everyday money decisions, not just how experts think they should.

briefs.title: How America Saves 2026: 25th Edition
briefs.summary: Vanguard compiles retirement-plan participation, savings rates, balances, withdrawal behavior, and default design data from a large defined-contribution base.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a practical benchmark for what real retirement saving behavior looks like inside employer plans at scale.

briefs.title: Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2023
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The Fed's annual household survey tracks inflation stress, bill-paying capacity, emergency savings, credit use, and retirement preparedness across a wide cross-section of Americans.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth using when you need a broad official read on where household balance sheets are holding up and where they are under strain.

briefs.title: Annuity selection in the presence of insurer default risk and government guarantees
briefs.authors: Searle P., Ayton P., & Clacher I.
briefs.summary: Using Chilean retirement-product data, the authors test whether annuity buyers respond rationally to insurer default risk after a change in government guarantees.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps show whether retirees actually price insurer safety when they lock in lifetime income.

briefs.title: How Does Tax Timing Affect Spending in Retirement?
briefs.authors: Austin C. R., Bobek D. D., Doxey M. M., & Stinson S. R.
briefs.publication: Journal of the American Taxation Association
briefs.summary: An experiment finds that people spend faster from deferred-tax retirement accounts than from after-tax accounts with the same after-tax purchasing power.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to see how tax framing can quietly change withdrawal behavior even when the economics are equivalent.

briefs.title: Plan Design and Participant Behavior in Defined Contribution Retirement Plans: Past, Present, and Future
briefs.summary: Reuter reviews what the evidence says about auto-enrollment, target-date defaults, liquid-savings sidecars, and other design choices inside workplace retirement plans.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a strong synthesis if you want to know which plan defaults actually raise saving and which gains fade over time.

briefs.title: Do Women Receive Worse Financial Advice?
briefs.authors: Bhattacharya U., Kumar A., Visaria S., & Zhao J. L.
briefs.summary: Using mystery-shopper visits to advisory firms, the paper finds that women were more likely to receive narrower and less diversified advice in financial planning settings.
briefs.whyItMatters: It turns a vague concern about advice quality into direct evidence about who gets steered toward worse portfolios.

briefs.title: Financial Literacy and Financial Education: An Overview
briefs.summary: Kaiser and Lusardi review who tends to lack financial knowledge, how that shows up in financial outcomes, and what randomized education studies have actually changed.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the cleaner recent overviews on what financial literacy does and does not seem to improve.

briefs.title: Financial literacy and household financial resilience
briefs.authors: Liu T., Fan M., Li Y., & Yue P.
briefs.summary: The paper links higher financial literacy to stronger household resilience, including a better ability to absorb shocks and manage cash-flow stress.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want evidence that money knowledge matters most when households get hit by volatility, not just in calm periods.

briefs.title: Financial Sophistication and Consumer Spending
briefs.summary: Using account-level data, Jorring shows that less sophisticated households react more to predictable income changes, save less, and carry thinner liquidity buffers.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why two households with similar income can have very different day-to-day financial stability.

briefs.title: The Causal Effects of Inflation Uncertainty on Households' Beliefs and Actions
briefs.authors: Georgarakos D., Gorodnichenko Y., Coibion O., & Kenny G.
briefs.summary: The paper studies how changes in inflation uncertainty alter household expectations and the actions people take around spending, saving, and price-setting behavior.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want the behavioral channel between messy inflation expectations and real household decisions.

briefs.title: Political Polarization Affects Households' Financial Decisions: Evidence from Home Sales
briefs.authors: McCartney W. B., Orellana-Li J., & Zhang C.
briefs.summary: Matching deeds records to voter rolls, the authors find that residents become more likely to sell after politically opposed neighbors move in nearby.
briefs.whyItMatters: This shows that partisanship can move one of the largest household financial decisions people make: when to sell a home.

briefs.title: Cash is king? Understanding financing risk in housing markets
briefs.summary: Los Angeles housing data show that cash buyers close faster and receive price discounts because sellers place real value on avoiding mortgage fallout risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when you want a cleaner explanation for why cash offers still matter even outside bidding-war headlines.

briefs.title: Refinancing cross-subsidies in the mortgage market
briefs.authors: Fisher J., Gavazza A., Liu L., Ramadorai T., & Tripathy J.
briefs.summary: Using administrative mortgage data, the authors estimate that slower, less active borrowers end up subsidizing faster refinancers through market design.
briefs.whyItMatters: This makes the distributional cost of refinancing frictions concrete instead of treating mortgage shopping as a purely individual problem.

briefs.title: When climate meets real estate: A survey of the literature
briefs.authors: Contat J., Hopkins C., Mejia L., & Suandi M.
briefs.summary: This survey reviews how floods, wildfires, sea-level rise, and transition risks show up in home prices, loan performance, migration, and affordability.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong starting point if you want one paper that maps climate risk into housing-market consequences households can actually feel.

briefs.title: Equity Return Expectations and Portfolios: Evidence from Large Asset Managers
briefs.summary: The paper shows that large asset managers' equity return expectations move against valuations and that those expectations show up in portfolio allocations.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives a cleaner read on how professional investors connect valuation views to actual positioning.

briefs.title: Robo advisors and access to wealth management
briefs.summary: Reher and Sokolinski examine whether robo advice broadens access to wealth-management services and how digital delivery changes who gets portfolio help.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to separate the marketing story around robo advice from evidence about actual access.

briefs.title: Strategic borrowing from passive investors
briefs.summary: The authors show that short sellers preferentially borrow shares from stocks with heavy passive ownership because the loans are more stable and recall risk is lower.
briefs.whyItMatters: This adds a market-structure channel to the passive-investing debate instead of treating index ownership as a side issue.

briefs.title: Treasury Bill Shortages and the Pricing of Short-Term Assets
briefs.summary: The paper argues that scarce Treasury bills and segmented money markets explain a large share of post-crisis short-term spread behavior.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good for understanding why tiny bond-market plumbing details can move cash-like yields in a big way.

briefs.title: Monetary Policy, Segmentation, and the Term Structure
briefs.authors: Kekre R., Lenel M., & Mainardi F.
briefs.summary: The authors build a segmented-markets model in which policy shocks change arbitrageur wealth and term premia, not just the path of expected short rates.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a useful bridge between Fed moves and the longer-duration bond yields households and investors actually care about.

briefs.title: The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing
briefs.authors: Larimore T., Lindauer M., & LeBoeuf M.
briefs.summary: A plain-language playbook for saving more, buying broad low-cost funds, and ignoring the noise that pushes households into expensive mistakes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want the Boglehead case for simple portfolio construction without advisor jargon.

briefs.title: The Bogleheads' Guide to Retirement Planning
briefs.authors: Larimore T., Lindauer M., Ferri R. A., & Dogu L. F.
briefs.summary: Extends the Boglehead approach into retirement with practical chapters on withdrawal planning, taxes, insurance, Social Security, and estate basics.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when the real problem is coordinating retirement decisions across accounts, taxes, and spending.

briefs.title: The Index Card
briefs.summary: Boils household money management down to a short list of high-leverage habits such as saving automatically, avoiding high fees, and using tax shelters well.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good for readers who need a compact ruleset that still respects the core evidence on saving and investing.

briefs.title: All About Asset Allocation
briefs.summary: Ferri turns diversification, correlation, and rebalancing into a practical asset-allocation manual rather than a theoretical lecture.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want to move from general diversification advice to an actual portfolio structure.

briefs.title: Lifecycle Investing
briefs.summary: Ayres and Nalebuff argue that young workers often carry too little market exposure over their lifetime and explore how leverage can smooth total lifetime risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want the strongest mainstream argument for thinking about risk across a lifetime instead of one account snapshot.

briefs.title: The Behavior Gap
briefs.summary: Richards focuses on the small behavioral errors that ruin decent plans, especially panic, overconfidence, and the urge to act at the wrong time.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful bridge between academic behavior findings and the mistakes households actually make with real money.

briefs.title: The Investor's Manifesto
briefs.summary: Bernstein distills the case for low-cost diversification, long horizons, and realistic expectations into a short book built for ordinary investors.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a compact statement of the disciplined, evidence-first investing worldview.

briefs.title: Expected Returns
briefs.summary: Ilmanen surveys the evidence on where long-run returns come from across stocks, bonds, credit, real assets, and strategy premia.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the more useful maps of which expected-return stories hold up once you compare asset classes side by side.

briefs.title: The Bond Book
briefs.summary: A practical field guide to Treasury bonds, munis, corporates, yield, duration, call risk, and the ways bond structures change what investors actually earn.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when bond allocation decisions need more than a vague sense that bonds are the safe part of a portfolio.

briefs.title: The Most Important Thing
briefs.summary: Marks explains second-level thinking, cycle awareness, and margin-of-safety discipline from the perspective of a credit investor who thinks in probabilities.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want a practical statement of value-investing judgment rather than a formula screen.

briefs.title: Capital Returns
briefs.summary: Collects Marathon Asset Management letters that frame value investing through capital cycles, industry structure, and the self-correcting nature of supply.
briefs.whyItMatters: This adds a supply-side lens to value investing that many stock-picking books barely touch.

briefs.title: The Price of Time
briefs.summary: Chancellor traces how suppressed interest rates distort saving, speculation, debt, and capital allocation across households and markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the bond and rate story connected to broader wealth effects rather than treated as a narrow policy topic.

briefs.title: The Algebra of Wealth
briefs.summary: Galloway frames wealth building around career durability, saving rate, low-cost investing, and the plain fact that time and income matter more than hustle theatrics.
briefs.whyItMatters: One of the clearer recent books on how earnings power and investment habits fit together over a working life.

briefs.title: Payout policy in the 21st century
briefs.authors: Brav A., Graham J. R., Harvey C. R., & Michaely R.
briefs.summary: The authors use a large manager survey and executive interviews to show why firms now favor repurchases over dividends and how payout choices reflect flexibility and signaling concerns.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearest explanations for why modern payout policy is not just about mailing out dividends.

briefs.title: The Dividend Disconnect
briefs.authors: Hartzmark S. M. & Solomon D. H.
briefs.summary: Hartzmark and Solomon show that investors often treat dividends and capital gains as if they were fundamentally different cash flows, even when standard theory says they are not.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a behavioral explanation for why dividend preferences remain strong despite the textbook irrelevance result.

briefs.title: Investor Sentiment and the Closed-End Fund Puzzle
briefs.authors: Lee C. M. C., Shleifer A., & Thaler R. H.
briefs.summary: The paper argues that discounts on closed-end funds reflect swings in sentiment among retail investors rather than neat fundamentals alone.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a classic piece of evidence that prices can move with mood and clientele effects, not just cash-flow news.

briefs.title: Anomalies: Closed-End Mutual Funds
briefs.authors: Lee C. M. C., Shleifer A., & Thaler R. H.
briefs.summary: Lee, Shleifer, and Thaler use the closed-end fund discount to challenge the idea that market prices always stay pinned to underlying asset values.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a simple market puzzle that reveals how limits to arbitrage and investor psychology can matter in practice.

briefs.title: Noise Trading, Costly Arbitrage, and Asset Prices: Evidence from Closed-end Funds
briefs.summary: Gemmill and Thomas show how sentiment-driven trading can move prices when arbitrage is expensive, risky, or slow to force convergence.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps explain why obvious mispricings can survive longer than clean theory suggests.

briefs.title: Long-Run Stock Returns: Participating in the Real Economy
briefs.summary: Ibbotson and Chen decompose long-run equity returns into inflation, real earnings growth, valuation change, and dividends to show what historically did the work.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a grounded way to think about stock returns beyond the slogan that equities just go up over time.

briefs.title: The Economics of Value Investing
briefs.authors: Hou K., Mo H., Chen X., & Zhang L.
briefs.summary: The paper argues that much of value investing can be understood through profitability, investment, and discount-rate mechanics rather than one vague cheapness story.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a modern economic account of why value strategies have worked and when they fail.

briefs.title: Money for Couples
briefs.summary: Sethi shifts personal finance from solo optimization to joint decision-making and gives couples scripts, account structures, and planning routines that keep both partners engaged in the numbers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when budgeting is not the hard part but staying aligned as a household is.

briefs.title: The White Coat Investor
briefs.summary: Dahle translates investing, insurance, debt payoff, and contract issues into a practical operating manual for high-income professionals who can still make expensive money mistakes early in their careers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Strong on the gap between high earnings and actual wealth building.

briefs.title: The Bogle Effect
briefs.summary: Balchunas explains how low-cost indexing moved from fringe idea to dominant default and documents the fee compression and power shift that followed across the fund industry.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful for understanding what passive investing changed beyond just investor costs.

briefs.title: Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk
briefs.summary: Bernstein traces how probability, insurance, statistics, and portfolio thinking turned risk from fate into something households, traders, and institutions could measure and price.
briefs.whyItMatters: This gives the long arc behind modern investing language about uncertainty, diversification, and expected return.

briefs.title: The Price You Pay for College
briefs.summary: Lieber breaks down how colleges set sticker prices, discount tuition, and use aid strategically, then shows families where negotiation and school selection matter most.
briefs.whyItMatters: College is one of the biggest household cash decisions many families will ever make.

briefs.title: The Opposite of Spoiled
briefs.summary: Lieber uses allowances, spending choices, chores, charity, and family tradeoffs to show how children learn money habits long before they open a brokerage account.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for households that want money behavior taught as a family practice, not left to chance.

briefs.title: The Wealth Ladder
briefs.summary: Maggiulli organizes financial choices by net-worth tier and argues that the right next move changes as households move from basic stability to portfolio management and legacy planning.
briefs.whyItMatters: Strong on matching tactics to financial stage instead of repeating one rule for every balance sheet.

briefs.title: Same as Ever
briefs.summary: Housel focuses on repeated human patterns such as fear, greed, patience, and tail events rather than on forecasting, and frames investing as a behavior problem more than an information problem.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the lesson is less about prediction and more about surviving incentives and emotion.

briefs.title: Capital Markets Fact Book 2025
briefs.summary: SIFMA compiles issuance, trading, outstanding balances, and investor participation across equity, bond, and securitized markets into one annual market-structure reference.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a fast way to ground claims about the scale and composition of U.S. capital markets.

briefs.title: Household Debt and Credit Report 2025: Q1
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The New York Fed tracks mortgages, student loans, auto debt, credit cards, new borrowing, and delinquency transitions using credit-panel data rather than surveys.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need a clean read on which parts of household leverage are actually deteriorating.

briefs.title: Highlights From the Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers 2024
briefs.authors: National Association of Realtors Research Group
briefs.summary: NAR summarizes who is buying and selling homes, how they finance purchases, what concessions they receive, and how first-time buyers are faring in the current market.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful for separating broad housing anecdotes from the actual buyer mix and financing conditions.

briefs.title: Distributional Financial Accounts
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The Fed combines macro balance-sheet data with survey evidence to estimate who owns assets and liabilities across the wealth distribution over time.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps anchor wealth-inequality discussions in balance-sheet data instead of headline net-worth anecdotes.

briefs.title: Making Ends Meet Survey
briefs.summary: The CFPB survey follows how households manage bills, income swings, liquidity stress, and credit use when regular budgeting is not enough to absorb shocks.
briefs.whyItMatters: Strong for understanding day-to-day financial fragility rather than only long-run wealth totals.

briefs.title: Periodic Table of Investment Returns
briefs.summary: Callan ranks major asset classes year by year and makes it obvious how often leaders and laggards swap places across public markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: A compact antidote to performance chasing and recent-winner bias.

briefs.title: IRS Data Book 2024
briefs.summary: The IRS Data Book tracks returns filed, audits, collections, taxpayer assistance, and enforcement activity, giving a grounded view of how the tax system actually operates at scale.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when tax discussions need operating facts instead of abstractions about rules alone.

briefs.title: Financial Accounts of the United States
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The Z.1 financial accounts show how household assets, debts, business financing, and sector balance sheets fit together across the entire U.S. economy.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the cleanest ways to connect household wealth stories to the broader credit and asset system.

briefs.title: Guide to Retirement 2025
briefs.summary: J.P. Morgan packages spending, longevity, Social Security timing, required minimum distributions, and market assumptions into one practitioner-focused retirement handbook.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need a current decumulation reference that ties multiple retirement constraints together.

briefs.title: Demographia International Housing Affordability 2025
briefs.summary: Demographia compares median house prices to median household income across major metropolitan markets using a simple affordability ratio that makes cross-city stress visible quickly.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when housing affordability claims need a consistent cross-market yardstick.

briefs.title: Investment Company Fact Book 2025
briefs.summary: ICI compiles mutual fund, ETF, and retirement-plan statistics covering assets, flows, ownership, and fund usage across U.S. households and institutions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for checking how large the fund complex is and how investors actually use it.

briefs.title: Personal Finance Index 2025
briefs.summary: The index measures how well adults understand borrowing, saving, earning, insurance, investing, and risk, then links those gaps to real financial behavior and stress.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good benchmark when claims about financial literacy need something more concrete than intuition.

briefs.title: Credit Card Banking
briefs.authors: Drechsler I., Jung H., Peng W., Supera D., & Zhou G.
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Reports
briefs.summary: Using account-level data covering most of the U.S. credit card market, the authors show that high card APRs reflect some default risk but also sizable pricing power, rewards economics, and operating margins.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when household borrowing costs look irrational and you want a cleaner picture of what card lenders actually earn.

briefs.title: Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025
briefs.summary: The Fed’s annual SHED report tracks savings, credit use, retirement progress, housing stress, fraud losses, and the share of adults who can cover emergency expenses with cash or its equivalent.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the broadest official snapshots of how U.S. households are actually handling money, debt, and financial shocks.

briefs.title: Household Debt Balances Grow Modestly; Early Delinquencies Level Out for Non-Housing Debts
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The New York Fed’s Q4 2025 debt report shows household liabilities reaching $18.8 trillion, with mortgage delinquencies rising while most early-stage delinquency rates outside housing largely steadied.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good baseline for checking whether rising consumer stress is broad or concentrated in a few debt categories.

briefs.title: Where Are Mortgage Delinquencies Rising the Most?
briefs.authors: Haughwout A. F., Lee D., Mangrum D., Scally J. W., & van der Klaauw W.
briefs.summary: This New York Fed analysis shows that recent mortgage delinquency deterioration is most pronounced in lower-income ZIP codes and in places with weaker labor and housing market conditions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when national delinquency averages hide where mortgage stress is actually building.

briefs.title: How vulnerable are Americans to unexpected expenses?
briefs.summary: Using banking data, the institute argues that many households can absorb a moderate shock only because disposable income and short-term credit supplement cash savings.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when survey claims about living paycheck to paycheck need a harder measure of actual liquidity.

briefs.title: Household Finances Pulse through June 2024: Balances Continue to Decline
briefs.summary: The Household Finances Pulse shows pandemic-era excess cash buffers fading, with most income groups continuing to draw balances down toward or below expected trends.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good context when resilience looks stable in surveys but liquid savings are still thinning underneath.

briefs.title: U.S. Persistence Scorecard Year-End 2025
briefs.authors: Ganti A. R., Di Gioia D., Didio N., & Flaherty L.
briefs.summary: S&P’s persistence study finds that even when active funds outperform for a year or two, very few stay in the top tier over longer periods.
briefs.whyItMatters: This sharpens the active-versus-passive debate by testing not just one-year wins, but whether skill persists.

briefs.title: Emergency Savings Protect Retirement Savings
briefs.authors: Goodman A., Hahn K., & Greig F.
briefs.summary: Vanguard finds that workers with accessible emergency savings contribute more consistently to retirement plans and are less likely to tap or cash out balances after shocks or job changes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when retirement shortfalls are really a liquidity problem upstream, not just a contribution-rate problem.

briefs.title: The Relationship Between Emergency Savings, Financial Well-Being, and Financial Stress
briefs.authors: Costa P., Martino M., & de la Fuente M.
briefs.summary: Survey evidence from Vanguard links even modest emergency reserves to materially better well-being scores, lower financial stress, and less time spent firefighting money problems.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong reference when small liquid reserves matter more than abstract budgeting advice.

briefs.title: U.S. House Price Index Report - 2026 Q1
briefs.summary: FHFA’s quarterly HPI report shows national house prices up 1.7 percent year over year in Q1 2026, with comparable breakout tables for states, metros, and census divisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when housing discussions need a broad official price benchmark rather than local anecdotes.

briefs.title: AANHPI Homeownership and Wealth-Building Trajectories
briefs.authors: Zhu L., Berry B., Pang D., & Zhu J.
briefs.summary: Urban traces how AANHPI households build, use, preserve, and transfer wealth through homeownership, with detail on equity growth, extraction, and barriers across the life cycle.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when homeownership is discussed as a wealth engine but the path differs sharply across groups and stages of life.
