briefs.title: Tangled Titles, Estate Planning, and the Digital Divide
briefs.authors: Neal M., Pruitt M., Walsh J., & Zinn A.
briefs.summary: This report explains how unclear title transfer and weak estate planning can trap families in heirs-property problems that block refinancing, repairs, and clean wealth transfer.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good reminder that property wealth can disappear through paperwork and legal frictions, not just price declines.

briefs.title: Measuring the True Cost of Economic Security
briefs.authors: Acs G., Dehry I., Giannarelli L., & Todd M.
briefs.summary: Urban builds a measure of what families need not just to survive, but to participate economically with enough income, support, and reserves to stay secure.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when standard poverty or income thresholds understate what durable household stability actually costs.

briefs.title: Do the Rich Really Save More? Answering an Old Question Using the Survey of Consumer Finances with Direct Measures of Lifetime Earnings and an Expanded Wealth Concept
briefs.authors: Llanes E., Thompson J. P., & Henriques Volz A.
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston Research Department Working Papers
briefs.summary: Using richer lifetime-earnings and wealth measures, the authors revisit whether higher-income households truly save more and show how that answer depends on what counts as wealth.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when wealth gaps are discussed as spending habits alone rather than a function of lifetime earnings, asset mix, and measurement choices.

briefs.title: Federal Student Loan Defaults Return After Pandemic Pause
briefs.authors: Jacob Z., Lee D., Mangrum D., Scally J. W., & van der Klaauw W.
briefs.summary: The New York Fed shows that once reporting resumed, federal student loan defaults surged, with millions of borrowers entering default after the pandemic-era pause unwound.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is useful when you need to separate a policy-timing cliff from a normal, gradual credit cycle.

briefs.title: Student Loan Delinquencies Are Back, and Credit Scores Take a Tumble
briefs.authors: Haughwout A. F., Lee D., Mangrum D., Scally J., & van der Klaauw W.
briefs.summary: After delinquent federal student loans reappeared on credit files, the New York Fed documented a sharp jump in past-due balances and large credit-score declines for affected borrowers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when student loan stress needs to be translated into downstream borrowing damage rather than delinquency headlines alone.

briefs.title: The Role of IRAs in US Households’ Saving for Retirement, 2025
briefs.summary: ICI’s annual IRA study tracks ownership, rollovers, contributions, and withdrawals, showing how IRAs function alongside workplace plans in household retirement balance sheets.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when retirement saving discussions need actual household participation and withdrawal behavior, not just account-size anecdotes.

briefs.title: How America Retires
briefs.summary: Vanguard’s retirement report studies how participants draw income, preserve balances, and behave once they move from saving into spending and distribution decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good context when retirement planning shifts from accumulation math to the harder question of how households actually spend portfolios down.

briefs.title: Household Financial Outlook Deteriorates; Short-Term Inflation Expectations Decline
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The May 2026 Survey of Consumer Expectations shows softer views on future credit access, household finances, and delinquency risk even as short-term inflation expectations eased slightly.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want the household side of the macro picture before distress fully shows up in realized delinquency data.

briefs.title: The Future of Homeownership and Housing Finance
briefs.summary: Urban outlines the main housing-finance problems ahead, including supply limits, access-to-close barriers, servicing resilience, and climate-related pressure on ownership costs.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful framing piece when housing affordability debates ignore the financing system that shapes who can buy and who can stay.

briefs.title: How Do Tax Incentives Influence Employer Decisions to Offer Retirement Benefits?
briefs.authors: Bloomfield A., Goodman L., Ramnath S., & Slavov S.
briefs.summary: Using tax data, the paper shows that the small-firm credit for starting a retirement plan is claimed far less often than policymakers likely intended, with take-up rising mostly when preparers learn the rules.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know why retirement-plan subsidies can look generous on paper yet move participation only modestly in practice.

briefs.title: Financial Wellness and Retirement Security: Understanding Financial Vulnerabilities to Deliver Better Outcomes
briefs.summary: Drawing on FINRA National Financial Capability Study data from 2012 to 2024, the report finds that retirement savers most often struggle with missing emergency savings, burdensome debt, overspending, and weak financial literacy.
briefs.whyItMatters: Retirement balances do not stand alone. This shows which day-to-day household weaknesses most often break long-run saving plans.

briefs.title: The Role of Health in Strengthening Retirement Security
briefs.summary: Pooling SHED data from 2021 through 2025, the analysis shows that health-related retirement is often early and involuntary, and is tied to weaker cash buffers, higher financial strain, and more skipped care.
briefs.whyItMatters: A retirement plan can fail long before markets do. Health shocks are one of the clearest channels through which that happens.

briefs.title: How Unequal Access to Employer-Sponsored Benefits Affects Worker Retention and Financial Stability
briefs.summary: Using Understanding America Study data from 2021 to 2023, the paper finds persistent gaps in benefit access by race and sex, and links paid leave, insurance, retirement plans, and work-from-home access to lower stress and lower turnover.
briefs.whyItMatters: Household resilience is shaped by job design as much as wages. Benefit access changes both saving capacity and shock absorption.

briefs.title: Making the Case: The Effect of Private Market Assets on Retirement Income in Cases of Disrupted Savings
briefs.summary: The report models caregivers, lower-income workers, job hoppers, and early retirees and finds that modest private-market exposure inside target-date funds can raise expected retirement income by roughly 7 to 8 percent net of fees.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when retirement-income debates assume a smooth career path that many workers do not actually have.

briefs.title: Quantifying the Value of the Federal Home Loan Bank System
briefs.authors: Berry B., Choi J. H., Goodman L., Pang D., Reynolds K., Visalli K., Walsh J., & Zhu J.
briefs.summary: Urban synthesizes three studies and estimates that the FHLBank system creates roughly $94 billion to $133 billion in annual value through liquidity support, added lending, and affordable-housing and community-development funding.
briefs.whyItMatters: The FHLBank system sits deep in housing finance plumbing. This gives a concrete estimate of how much that plumbing may matter.

briefs.title: The Value of the FHLBank System to Promote Housing and Community Development Lending
briefs.authors: Choi J. H., Zhu J., Goodman L., Walsh J., Visalli K., & Berry B.
briefs.summary: Using more than two decades of member data, the report finds that FHLBank advances and membership are associated with more lending not only for mortgages but also for community development, agriculture, and small business credit.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearer attempts to measure whether wholesale housing-finance liquidity actually changes credit supply in the real economy.

briefs.title: How Expanding Housing Supply and Supporting Demand Can Increase Homeownership
briefs.authors: Cusella C., Balu R., & Kumari S.
briefs.summary: The brief argues that homeownership policy works best when it pairs lower-cost supply expansion with targeted demand support, rather than treating down-payment help as a complete solution to affordability problems.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful counterweight to one-sided homeownership debates that talk only about subsidies or only about zoning.

briefs.title: Moving Beyond Aggregate Measures to Understand AANHPI Homeownership Dynamics in the US Housing Market
briefs.authors: Zhu L., Pang D., Berry B., & Zhu J.
briefs.summary: Using disaggregated subgroup data, the report shows that AANHPI homeownership patterns differ sharply by origin, geography, and household structure, which broad national averages often hide.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when broad racial aggregates blur where homeownership and wealth-building barriers actually sit.

briefs.title: The Evolution of Residential Transition Lending
briefs.summary: The report documents how residential transition lending has become a key source of short-term capital for small builders and rehab projects that larger banks and capital markets often do not serve well.
briefs.whyItMatters: Small-balance construction finance is easy to ignore until supply stalls. This explains one of the channels keeping incremental housing production alive.

briefs.title: Housing Finance at a Glance: A Monthly Chartbook, May 2026
briefs.authors: Goodman L., Neal M., Choi J. H., Zhu L., Walsh J., Pang D., Visalli K., Mehrotra A., Pruitt M., Berry B., Rincon A., Hill T., Barcus A., & Koons E.
briefs.summary: Urban's monthly chartbook compiles more than 80 figures on mortgage affordability, delinquencies, credit availability, insurance activity, and first-time-buyer participation, with a current read on where the market is tightening and easing.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a compact operating dashboard when one headline about housing misses the financing side of the market.

briefs.title: Housing Capital and Intergenerational Mobility in the United States
briefs.authors: Binder A. J., Risch M., & Voorheis J. L.
briefs.summary: Linking census, tax, and property records for more than 3.4 million families, the paper finds that housing capital is more persistent across generations than earnings and that supply constraints widen those wealth gaps.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is strong evidence that housing wealth is not just a reflection of income. It is its own transmission channel across families.

briefs.title: Screen More, Sell Later: Screening and Dynamic Signaling in the Mortgage Market
briefs.authors: Adelino M., Wei B., & Zhao F.
briefs.summary: The paper shows that mortgages with longer processing times tend to be sold later and default less, consistent with lenders using costly screening to signal loan quality in securitized mortgage markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful lens on how underwriting incentives and securitization interact, especially when mortgage fragility looks hidden until late in the cycle.

briefs.title: Interest Rates and Equity Valuations
briefs.summary: The authors decompose real-rate moves into growth, risk, and pure discounting shocks and find that only the discounting component maps cleanly into higher or lower equity valuations.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when commentators treat all rate moves as equivalent for stocks even though the driver of the rate move matters a great deal.

briefs.title: The Response of Debtors to Rate Changes
briefs.authors: Fuster A., Gianinazzi V., Hackethal A., Schnorpfeil P., & Weber M.
briefs.summary: Using German mortgage data, a field intervention, and surveys, the paper shows that borrowers actively prepare for reset risk and can blunt payment shocks through refinancing and other adjustments.
briefs.whyItMatters: Interest-rate transmission depends on how borrowers behave, not only on the size of the rate move itself.

briefs.title: Financial conditions and the macroeconomy: a two-factor view
briefs.authors: Lombardi M. J., Manea C., & Schrimpf A.
briefs.summary: The BIS paper builds a more interpretable U.S. financial-conditions index that separates the price of financing from broader risk appetite, improving how analysts link markets to the real economy.
briefs.whyItMatters: A single conditions index often hides the mechanism. This one is useful because it splits financing stress into more decision-ready pieces.

briefs.title: Europe Persistence Scorecard: Year-End 2025
briefs.authors: Edwards T., Di Gioia D., & Smith E.
briefs.summary: The scorecard finds that very few Europe-focused active funds sustain top-half performance across multi-year periods, with persistence generally weak across both equity and fixed-income categories.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want evidence on whether active outperformance in Europe repeats often enough to justify manager selection risk.

briefs.title: Canada Persistence Scorecard: Year-End 2025
briefs.authors: Nelesen J., Hyman L., & Di Gioia D.
briefs.summary: S&P shows that Canadian active funds rarely keep top-quartile or top-half rankings over consecutive years, even when short-run outperformance briefly appears.
briefs.whyItMatters: This helps separate one good year from evidence of repeatable manager skill in the Canadian fund market.

briefs.title: Young Adults' Perspectives on Wealth Building
briefs.authors: Martinchek K., Atherton S., McKernan S.-M., & Brown M.
briefs.summary: Based on interviews with young adults, the report finds that many see stable income, emergency reserves, retirement access, and achievable housing costs as prerequisites for wealth building, not side issues.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when discussions of wealth building skip the balance-sheet constraints that younger households say come first.

briefs.title: How Wealth-Building Accounts Can Help Families Access Capital Markets
briefs.authors: Webley H., Cusella C., Brown M., & Ford L. D.
briefs.summary: Urban argues that seeded wealth-building accounts can give low-wealth families earlier exposure to long-term compounding and estimates meaningful gains for education, homeownership, entrepreneurship, and retirement over the life cycle.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a practical bridge between abstract wealth-gap debates and one concrete mechanism for getting more families invested earlier.

briefs.title: Does Homeownership Matter? The Long-Term Consequences of Losing a House during the Great Recession
briefs.authors: Artigue H., Bayer P., Ferreira F. V., & Ross S.
briefs.summary: Using mortgage-modification variation during the Great Recession, the paper finds that households that kept their homes retained much larger housing gains years later, but saw little lasting edge in credit scores or neighborhood quality.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when homeownership debates assume the wealth case automatically carries over to every other household outcome.

briefs.title: Income and Wealth Inequality in the United States: An Update Including the 2022 Wave
briefs.summary: Using the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, the paper updates how earnings, income, and wealth are spread across households and shows that the top 1 percent still controls a very large share even after housing gains lifted middle-class balance sheets.
briefs.whyItMatters: A current inequality baseline helps separate broad wealth growth from who actually captured it.

briefs.title: Financial Advisors and Investors' Bias
briefs.authors: Andries M., Bonelli M., & Sraer D.
briefs.summary: Studying a brokerage-platform change, the paper finds that removing advisers' visibility into unrealized gains and losses sharply reduced clients' disposition effect, especially among heavily advised investors.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is concrete evidence that choice architecture inside advice channels can change real investor behavior.

briefs.title: Student Loan Forgiveness
briefs.authors: Dinerstein M., Earnest S., Koustas D. K., & Yannelis C.
briefs.summary: Using credit-bureau data around large federal forgiveness episodes, the paper finds that forgiven borrowers increased other borrowing and saw lower employment and earnings relative to comparison groups.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong addition when student-debt relief is discussed as a pure balance-sheet win with no behavioral response.

briefs.title: Pricing Residential Mortgage Credit Risk in the Post-GFC Era
briefs.authors: Capponi A., Van Nieuwerburgh S., & Wu X.
briefs.summary: The paper models the post-crisis credit-risk-transfer market and finds that mortgage credit is priced roughly fairly on average, while showing where low-risk and high-risk borrowers are cross-subsidized.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how mortgage pricing, guarantee fees, and borrower risk now connect after the crisis-era redesign.

briefs.title: Stimulus through Insurance: the Marginal Propensity to Repay Debt
briefs.authors: Kosar G., Melcangi D., Pilossoph L., & Wiczer D. G.
briefs.summary: The authors show that heavily indebted households often use transfer payments to pay down debt rather than spend immediately, because reducing future interest costs can dominate near-term consumption.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when fiscal-transfer debates treat every extra dollar as if it will be spent the same way across households.

briefs.title: Moral Hazard and the Sustainability of Income-Driven Repayment Plans
briefs.authors: Fu C., Li X., & Zafar B.
briefs.summary: Survey and model evidence suggest that income-driven repayment softens some underinvestment caused by debt, but also changes job choices in ways that can increase expected forgiveness costs.
briefs.whyItMatters: This captures the tradeoff between easing borrower strain and creating new incentives inside student-loan policy.

briefs.title: College Loans and Human Capital Investment
briefs.authors: Fu C., Lin H.-C., & Tanaka A.
briefs.summary: This structural paper models how borrowing limits and repayment rules affect schooling and later skill investment, concluding that income-driven plans can modestly raise attainment and lifetime earnings.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want student-loan policy tied back to education and earnings rather than balance totals alone.

briefs.title: How Do Financial and Longevity Literacy Affect Annuity Demand?
briefs.summary: Brown reviews the evidence on annuity decisions and shows that financial and longevity literacy do not cleanly explain take-up rates, but do shape planning quality and how retirees react to framing and choice design.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good addition for readers who want to know why annuities remain underused even when longevity risk is obvious.

briefs.title: Wealth Heterogeneity and Consumer Spending
briefs.authors: Beach S., Gamber W., & Moran P.
briefs.summary: The note argues that rising wealth concentration lowers the average propensity to consume out of wealth, making household spending less responsive to asset-price gains than older models imply.
briefs.whyItMatters: A balance-sheet boom does not mean a proportionate spending boom. This explains one reason why.

briefs.title: The State of Retirement Withdrawal Strategies for 2025
briefs.summary: Morningstar's annual report updates safe starting withdrawal guidance using forward-looking capital-market assumptions and compares static and flexible drawdown methods under current valuations and yields.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the 4 percent rule is quoted without checking whether current market conditions support it.

briefs.title: Assessing Black Wealth Using Public Datasets and Case Study Interviews
briefs.summary: Urban combines public data with interviews to show how asset ownership, debt burdens, and local conditions continue to hold down Black wealth relative to white households even when income measures look less extreme.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful reminder that wealth gaps cannot be read off income gaps alone.

briefs.title: Evaluating Paths to Building Black Wealth through Education and Entrepreneurship
briefs.summary: The report compares the wealth outcomes associated with professional education and business ownership and finds that both paths correlate with higher net worth, though racial gaps persist at each stage.
briefs.whyItMatters: It adds structure to wealth-building debates by showing which channels have historically moved net worth and where they still fall short.

briefs.title: Student Loan Balance and Repayment Trends Since the Pandemic Disruption
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The New York Fed tracks how payment pauses, resumed interest, and later forgiveness programs broke long-running repayment trends and left an unusually large share of borrowers with flat or rising balances.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong operating read on how the student-loan market changed after the pandemic rather than simply returning to its old path.

briefs.title: Credit Score Impacts from Past Due Student Loan Payments
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: Using credit-bureau histories, the post estimates that the return of negative reporting on delinquent student loans could knock more than 150 points off scores for many previously prime borrowers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Student-loan delinquency does not stay inside the loan itself. It spills into borrowing costs and credit access across the household balance sheet.

briefs.title: Change in Household Debt Balances Mixed; Student Loan Delinquencies Rise Sharply
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The New York Fed's quarterly household-debt release shows overall debt still growing in early 2025 while reported serious student-loan delinquency jumps back after the credit-reporting pause ended.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful reference point for where U.S. household leverage and repayment stress actually stood once student-loan reporting resumed.

briefs.title: Household Debt Growth Remains Steady; Auto Loan Originations Pick Up
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The Q2 2025 debt release shows mortgage and credit-card balances still rising, auto originations recovering, and student-loan stress continuing even as aggregate household debt growth looks moderate.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when broad debt totals look calm but the composition of new borrowing and delinquency pressure is shifting underneath.

briefs.title: Homeownership and Housing Equity in the Mid-Twentieth Century
briefs.authors: Frydman C., Molloy R., & Palis A.
briefs.summary: Using historical census microdata, the note shows how the postwar jump in homeownership changed housing-equity accumulation and helps explain why owner-occupied housing became central to middle-class wealth.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful historical anchor for today's arguments about whether housing wealth is a policy choice, a market outcome, or both.

briefs.title: Black Housing Wealth Varies across Local Markets, Despite Recent Improvement in the Black Homeownership Rate Nationally
briefs.summary: Urban shows that the national rise in Black homeownership masks large local differences in how much housing wealth Black households actually hold relative to their share of households.
briefs.whyItMatters: National ownership rates can look better while local wealth gaps remain severe. This piece shows where that split matters.

briefs.title: High Interest Rates and Expensive Home Prices Continued to Make Homeownership Less Affordable in 2025, New Data Show
briefs.summary: Using newly released HMDA data, Urban documents how high rates and elevated prices kept debt-to-income ratios, cash-to-close burdens, and first-time-buyer pressure uncomfortably high through 2025.
briefs.whyItMatters: A clear data point on why affordability stayed broken even without another obvious boom in home sales.

briefs.title: How Do State Auto-IRA Policies Affect Household Balance Sheets?
briefs.authors: Bloomfield A., Dao N., Lee K. M., & Slavov S.
briefs.summary: Using Oregon's auto-IRA rollout as a natural experiment, the paper finds that automatic retirement-saving mandates raise retirement account ownership and balances while also changing checking balances and credit-card borrowing.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when retirement-plan defaults are framed as narrow pension policy even though they spill into day-to-day household balance-sheet behavior.

briefs.title: Real Effects of Nominal Interest Rates
briefs.authors: Hausman J. K., Leahy J. V., Mondragon J., & Wieland J.
briefs.summary: The paper argues that higher nominal rates matter directly for households because fixed mortgage payments and payment-to-income constraints reduce how much people can borrow even when real rates tell a murkier story.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good anchor for why mortgage affordability can tighten fast when nominal rates rise, even before house prices fully adjust.

briefs.title: Did the Modern Mortgage Set the Stage for the U.S. Baby Boom?
briefs.authors: Dettling L. J. & Kearney M. S.
briefs.summary: Dettling and Kearney show that FHA and VA mortgage insurance expanded young-family homeownership enough to help explain roughly a tenth of excess baby-boom births between 1935 and 1957.
briefs.whyItMatters: This connects mortgage design to family formation and long-run housing demand instead of treating home finance as a narrow pricing issue.

briefs.title: Self-assessed Life-Cycle Saving Behavior in the U.S. and Singapore: Procrastination Versus Economic Shocks
briefs.authors: Rohwedder S., Hurd M. D., & Boersch-Supan A.
briefs.summary: Survey evidence from older Americans and Singaporeans suggests regret about under-saving is tied more to economic shocks than to simple procrastination stories.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when retirement shortfalls are blamed on self-control alone and the bigger risk is repeated shocks households never fully absorb.

briefs.title: Who Benefits from Retirement Saving Incentives in the U.S.? Evidence on Gaps in Retirement Wealth Accumulation by Race and Parental Income
briefs.authors: Choukhmane T., Colmenares J., O'Dea C., Rothbaum J. L., & Schmidt L. D. W.
briefs.summary: Using linked employer-employee retirement data, the paper shows that tax breaks and matching incentives disproportionately build retirement wealth for workers from richer families and for White and Asian workers relative to similar-income peers.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is a strong corrective when retirement policy is discussed as if the same subsidy reaches every worker equally.

briefs.title: Ricardian Non-Equivalence
briefs.authors: Eichenbaum M. S., Guerreiro J., & Obradovic J.
briefs.summary: New survey evidence suggests households plan to spend transfers in ways that do not fully offset future tax liabilities, pointing to a much more cash-flow-driven response than textbook Ricardian logic predicts.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when fiscal checks or transfer policies are debated as if households calmly net out future taxes before spending.

briefs.title: Self-Fulfilling Credit Scores
briefs.summary: The paper finds that small score hits caused by how inquiries are counted can themselves raise later default rates for already fragile borrowers, making part of the score-default link self-fulfilling.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading when credit scores are treated as passive measurements rather than rules that can worsen the behavior they predict.

briefs.title: The Effect of Foreclosures on Homeowners, Tenants, and Landlords
briefs.authors: Diamond R., Guren A., & Tan R.
briefs.summary: Using random judge assignment and matched comparisons, the paper finds foreclosure imposes large financial and non-financial costs on owners while renters and landlords experience a different mix of damage.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong reminder that mortgage distress is not just a balance-sheet event. It also changes housing stability, neighborhoods, and family outcomes.

briefs.title: How Annuities Could Improve Retirement Security amid Economic Uncertainty
briefs.summary: Urban reviews annuity ownership, wealth gaps, and product design to show how guaranteed lifetime income could help households handle longevity risk but remains concentrated among wealthier families.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when annuities are dismissed wholesale even though the real question is which designs make retirement income more durable and more accessible.

briefs.title: Many Families Rely on Credit and Savings to Afford Groceries
briefs.authors: Martinchek K., Karpman M., Kennedy N., & Waxman E.
briefs.summary: Using a large 2025 survey, Urban shows that many households are leaning on credit cards, BNPL, payday loans, and emergency savings just to cover groceries, with repayment trouble most visible among lower-income families.
briefs.whyItMatters: A concrete signal that everyday price pressure is spilling into debt use and savings depletion, not just sentiment surveys.

briefs.title: Why Funding a Down Payment with Retirement Funds Is a Winning Proposition
briefs.summary: The brief compares long-run housing and stock returns and argues that using retirement assets for a first-home down payment can be financially attractive for many borrowers, especially when leverage and refinancing matter.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when the retirement-versus-homeownership tradeoff is discussed as a simple stock-market comparison instead of a financing problem.

briefs.title: Financial Nihilists or Savvy Strategists? Understanding Gen Z's Financial Attitudes and Behaviors
briefs.authors: Garon T., Wu R., Axelrod J., Godinez-Puig L., & Ramos K.
briefs.summary: Urban finds that Gen Z mixes conventional saving with speculative behavior, with many young adults using retirement accounts and savings products even while some also reach for crypto, retail trading, and sports betting.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good check against caricatures that portray younger households as either reckless gamblers or perfectly disciplined savers.

briefs.title: How and Why People Are Using Emerging Financial Technologies
briefs.authors: Godinez-Puig L., Garon T., Axelrod J., Wu R., & Ramos K.
briefs.summary: This fact sheet uses new consumer survey evidence to map how households are approaching crypto, sports betting, and other new financial tools as part of broader saving, borrowing, and wealth-building decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when fintech adoption is framed as a niche story rather than part of mainstream household finance behavior.

briefs.title: The Importance of Life Insurance Policies Among Senior Black Families
briefs.summary: Using Survey of Consumer Finances data, the brief shows that life-insurance coverage is a meaningful but often omitted source of transferable capital for older Black families.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading when wealth is defined too narrowly and intergenerational transfer is reduced to homes, stocks, and retirement accounts.

briefs.title: Credit Insecurity and ALICE Households in the United States
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The report shows that households living just above or below basic-needs thresholds often face weaker access to mainstream credit, thinner revolving-credit availability, and deeper delinquency pressure.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful map of where credit access breaks down before families show up in outright poverty statistics.

briefs.title: Sizing the Community Development Financial Institution Industry: 2011-2025
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The report tracks how CDFIs grew through 2024 and then saw modest asset and institution-count declines by mid-2025, giving a clearer view of the scale of mission-driven finance in underserved markets.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when community finance is discussed abstractly and you need a real sense of industry size, concentration, and recent momentum.

briefs.title: Household Debt Balances Rise Slightly as Delinquency Transition Rates Hold Steady
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The New York Fed's Q1 2026 debt release shows overall household debt still edging higher while mortgage, HELOC, and auto balances rise and student-loan stress continues to normalize upward after the payment pause.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good baseline for where broad household leverage and delinquency transitions actually stood heading into mid-2026.

briefs.title: 2026 SCE Housing Survey (Fielded in February): One-Year Expectations for Rent Increases Are Stable at 8 Percent; Expected Probability of Refinancing Climbs
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The survey shows households still expect solid home-price growth and very high rent increases while the perceived odds of moving stay soft and refinancing interest edges up.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you need a direct read on household housing expectations rather than a view inferred from sales or permits alone.

briefs.title: June Survey: Consumers' Credit Application Rates Increase, Rejection Rates Up Slightly
briefs.authors: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: The June credit-access survey finds more households applying for credit than earlier in the year while rejection rates tick higher and emergency-cash pressure remains elevated.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful snapshot of whether credit demand is rising because households feel stronger or because they are under more strain.

briefs.title: Buy Now, Pay Later Beyond Pay in 4, A Comprehensive Product Overview
briefs.authors: Acree N. R., Barnes K., Bruce A., & Hannon S. M.
briefs.summary: The note expands BNPL measurement beyond classic pay-in-four plans and estimates roughly $157 billion of BNPL credit issuance in 2025 across short- and longer-term products.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when BNPL is treated as a tiny checkout gimmick rather than a meaningful and fast-growing slice of consumer credit.

briefs.title: Measuring Renters in Credit Data: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
briefs.summary: Linking survey and credit-bureau data, the note shows that common renter proxies misclassify large numbers of households and can overstate renter credit quality by mixing them with mortgage-free owners.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful warning when analysts draw renter-finance conclusions from credit files that were not built to identify renters cleanly.

briefs.title: Measuring Mutual Fund Liquidity with N-PORT
briefs.authors: Larsson E., Kawamura T., & Shin C.
briefs.summary: Using SEC N-PORT filings, the note builds a practical liquidity metric for corporate-bond mutual funds and shows how cash-like buffers are rebuilt and drawn down across stress episodes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when fund liquidity is discussed vaguely and you need a concrete view of how bond funds actually manage redemption risk.

briefs.title: Australia Persistence Scorecard: Year-End 2025
briefs.summary: The scorecard shows that most Australian active equity funds failed to sustain top-quartile or top-half rankings, while bond funds showed somewhat stronger persistence than equities.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good regional test of whether recent outperformance is repeating skill or just another short-lived stretch of good positioning.

briefs.title: Latin America Persistence Scorecard Year-End 2025
briefs.summary: Across Brazil, Chile, and Mexico, the scorecard finds that active-fund winners rarely stayed winners for long, with persistence generally weak across both local equity and bond categories.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when allocator discussions lean too heavily on short recent rankings in markets where persistence has been consistently scarce.

briefs.title: Private Credit and Leveraged Loan Markets: Similarities, Differences, and Substitution
briefs.authors: Banegas A., Castelo S., Degerli A., Dobridge C., & Kennedy W.
briefs.summary: The note compares private-credit funds with leveraged-loan markets and shows that the two channels increasingly overlap as lower-rated middle-market borrowers move between them depending on pricing, structure, and lender appetite.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when private credit is treated as a separate universe rather than a substitute for syndicated leveraged lending.

briefs.title: The Price of Bank Funding Behind Private Credit: Evidence from Business Development Companies
briefs.summary: Looking at business development companies, the note shows that a large share of private-credit lending still depends indirectly on bank funding, so changes in bank financing costs can flow through to supposedly nonbank credit.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when investors assume private credit is insulated from the banking system that still helps finance it.

briefs.title: Examining the Sensitivity of Regional Banks to Macroeconomic Shocks
briefs.authors: Achugamonu F., Afanasyeva E., Schmidt-Eisenlohr T., & Seay M. P.
briefs.summary: The authors test how regional-bank balance sheets react to severe macro shocks and show why mid-sized lenders can still transmit broader stress even without the scale of the largest banks.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good reference when post-SVB debate slips into assuming only megabanks matter for systemic fragility.

briefs.title: Decomposing Hedge Funds’ U.S. Treasury Exposures
briefs.summary: Using Form PF data, the note breaks hedge-fund Treasury exposure into basis trades, swap-spread trades, yield-curve positions, and liquidity holdings, and estimates that the cash-futures basis trade was about $830 billion by September 2025.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when Treasury-market leverage is discussed abstractly and you need a concrete decomposition of where the exposure sits.

briefs.title: Mortgage Servicing Right Valuations Under Stress
briefs.authors: Elul R., Pence K., Ranish B., & Suher M.
briefs.summary: The note estimates how mortgage servicing right values could fall in a severe downturn as defaults and prepayments shift, showing another channel through which housing stress can hit bank capital.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong primer on why servicing assets can amplify mortgage stress even when headline home prices are not the whole story.

briefs.title: Investor Composition of Money Market Funds and Its Implications for Flow Dynamics
briefs.authors: Li Y., Panetta N., & Watts W.
briefs.summary: The note shows that money market fund flow behavior depends heavily on who owns the fund, with different investor mixes producing meaningfully different run and redemption patterns under stress.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when cash-like funds are discussed as homogeneous even though investor mix can change how stable they really are.

briefs.title: Subprime Auto Lending: Trends in Buy Here Pay Here Auto Lending
briefs.authors: Chyruk O., Cox D., Liu L., Wang J., & Zoulalian S.
briefs.summary: The note maps the Buy Here Pay Here segment of auto lending, showing how dealership-based financing remains a distinct and expensive credit channel for riskier borrowers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when auto-credit stress is discussed only through prime lenders and misses the hardest-credit segment entirely.

briefs.title: Monitoring High Credit Growth: The Link Between Local Deposits and CRE Lending
briefs.authors: Lopez Cruz D., Paligorova T., & Yorozu T.
briefs.summary: The authors link unusually strong local deposit growth to later commercial real-estate lending expansion, offering a simple signal for where credit booms may be building.
briefs.whyItMatters: A practical early-warning lens for regions where deposit growth may be feeding real-estate risk too quickly.

briefs.title: How U.S. Bank Stock Prices Respond to Geopolitical Risk
briefs.authors: Niepmann F., Shen L. S., & Walker J.
briefs.summary: The note finds that banks with weaker earnings, thinner liquidity buffers, and larger exposure to stressed regions see larger equity declines when geopolitical risk jumps.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when geopolitical shocks are framed as a general market story rather than a bank-specific balance-sheet filter.

briefs.title: Trade Finance Activities of U.S. Banks: What the Data Can Tell Us
briefs.summary: Drawing on regulatory data, the note shows that trade finance supports a meaningful share of cross-border commerce but is concentrated in large U.S. banks and has trended down over time.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when global trade exposure is discussed without the financing layer that still runs through a narrow slice of banks.

briefs.title: A Note on Recent Dynamics of Consumer Delinquency Rates
briefs.authors: Adams R., Barnes C., Bopst C., & Sommer K.
briefs.summary: Using New York Fed credit-panel data, the note tracks how post-pandemic delinquencies in credit cards and auto loans moved back toward Great Financial Crisis-era ranges by the third quarter of 2025.
briefs.whyItMatters: A clear baseline for whether rising household stress is broad, temporary, or concentrated in specific loan types.

briefs.title: Implications of Growth in ETFs: Evidence from Mutual Fund to ETF Conversions
briefs.summary: The note studies mutual-fund-to-ETF conversions and asks how the migration into ETF wrappers may affect the trading and ownership patterns of the underlying stocks.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when ETF growth is treated as just a fee story rather than a market-structure shift in how assets are held and traded.

briefs.title: What Drives the Substitution Between Bank Deposits and Money Market Funds?
briefs.authors: Im J., Li Y., & Wang A.
briefs.summary: The note studies why cash moves between bank deposits and money market funds and shows how rates, convenience, and perceived safety all shape the substitution.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when cash migration is reduced to yield chasing and ignores the funding implications for banks and short-term markets.

briefs.title: Order Flow Imbalances and Amplification of Price Movements: Evidence from U.S. Treasury Markets
briefs.authors: Dobrev D., Liu E., Kim J., & Rodriguez M.
briefs.summary: The authors show that large one-sided order flow can amplify Treasury price moves when liquidity is thin, offering a cleaner read on how stress episodes snowball in the rates market.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when Treasury volatility is discussed as a macro surprise without enough attention to market microstructure and strained liquidity.

briefs.title: The Cross-Border Trail of the Treasury Basis Trade
briefs.authors: Barth D., Beltran D., Hoops M., Kahn J., Liu E., & Perozek M.
briefs.summary: The note follows Treasury basis-trade exposure across official cross-border datasets and shows why standard capital-flow measures can miss how the trade is actually housed offshore.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong complement to basis-trade discussions that rely too heavily on one data source and miss the offshore chain of custody.

briefs.title: Examining the Relationship Between Loan Pricing and Credit Risk
briefs.authors: Abdymomunov A., Elul R., Ruffino D., & Wang J.
briefs.summary: The note studies how banks price risk into loans and shows where higher interest rates really compensate for expected losses versus where pricing looks less tightly linked to underlying risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when borrowers are told high rates simply reflect risk and you want a cleaner empirical check on that claim.

briefs.title: Rising Property Insurance Costs and Pass-Through to Rents for Apartment Buildings
briefs.summary: The note shows how higher insurance costs for apartment buildings feed into rents, adding a less visible channel through which climate and catastrophe pricing can hit tenants.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when rent inflation is discussed only in terms of supply and rates, not the insurance bill embedded in operating costs.

briefs.title: Debt Payments and Spending: Evidence from the 2023 Student Loan Payment Restart
briefs.authors: Aladangady A., Crawley E., Gamber W., Moran P., & Nino J.
briefs.summary: The note measures how the 2023 restart of federal student-loan payments cut disposable income and traces the spending response of borrowers once monthly bills resumed.
briefs.whyItMatters: A useful empirical anchor for claims about how student-debt payment burdens spill into everyday consumption.

briefs.title: What Do Bank Stock Returns Say About Monetary Policy Transmission?
briefs.authors: Ehresmann P., Morelli J. M., & Wang J. J.
briefs.summary: Using a factor framework for bank equities, the note studies what stock-price reactions reveal about how monetary-policy shocks move through bank profitability and credit supply.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when monetary transmission is discussed in the abstract and you want a market-based read on which bank channels investors focus on.

briefs.title: Estimating the importance of monetary policy shocks for variation in the U.S. homeownership rate
briefs.summary: The note estimates how much of the movement in the U.S. homeownership rate can be traced to monetary-policy shocks rather than slower structural forces alone.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when housing-wealth debates ignore how much rate policy can alter who gets to own in the first place.

briefs.title: Liquidity Transformation Risks in U.S. Bank Loan and High-Yield Mutual Funds: A 2026 Update
briefs.authors: Anadu K. E., Baker S., Cai F., George L., & Larsson E.
briefs.summary: The note updates simple monitoring ratios for bank-loan and high-yield mutual funds and finds that bank-loan funds have crept back toward pandemic-era illiquidity levels even while liquid buffers stayed fairly steady.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to know where redemption risk is building inside credit funds before the next real stress test arrives.

briefs.title: Inequality in Comprehensive Wealth
briefs.authors: Landel H., Love D., & Smith P. A.
briefs.summary: This paper broadens the usual net-worth lens by adding Social Security, pensions, annuities, insurance, and other future payment streams, then shows how retirement resources diverge across education, race, and household structure.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when plain net-worth snapshots miss the retirement-income machinery that actually supports later-life spending.

briefs.title: Price-Segmented Beliefs and the U.S. Housing Boom
briefs.summary: Jacobson shows that expected house-price gains were especially elevated in lower-priced segments during the 2000s boom, tying housing beliefs more tightly to credit-sensitive buyers.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong corrective to housing-boom stories that treat credit loosening and buyer beliefs as separate forces.

briefs.title: Does Banking Consolidation Harm Households?
briefs.authors: Brunetti C., Harris J. H., & Spyridopoulos I.
briefs.summary: Using 44 million mortgage records across thousands of bank mergers, the paper finds little evidence that consolidation raised mortgage rates, cut approval rates, or worsened delinquency outcomes for borrowers.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when broad anti-merger claims are made without checking whether household mortgage outcomes actually deteriorated.

briefs.title: Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The 2025 SHED report tracks how U.S. adults handled savings, bills, housing, credit, and financial shocks, using a national survey fielded in October 2025.
briefs.whyItMatters: This is one of the clearest annual snapshots of how household finances actually feel on the ground, not just how aggregates move.

briefs.title: SPIVA Institutional Scorecard Year-End 2025
briefs.authors: Ganti A. R., Di Gioia D., & Flaherty L.
briefs.summary: This scorecard extends the active-versus-index comparison into institutional and SMA accounts, asking whether manager skill looks more durable once the usual mutual-fund fee noise is stripped out.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when someone claims the active-passive evidence is only a retail mutual-fund story.

briefs.title: Chapter 1: Enhancing Resilience amid Global Trade Uncertainty
briefs.summary: The IMF chapter reviews how stretched valuations, rising household equity exposure, and uneven housing affordability leave markets and balance sheets more exposed when policy and trade shocks hit together.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good macro-finance bridge when you want household vulnerability placed inside the broader market-risk backdrop.

briefs.title: Chapter 1: Steadying the Course: Financial Markets Navigate Uncertainty
briefs.summary: This IMF chapter surveys how rate volatility, credit spreads, and still-elevated house prices shaped global financial conditions as markets adjusted to slower disinflation and uneven growth.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when you need a disciplined baseline for what late-2024 market stress actually looked like across credit, housing, and risk assets.

briefs.title: International finance through the lens of BIS statistics: bond markets, domestic and international
briefs.authors: Chan T., von Peter G., & Wooldridge P.
briefs.summary: The BIS overview shows how debt financing has shifted toward bond markets since the global financial crisis, with government issuance driving size while cross-border and private borrowing changed the market mix.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when you want a clean map of how modern bond markets grew and who now sits on the creditor side.

briefs.title: The safe haven properties of US Treasuries and portfolio flows of global investors
briefs.summary: This BIS note studies whether U.S. Treasuries still behave like the world’s default refuge and documents a recent weakening in their usual correlation pattern during stress.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want evidence on whether the classic Treasury safe-haven assumption is still as dependable as investors think.

briefs.title: Understanding Preferences for Payment Cards using Household Scanner Data
briefs.authors: Rysman M., Wang S., & Wozniak K.
briefs.summary: The paper uses scanner-panel data to show that household payment habits are persistent and idiosyncratic, with transaction size mattering less than many standard models assume.
briefs.whyItMatters: Helpful when payment-policy debates ignore how sticky real household checkout behavior can be.

briefs.title: Illiquid Homeownership and the Bank of Mom and Dad
briefs.summary: Brandsaas models how parental transfers now help a large share of young households clear the barrier into homeownership and then keep holding an illiquid housing asset.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when housing access is framed as only a rates-and-supply problem rather than a family-balance-sheet problem too.

briefs.title: Do the Rich Really Save More? Answering an Old Question Using the SCF with Direct Measures of Lifetime Earnings and an Expanded Wealth Concept
briefs.authors: Llanes E., Thompson J., & Henriques Volz A.
briefs.summary: Using the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, this paper finds that saving gradients are steep mainly at the top of the lifetime-earnings distribution and remain visible even after stripping out unrealized capital gains.
briefs.whyItMatters: A better answer to the "do the rich just earn more or actually save more" question than the usual social-media shorthand.

briefs.title: The Composition and Draw-down of Wealth in Retirement
briefs.authors: Poterba J. M., Venti S. F., & Wise D. A.
briefs.summary: The paper studies what retirees actually hold at the start of retirement and shows how slowly many households run down both financial assets and housing equity unless a major shock forces the issue.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when retirement plans assume home equity and portfolio assets will be spent down smoothly just because they are available on paper.

briefs.title: The Retirement-Consumption Puzzle: New Evidence from Personal Finances
briefs.summary: Using detailed personal-finance data, the paper finds that people often cut spending, pay down consumer debt, and build liquid savings when they retire rather than simply glide into planned dissaving.
briefs.whyItMatters: A good antidote to overly tidy retirement models that assume households behave like frictionless life-cycle optimizers.

briefs.title: Nudging Retirement Savings: A Field Experiment on Supplemental Plans
briefs.authors: Clark R. L., Hammond R. G., Morrill M. S., & Khalaf C.
briefs.summary: This field experiment finds that simple informational nudges can raise supplemental-plan contributions among workers who are already enrolled, while doing much less for those who have not started saving at all.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want evidence on where low-cost retirement nudges help and where they plainly do not.

briefs.title: Asset Allocation and Asset Location: Household Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances
briefs.summary: Bergstresser and Poterba use SCF data to show that many households face meaningful decisions not just about what to own, but where to hold it across taxable and tax-deferred accounts.
briefs.whyItMatters: A strong reminder that portfolio design without account location can leave obvious tax value on the table.

briefs.title: Pre-Retirement Cashouts and Foregone Retirement Saving: Implications for 401(k) Asset Accumulation
briefs.authors: Poterba J. M., Venti S. F., & Wise D. A.
briefs.summary: The paper asks how much 401(k) wealth is lost when workers cash out before retirement and concludes that the drag is real but smaller than many critics assumed because many balances stay inside the retirement system.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when early-withdrawal behavior is cited as proof that defined-contribution saving never compounds into meaningful retirement assets.

briefs.title: Personal Retirement Saving Programs and Asset Accumulation: Reconciling the Evidence
briefs.authors: Poterba J. M., Venti S. F., & Wise D. A.
briefs.summary: This paper revisits the long-running dispute over whether IRA and 401(k) contributions mostly reshuffle existing money or create new saving and argues that much of the contribution flow represented genuine additional saving.
briefs.whyItMatters: A core reference for debates about whether tax-advantaged retirement accounts actually change household wealth accumulation.

briefs.title: Distribution of Household Wealth in the U.S. since 1989
briefs.authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
briefs.summary: The Federal Reserve’s distributional wealth table tracks who holds household wealth over time, making it easy to separate broad market gains from concentration at the top of the distribution.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when aggregate net-worth headlines obscure how unevenly asset gains are actually distributed.

briefs.title: Debt Burdens Among Credit-Linked Consumers in the United States
briefs.summary: CFPB links consumers who share credit with likely household members and shows that a household-style credit view captures different debt burdens and risk patterns than an individual-only file.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good for reading leverage through a shared-household lens instead of assuming every debt decision is individual.

briefs.title: How the Basel Re-Proposal Will Impact the Mortgage Market
briefs.authors: Parrott J., Goodman L., & Zandi M. M.
briefs.summary: Parrott, Goodman, and Zandi argue that the March 2026 Basel re-proposal would modestly shift banks toward lower-risk mortgages and could pull more bank capital back into housing finance if key definitions are clarified.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want to know how capital rules can change mortgage pricing and who originates loans.

briefs.title: When the Mortgage Becomes the Backup Plan: Debt and Disaster Insurance
briefs.summary: Phan explains how highly leveraged homeowners can treat default as an implicit substitute for flood insurance, concentrating uninsured disaster risk in the mortgage market rather than the insurance system.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when home-insurance stress is discussed as a climate story without tracing the balance-sheet consequences for borrowers and lenders.

briefs.title: A Check-In on the Mortgage Market
briefs.authors: Haughwout A. F., Lee D., Lee J., Scally J., & van der Klaauw W.
briefs.publication: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
briefs.summary: Using the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, the authors show mortgage balances kept rising in 2025 while delinquency and product risks remained uneven across regions and loan types.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when aggregate mortgage growth obscures where credit risk is actually building.

briefs.title: Technical correction and update to the CFPB's credit invisibles estimate
briefs.summary: CFPB revises its widely cited credit-invisibility estimate, cutting the 2010 share roughly in half after data corrections and showing that more adults held scored credit files by 2020.
briefs.whyItMatters: A reminder that baseline claims about who is outside the credit system can drift when the measurement changes.

briefs.title: Auto Lending to Servicemembers
briefs.summary: Using loan-level data from six lenders, CFPB finds servicemembers face elevated risks across the auto-loan life cycle, including downstream financial strain that can affect military careers and clearances.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for anyone who treats auto debt as generic consumer credit without the added institutional risks servicemembers face.

briefs.title: An Introduction to the CFPB’s Rental Payment Data and Analysis
briefs.summary: This technical report introduces CFPB rental-payment data on leases, delinquencies, inquiries, and collections, and benchmarks the coverage against outside housing sources.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good background if you want higher-frequency evidence on rent stress instead of waiting for slower household surveys.

briefs.title: Behind on Rent? Examining Rental Housing Delinquencies in New Payment Data
briefs.summary: Witzen uses CFPB rental-payment data to show late-fee incidence rose sharply into early 2023 before easing by late 2024, while repeated late and NSF fees remained common among struggling renters.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful because rent delinquency often shows up before more visible housing distress.

briefs.title: Cash-Out Refinances and Paydown Behavior of Non-mortgage Debt Balances
briefs.summary: CFPB tracks 2014 to 2021 cash-out refinance borrowers and finds many use extracted home equity to reduce credit card and other nonmortgage balances, with credit scores improving after the refinance event.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when home equity is treated as abstract wealth rather than a source of household debt restructuring.

briefs.title: Consumer Use of Buy Now, Pay Later and Other Unsecured Debt
briefs.summary: Using matched BNPL applications, originations, and credit records from six large firms, CFPB shows how loan stacking and unsecured debt exposure build outside traditional credit reporting.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good for understanding why headline credit-bureau balances can miss a growing layer of short-duration consumer borrowing.

briefs.title: Flood Risk and the U.S. Mortgage Market
briefs.summary: CFPB merges HMDA mortgage data with FEMA and First Street flood measures and finds mortgage-market flood exposure is broader and more inland than traditional maps imply, leaving many borrowers underinsured.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful if you want to see how climate-linked property risk leaks into mortgage underwriting and household resilience.

briefs.title: The Financial Security of Small Business Owners: Evidence from the Making Ends Meet Survey
briefs.authors: Brennecke C., Caldwell I., & Witzen B. H.
briefs.summary: Using the Making Ends Meet survey, the authors find small business owners tend to have higher income and wealth than nonowners but also face more month-to-month income volatility and more credit friction.
briefs.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you want the household-finance tradeoff behind the small-business success story.

briefs.title: 2023 Mortgage Market Activity and Trends
briefs.summary: This CFPB HMDA review maps 2023 mortgage originations, application outcomes, borrower characteristics, and pricing, giving a clean snapshot of who received housing credit and on what terms.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful as a broad reference point for mortgage access, pricing, and lending composition after the rate shock.

briefs.title: An analysis of the first seven months of the federal student loan return to repayment
briefs.summary: Using credit-record data after the payment pause ended, CFPB finds around 40 percent of borrowers were making payments by April 2024 while roughly 30 percent missed a payment and millions used the on-ramp policy.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful for gauging how quickly student debt payment stress returned once the emergency pause ended.

briefs.title: Making Ends Meet in 2024: Insights from the Making Ends Meet Survey
briefs.summary: CFPB reports that household financial stability and well-being deteriorated from 2023 to 2024, with more trouble paying bills, weaker emergency resilience, and persistent gaps across income and racial groups.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good baseline evidence when claims about consumer resilience rely too heavily on aggregate spending or labor-market headlines.

briefs.title: Insights from the 2023-2024 Student Loan Borrower Survey
briefs.summary: This borrower survey finds repayment difficulty is widespread, many borrowers do not understand or access income-driven repayment options, and debt relief often changes major life decisions.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when student debt is framed only as a balance-sheet number instead of an administrative and behavioral problem.

briefs.title: Data Spotlight: The Impact of Changing Mortgage Interest Rates
briefs.summary: CFPB shows that the jump in mortgage rates from 2021 to 2023 raised principal-and-interest payments dramatically, squeezed affordability, and left a large stock of borrowers locked into older low-rate loans.
briefs.whyItMatters: Good context for why even modest rate declines do not quickly fix housing affordability or mobility.

briefs.title: Borrower Experiences with Mortgage Servicing During the COVID-19 Pandemic
briefs.summary: Using the 2020 American Survey of Mortgage Borrowers, CFPB finds distressed borrowers often struggled to access loss-mitigation programs, understand forbearance exits, and navigate servicing in languages other than English.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful because mortgage distress depends on servicing frictions, not just whether a hardship program exists on paper.

briefs.title: Negative Equity Findings from the Auto Finance Data Pilot
briefs.summary: This first report from CFPB's auto-finance data pilot examines how rolled-over negative equity pushes borrowers deeper underwater on replacement vehicles and raises future distress risk.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful when used-car affordability is discussed without looking at how trade-in debt compounds the next loan.

briefs.title: Repossession in Auto Finance
briefs.summary: CFPB uses its auto-finance data pilot to measure repossession patterns, showing how pandemic-era servicing changes and later vehicle-price swings affected defaults, losses, and borrower outcomes.
briefs.whyItMatters: Useful because repossession is a severe consumer-credit failure point that standard delinquency tables often understate.
